item.title: 政治
item.description:
The world this week

Israel and Lebanon agreed to renew a truce negotiated by America between Israel and Hizbullah, the Iran-backed militia. Israeli troops made their deepest advance into Lebanon in a quarter of a century, capturing Beaufort Castle, a crusader fortress last held in 2000. It also struck Beirut, the capit...
item.content:encoded:
政治

本周世界以色列和黎巴嫩同意续签由美国斡旋的以色列与伊朗支持的民兵组织真主党之间的停火协议。以色列军队推进至黎巴嫩境内四分之一世纪以来最深处，占领了博福特城堡（Beaufort Castle），这是一座十字军堡垒，上次被占领是在2000年。以色列还三周来首次袭击了首都贝鲁特。但在一次明显充满脏话的电话中，唐纳德·特朗普命令本雅明·内塔尼亚胡暂停进一步开火。该协议与5月达成的一项协议类似，取决于真主党也停止对以色列的袭击。伊朗外交部警告说，如果以色列袭击贝鲁特，将“全面恢复”战争。

美国与伊朗之间的谈判在外交上几乎没有进展。相互袭击不断升级。伊朗无人机袭击科威特国际机场，造成1人死亡、60多人受伤。美国拦截了其他射向科威特以及巴林的导弹，伊朗数周来未对这些国家发动过袭击。伊朗表示，这些袭击是对美国攻击霍尔木兹海峡（Strait of Hormuz）的格什姆岛（Qeshm Island）和一艘油轮的报复。特朗普先生表示，和平谈判仍在继续，但“变得非常无聊”。

埃塞俄比亚人参加了投票，但这次选举因主要反对党被排除、媒体受到压制以及部分地区发生反政府暴力事件而蒙上阴影。官方结果预计几天后才能公布，但总理阿比·艾哈迈德（Abiy Ahmed）领导的执政党繁荣党（Prosperity Party）预计将轻松获胜。

津巴布韦政府向一项有争议的宪法修正案迈出了一步，该修正案将把总统任期延长两年，并以立法者选拔取代总统选举。这项由司法部长在议会提出的法案，仍面临宪法法院的多项法律挑战。

肯尼亚高等法院再次阻止开设一个面向美国人的埃博拉隔离中心三周。该设施已获肯尼亚政府批准，但引发了抗议活动，导致两人死亡。特朗普政府表示，将阻止感染该病毒的人返回。

皮特·赫格塞斯（Pete Hegseth）在香格里拉对话会上称赞美国与中国的关系是“多年来”最好的。他在新加坡向其他国防部长发表讲话时，建议地区盟友增加军费开支。他没有提及台湾。

印度尼西亚总统普拉博沃·苏比安托（Prabowo Subianto）解雇了其免费学校午餐计划负责人。政府这项为8000万儿童提供食物的旗舰计划被认为已导致数万名儿童患病。运行该计划的机构办公室在一次反腐突击检查中被关闭。

2025年日本出生人口连续第十次创下新低，为67.1万。厚生劳动省还表示，女性一生平均预计生育1.14个孩子。早期人口普查数据显示，2020年至2025年间，日本人口减少了300万，为有史以来最大降幅。

英国爆发抗议活动，涉及警方对亨利·诺瓦克（Henry Nowak）的处理方式。这名18岁少年在被戴上手铐时因一名锡克教男子造成的刀伤死亡，当时警方正在应对一起关于种族主义袭击的虚假报告。英国改革党（Reform UK）领袖奈杰尔·法拉奇（Nigel Farage）抨击警方存在“反白人偏见”。内政大臣沙巴娜·马哈茂德（Shabana Mahmood）指责抗议者“劫持”这起谋杀案以“煽动暴力和混乱”。

民粹主义右翼的阿韦拉多·德·拉·埃斯普列利亚（Abelardo de la Espriella）赢得了哥伦比亚总统选举的第一轮。特朗普先生的盟友出人意料地……（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

item.title: 商业
item.description:
The world this week

Anthropic filed paperwork for an initial public offering of its shares. The listing is expected to value it at around $1trn. Anothergiga-IPO, for SpaceX, is due on June 11th. Elon Musk’s rocketry firm is trying to raise as much as $75bn at a valuation of $1.8trn. Alphabet, meanwhile, has said it int...
item.content:encoded:
商业

本周世界Anthropic提交了首次公开募股（IPO）的文件。此次上市预计将使其估值达到约1万亿美元。另一场超级IPO——SpaceX——定于6月11日进行。埃隆·马斯克的火箭公司正试图以1.8万亿美元的估值筹集高达750亿美元。与此同时，Alphabet表示计划发行价值850亿美元的新股。所有这些公司都在利用股市的活跃表现：美国标普500指数（S&P 500）长期上涨，并于6月2日首次收于7600点以上。高盛（Goldman Sachs）老板表示：“我们绝对处于一个贪婪多于恐惧的时刻。”

在准备上市之际，Anthropic还更广泛地推广其Mythos AI模型。由于Mythos在黑客攻击计算机系统方面有着惊人的能力，该公司最初将其访问权限限制在约50家公司，主要在美国。现在，它将与更多组织共享，包括北约（NATO）、SWIFT和纽约证券交易所（New York Stock Exchange）的母公司。

英国竞争与市场管理局（Competition and Markets Authority）命令谷歌允许出版商阻止其材料被用于AI搜索摘要。谷歌还必须允许出版商防止其输出被用于微调其AI模型，并且不得对选择这样做的出版商进行报复。

博通（Broadcom）在发布财报后，股价在盘后交易中下跌14%。这家芯片制造商表示，预计本季度营收为294亿美元——高于分析师共识预期，但低于最乐观的预测。博通的市值下跌了超过3000亿美元。

英伟达（Nvidia）开发了一款用于个人电脑的新芯片。RTX Spark旨在帮助个人设备运行AI模型。这与该公司其他AI芯片形成对比，后者大多用于数据中心。

另一家AI公司中国深度求索（DeepSeek）即将完成自己的融资交易。它正在向包括腾讯在内的投资者寻求约500亿元人民币（74亿美元）。

唐纳德·特朗普的白宫表示，计划对包括英国、加拿大、中国、欧盟、日本和墨西哥在内的60个贸易伙伴征收10-12.5%的新关税。美国贸易代表办公室（Office of the US Trade Representative）表示，征收这些关税是因为其他国家在阻止使用强迫劳动生产的商品进口方面做得不够。但巧合的是，这些关税是在最高法院推翻先前一批关税后，其设定的限时关税到期前几周宣布的。

英国金融行为监管局（Financial Conduct Authority）警告英超足球俱乐部，与加密货币公司的“可疑赞助协议”存在风险。几家未获金融监管机构授权的加密货币公司已与顶级球队签署了此类协议。FCA表示，这些协议“可能使俱乐部面临法律责任、洗钱风险和严重的声誉损害”。

由先锋集团（Vanguard）管理、追踪美国标普500指数的一只交易所交易基金（ETF）成为首只管理资产超过1万亿美元的ETF。

美国做空者安德鲁·莱夫特（Andrew Left）被判证券欺诈罪。检察官称，莱夫特先生在建立头寸后利用社交媒体帖子试图影响股价，然后在不告知粉丝的情况下反向操作。莱夫特先生表示，这一判决标志着“言论自由悲伤的一天”。

根据欧洲中央银行（European Central Bank）的一份报告，黄金现在比美国国债更受欢迎作为储备资产。报告发现……（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

item.title: 如何反击Z世代社会主义
item.description:
Leaders

Something new is stirring on the left. A fresh crop of socialists want to remake the economy with price controls, hefty wealth taxes and a spree of nationalisations. Supercharged by fury over Gaza, they are winning voters at a formidable pace. Many rose to prominence only recently, like Zack Polansk...
item.content:encoded:
如何反击Z世代社会主义

leaders | 我们的封面左翼正在酝酿新的动向。一批新生的社会主义者希望通过价格管制、巨额财富税和一波国有化浪潮来重塑经济。在加沙问题的愤怒推动下，他们正以惊人的速度赢得选民。许多人最近才崭露头角，比如英国绿党领袖扎克·波兰斯基（Zack Polanski），或者纽约市长佐兰·马姆达尼（Zohran Mamdani）。另一些则是长期的政治常客：年逾七旬的让-吕克·梅朗雄（Jean-Luc Mélenchon）正在第四次冲击法国总统宝座，但来自“Z世代”二十多岁年轻人的大力支持，让他再次将爱丽舍宫纳入视野。

称之为Z世代社会主义。并非因为所有追随者都年轻——也不是因为年轻人向左转是新鲜事——而是因为这是为TikTok时代打造的左翼主义品牌，正是当今年轻革命者所支持的。

忘掉沉重的集体主义理想或夺取生产资料吧。Z世代社会主义是一种“我优先”的信条。气候变化和种族问题——2010年代和2020年代初的关注焦点——现在已变得非常边缘。社会议题也是如此，除了加沙。对通胀、住房和人工智能的焦虑已经取代了这一切，变得更为原始。“这个国家财富泛滥，”加拿大新民主党刚刚当选的领袖阿维·刘易斯（Avi Lewis）说——加拿大这个国家的生产率十年来几乎停滞不前。“我们可以拥有美好的东西。”声称应该限制价格以降低你的账单，同时让别人为你的公共服务买单——这是一个诱人且易于传播的信息。

激发Z世代社会主义者的许多不满确实源于现实问题。通胀太高，大城市的租金现在往往难以承受，人工智能可能颠覆劳动力市场。忽视这些担忧将是愚蠢的。然而，Z世代社会主义在如何解决资本主义问题上是错误的。必须抵制它，因为它对繁荣构成了深远的威胁。

没有一个国家的Z世代社会主义者是完全相同的。权力的现实迫使一些人，比如马姆达尼先生，变得更加温和。但他们大致同意三个核心原则。首先，增长对普通人帮助不大。他们是零和思维，认为更好的结果不是来自创造，而是来自夺取——因为他们担心人工智能巨头很快会大规模这样做。其次，支出可以由最富有的人承担。过去左派希望每个人都缴纳更高的税；Z世代社会主义者则要求由亿万富翁资助的施舍。第三个原则是对私营企业的显著敌意。Z世代社会主义者对让市场自由发展并再分配收益不感兴趣。他们希望从住房到食品杂货等日常生活的方方面面都受国家指令支配。

政治总是有古怪的边缘。极右翼同样疯狂——而且更危险。但Z世代社会主义者令人担忧之处在于，他们的想法如此深入地渗透到中左翼之中。为了竞争，即使是美国的主流民主党人现在也提出疯狂的计划，比如免除超过一半纳税人的联邦所得税。在英国，工党曾以中间派纲领赢得权力，但被绿党吓到，重新燃起了对更高税收和国家控制的热情。越来越明显的是，即使Z世代社会主义者的候选人落败，他们的想法也能获胜。

这是坏消息。租金管制会通过抑制建房动力来加剧住房短缺。大型连锁超市的利润率……（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

item.title: 印度令人意外的婴儿潮消退是对世界的警告
item.description:
Leaders

YOU ARE having too many babies. For decades that crude message was drilled into the minds of Indians by their rulers, abetted by inept foreign donors. In the 1960s slogans on school buildings chided parents, telling them: “Two or three children, enough”. By the 1970s officials had taken a crueller t...
item.content:encoded:
印度令人意外的婴儿潮消退是对世界的警告

leaders | 我们的封面你们生的孩子太多了。几十年来，印度统治者及其无能的国外捐助者将这条粗鲁的信息灌输给印度人的脑海。20世纪60年代，学校建筑上的标语责备父母，告诉他们：“两三个孩子，够了”。到20世纪70年代，官员们采取了更残酷的做法，监督了数百万年轻成年人的绝育，通常是穷人，许多是强迫的。但今年夏天印度学校教科书重印时，将传递一个截然不同的信息。他们将警告的不是孩子太多的危险，而是孩子太少的风险。

这是因为这个世界上人口最多的国家正在经历婴儿潮消退。印度的总和生育率（TFR，衡量每名妇女生育子女数的指标）为1.9，并且还在下降。这低于长期人口稳定所需的更替水平（约2.1）。在印度几个邦，TFR现在与你在富裕欧洲国家看到的低迷水平相当。南部的工业化邦泰米尔纳德邦（Tamil Nadu）和东部人口众多的西孟加拉邦（West Bengal）的生育率（均为1.3）与芬兰相同。涵盖孟买的西部大邦马哈拉施特拉邦（Maharashtra）与挪威（1.4）持平。如果你想到印度的人口统计，斯堪的纳维亚并不是自然的参照点。但未来将越来越是。

印度人口仍将从目前的14.5亿继续增长：较少的出生人数转化为较少的总人口需要时间。但出生人数已比2001年的峰值下降了五分之一。在泰米尔纳德邦，去年有1200所学校因没有足够的学生填充教室而关闭。那些上学的孩子越来越经常没有兄弟姐妹。政府担心印度会在富起来之前变老——即该国正走上与中国的类似道路，中国人口已经达到峰值并开始下降。一些政治家正在提供现金以鼓励印度人生育。

印度的人口转变是全球趋势中最引人注目的例子。因为现在不再仅仅是富裕地区生育少或不生育。超过三分之二的国家现在低于更替水平。巴西、伊朗、泰国和土耳其等中等收入国家多年来一直远低于该水平。较贫穷的国家正稳步加入他们的行列。斯里兰卡的TFR仅为1.3；突尼斯为1.6。摩洛哥已降至更替水平以下。肯尼亚首都内罗毕可能接近这一点。在许多地方，尽管婚姻几乎普遍存在，而且很少有女性拥有正式工作，出生率仍在急剧下降。

印度也体现了为什么会出现这种全球性下滑。儿童死亡率下降提供了一个解释：如果父母确信所有孩子都能活到成年，他们就不必生那么多孩子。但人口统计学家长期以来一直表明，真正重要的是女童教育。教育意味着女孩获得更多自主权，在人生决策中拥有更大发言权。20世纪90年代，印度和非洲大部分地区都出现了女童入学人数激增，这并非巧合。只有在少数女童仍然不上正规学校的地方——如尼日尔、尼日利亚北部或乍得——生育率几乎没有变化。

教育还通过另一种方式压低生育率。父母越有抱负，他们就越需要投资于每个孩子。当公立学校糟糕时，这种动力会加速。值得注意的是，39%的印度儿童上的是付费……（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

item.title: 乌克兰不是慈善案例
item.description:
Leaders

GIVE EUROPE credit for stepping up when many doubted it could. Since Donald Trump cut American military aid to Ukraine, Europe has managed to fill the breach. It is accelerating the flow of money and arms eastward, while stiffening sanctions on the Russian aggressor. Partly as a result of European h...
item.content:encoded:
乌克兰不是慈善案例

社论 | 关键的安全伙伴当许多人怀疑欧洲能否挺身而出时，它做到了，值得称赞。自唐纳德·特朗普切断美国对乌克兰的军事援助以来，欧洲已设法填补了缺口。它正在加速向东输送资金和武器，同时加强对俄罗斯侵略者的制裁。部分由于欧洲的帮助，俄罗斯在战场上的惨重损失正在对弗拉基米尔·普京施加压力。随着美国通过外交努力结束战争的希望破灭，一些欧洲人开始质疑，是否到了由他们带头并与俄罗斯领导人对话的时候。

那个时刻可能会到来，但还不是现在。对于欧洲而言，更紧迫的问题涉及它与其一个从西方庇护者转变为关键安全伙伴的国家的关系。乌克兰久经沙场的军队正在取得进展，其创新的国防工业也在增长。如果欧洲要保卫自己的边界并摆脱对跨大西洋援助的依赖，它需要乌克兰的程度与乌克兰需要它的程度一样大。欧洲的优先事项应该是全面拥抱乌克兰，而且要快。

对于乌克兰本身而言，目标早已明确：成为欧盟正式成员国，以巩固与西方的联系，并弥补被俄罗斯夺走的领土。在接纳乌克兰成为候选国四年后，欧盟预计将于本月开启第一个谈判“集群”，涵盖民主和法治等议题。基辅的一些人希望正式成员国资格最快能在明年实现。然而，在欧盟内部，即使是热心支持者也怀疑能否在十年内实现。双方预期之间的鸿沟是危险的。

部分责任在于乌克兰总统弗拉基米尔·泽连斯基。他应该做出更多努力来加强国内独立机构，特别是打击腐败。他应该对让乌克兰以创造性方式尽早踏入欧盟的提议更加开放。德国总理弗里德里希·默茨最近提出了一种“准成员国”身份，拥有有限的投票权，作为正式入盟的中转站。泽连斯基轻率地断然拒绝了这一提议。

但更大的任务落在欧洲人身上。仍然有太多人将乌克兰视为某种慈善案例。实际上，欧洲可以从乌克兰的成就中学到很多东西，尤其是在无人机技术、生产和部署方面。欧洲的军队可以通过投资邻国来增强自身安全。瑞典国防部长表示，在乌克兰测试武器系统能在数周或数月内带来创新，而在国内这样做则需要数年或数十年。

一些欧洲人担心速度过快。他们谈论匆忙将一个庞大、贫穷、制度薄弱的国家纳入联盟的风险。这些担忧并非毫无根据，但它们忽略了全局：欧洲必须迅速采取行动，以获取在日益敌对的世界中自卫所需的更多硬实力。将乌克兰纳入欧洲怀抱是应对明显地区威胁——俄罗斯——的一种手段。扩大不仅仅是官僚程序。对于一个在更具掠夺性的大国面前显得脆弱的欧洲大陆来说，它是一种地缘政治工具。

其他想法，例如可能包括英国在内的欧洲安全理事会，可能有助于更快地正式确定与乌克兰的安全伙伴关系。但优先事项必须是加快乌克兰的入盟进程。欧盟现在就应该开始起草入盟条约，作为对乌克兰厌倦战争的民众以及将为战后重建提供资金的投资者的一种意向信号。post-...

item.title: 英国禁止像Hasan Piker这样的演讲者是错误的
item.description:
Leaders

“I’ve been banned for criticising Israel. Are we free any more?” Cenk Uygur’s question, posed to his followers on X this week, has some merit. Mr Uygur and Hasan Piker, two controversial American left-wing influencers, were both blocked by the British government from entering the country to speak at...
item.content:encoded:
英国禁止像Hasan Piker这样的演讲者是错误的

社论 | 被钳口的英国“我因为批评以色列而被禁言。我们还有自由吗？”Cenk Uygur本周在X上向他的追随者提出的问题有一定道理。Uygur和Hasan Piker这两位有争议的美国左翼影响者，都被英国政府阻止入境，无法在伦敦的SXSW音乐节和牛津大学发表演讲。对于一个自视为言论自由诞生地、自由民主基本支柱之一的国家来说，这一决定是糟糕的行为。人们能够自由表达和思考自己想要的，不仅是公民的权利；它是一种文化规范，如果来自国外的演讲者经常在边境被拒之门外，这种规范就会受到侵蚀。

Piker和Uygur被阻止入境是因为内政大臣Shabana Mahmood判断他们的存在“可能不利于公共利益”。这一极其模糊的标准似乎正越来越多地被用来禁止政府不欢迎其观点的高调外国人。今年4月，这一理由被用来阻止Kanye West——一位曾有过疯狂纳粹胡言乱语（此后他已为此道歉）的说唱歌手——在音乐节上表演。今年5月，它被引用来作为禁止几名极右翼分子参加并演讲由白人种族主义煽动者Tommy Robinson在伦敦组织的集会的理由。

所有这些都令人担忧地积极应用了授予内政大臣的自由裁量权。这种权力应该非常谨慎地使用。直接和蓄意煽动暴力是非法的；排除有此类行为记录的人很可能是正确的。伤害性、令人不安或令人厌恶的观点——其中一些在本周因警方对一名叫Henry Nowak的学生遭到致命袭击的反应而引发的轩然大波中显露出来——并未达到那个门槛。

Piker有很多观点让理智的人感到冒犯或干脆就是疯狂。他认为银行抢劫“很酷”；说他理解为什么有人可能想谋杀一家健康保险公司的老板；并曾评论道：“每一次我都会投票给哈马斯而不是以色列。”但他对英国并不构成威胁，就像那些仅仅因为举着写有“我支持巴勒斯坦行动”牌子而被捕的抗议者一样。这个曾经为卡尔·马克思提供庇护的国家不应该害怕他现在的社交媒体门徒。

对West和Piker等人实施签证禁令也不会阻止英国人听到他们的观点。任何人都可以收看他们的社交媒体账号。事实上，压制他们言论的企图更有可能让英国人主动去寻找他们。本周英国地区在谷歌上对Piker和Uygur的搜索量达到了历史最高水平。作为靠点击量谋生的煽动者，他们无疑会感到高兴。

英国并非唯一使用签证禁令阻止政府不喜欢的演讲者入境的国家：美国、澳大利亚、德国和其他许多国家也在做同样的事情。但这不是借口。议会应该敦促政府不要如此随意地使用其权力。

它还应该采取更多措施来削弱富人和有权势者用来恐吓或压制批评者的工具，例如旨在让他们承担巨额费用的诉讼（即“针对公众参与的战略诉讼”，或SLAPPs）。刚刚过去的周末就提供了一个恶劣的例子：前Meta员工、后来成为举报人的Sarah Wynn-Williams不得不在舞台上保持沉默……on a stage...

item.title: 美国衰落的国债市场需要修复
item.description:
Leaders

SINCE RICHARD NIXON broke the link between the American dollar and gold in 1971, global finance has floated on a sea of Treasuries. No asset is more important than America’s government debt. It provides a haven for investors at dangerous moments. Trillions of dollars of contracts and securities worl...
item.content:encoded:
美国衰落的国债市场需要修复

社论 | 珍视它自1971年理查德·尼克松切断美元与黄金的联系以来，全球金融一直漂浮在国债的海洋上。没有比美国政府债务更重要的资产了。它在危险时刻为投资者提供避风港。全球数万亿美元的合约和证券都以美国国债为定价参考。

遗憾的是，正如我们的特别报道所解释的，这个全球安全资产已经风光不再。过去十年间，未偿还国债的数量增长了126%，达到近32万亿美元，远远超过了外国央行等稳定需求的增长速度。结果，在杠杆的推动下，追逐收益的私人投资者和对冲基金占据了市场越来越大的份额。偶尔——最显著的是在2020年3月——这种需求突然枯竭，导致短期融资成本飙升，迫使美联储购买债券，实际上是为市场提供担保。

经济和地缘政治趋势也正在损害对国债的需求。自2021年以来通胀的复苏常常导致股票和政府债券同时抛售，这意味着国债已不再扮演高风险投资组合压舱石的有价值角色。与此同时，美国好斗的贸易政策及其反复动用金融制裁（无论其优点如何）已使外国买家在成为山姆大叔的长期债权人之前三思而行。

如果这些模式持续下去，市场就有可能失去一种特殊地位，而这种地位为美国和整个世界都提供了至关重要的利益。挽救这一局面给新任美联储主席Kevin Warsh、财政部长Scott Bessent以及国会提出了棘手的问题。

Warsh已表明他打算减少美联储持有的国债。这是一个可以实现的目标，即使这将需要更多的私人需求。然而，Warsh还必须随时准备购买债券以平息突然的恐慌。任何此类干预都需要比美联储以往更灵活的手法——过去它未能区分量化宽松（QE）（旨在刺激经济的债券购买）和旨在防止恐慌性抛售的短暂“市场运行”干预。过去它不需要区分：例如在2020年3月，两个目标同时发挥作用，并且通胀处于低迷状态。

如今，经济并不缺乏刺激，但债券市场仍可能需要救助。如果为了疏通金融管道而进行的债券购买被解读为美联储向唐纳德·特朗普总统对宽松货币的渴望低头，那将是一场灾难。因此，Warsh必须为精准干预制定好作战计划。英格兰银行是一个可供效仿的模型：在2022年英国国债因灾难性的“迷你预算”而遭到抛售期间，该银行积极购买债券，但承诺尽快退出市场。它在几个月内兑现了承诺，并且最终还为纳税人带来了利润。

改革市场将需要美国众多其他监管机构与美联储协同行动。目前交易通过交易商银行进行，这些银行在压力时期难以清理市场。交易数据每天公布，不像公司债券市场那样实时报告。更快的报告将允许所谓的全对全交易的发展。像股票市场一样，任何投资者都可以直接买卖……buy and sell direct...

item.title: 如何让足球更精彩

The World Cup, which starts on June 11th, is being hosted by America, Canada and Mexico, the international equivalent of going to a dinner party and hearing the hosts rowing in the kitchen. The tournament will feature 48 teams play...
item.content:encoded:
如何让足球更精彩

社论 | 更美丽的比赛足球是美丽的比赛。但它通常也是无聊的比赛。将于6月11日开幕的世界杯由美国、加拿大和墨西哥联合主办，这相当于去参加一个晚宴却听到主人在厨房里争吵。本届赛事将有48支球队在六个半星期内进行104场比赛。虽然观看自己国家的比赛确实令人兴奋，但对于中立球迷来说，平均每场比赛可能相当乏味。世界杯的赌注太高，球员不敢冒太大风险，而对于不被看好的球队来说，保平往往很划算。

让足球变得更有趣的想法已经在流传。主教练阿尔塞纳·温格（他的资历包括让阿森纳变得值得一看）提出了修改越位规则、将界外球改为踢球等建议。但这些想法还不够激进。《经济学人》想提出以下改动，让世界足球令世界为之激动。

如果一支球队击中门柱或横梁三次，将算作一个进球。进攻意图应该得到充分奖励。这将有利于那些真正全力进攻的球队。

未晋级国家的球员组成一支自己的球队。一些伟大的足球运动员从未参加过世界杯，因为他们效力的国家没有晋级。一支由这些国家中排名最高球员组成的中立球队，将给每个人一个第二喜欢的球队。

随着比赛进行，守门员被允许使用身体部位扑救的范围越来越小。首先一只手被禁止，然后另一只手。在伤停补时阶段，守门员唯一能用来阻挡球的部位就是他的脸。

任何假装受伤的人都有更高的真正受伤风险。看着一个人在地上连续几分钟假装痛苦地翻滚，无聊得令人难以置信。如果一名球员被判定为假装受伤，那么之后对他进行的下一次犯规将不受惩罚。要么地上打滚的情况减少，要么会出现暴力报复的戏剧性场面。无论哪种方式，足球都是赢家。

在上半场的十分钟内，随机选出一名观众为每支球队参赛。观众很可能会被选入他们不支持的球队；没有人知道他们的偏好，包括他们的新队友。他们如何利用这段时间由他们自己决定。

角球已经变成了摔跤比赛。为了让它们更有趣，场上每个人，包括踢角球的球员，都必须蒙上眼睛。比赛将持续进行，直到球出界或观众开始发出嘘声。

没有什么比永久居留权的承诺更能让体育比赛激动人心了。除了通常的黄牌和红牌，裁判还可以向在美国土地上比赛时带球过掉对手的任何球员出示一张绿牌。

世界杯上最令人难忘的人物之一是喀麦隆球员罗杰·米拉，他在进球后在角旗区跳舞。如果这让足球听起来无聊，那就证明了我们的观点。不过，有创意的进球庆祝活动可以很有趣；为了鼓励它们，如果庆祝活动特别有想象力，裁判可以取消因犯规行为出示的黄牌。

竞争总是一件好事，这一原则可以通过同时在场上放置两个球来应用于比赛中。这之所以有趣，主要是因为这对裁判的影响……effect that it will have on ref...

item.content:encoded:
大多数名人读书俱乐部令人厌烦吗？

读者来信 | 精选信件欢迎通过电子邮件发送信件至 letters@economist.com

了解更多关于我们如何处理您的信件的信息

“从红毯到阅读清单”（5月9日）指出，大多数名人读书俱乐部令人厌烦，但正如一位学者所言，这类俱乐部让阅读不再孤独，将“一种孤独的体验……转变为一种集体体验”。这正是Charmaghz（一家与阿富汗女孩合作的非营利组织）的职能。该组织由一位阿富汗女孩教育活动家创立，在塔利班禁止女孩上中学和大学的地方，Charmaghz运营着线上读书俱乐部。

阿富汗的女孩和妇女现在通常被排除在大多数公共场所之外。她们缺少的是同龄读者的陪伴，以及一个她们对小说或其他任何事物的观点都值得被倾听的环境。由阿富汗女性主持的每周90分钟讨论《汤姆·索亚历险记》或《八十天环游地球》的会议，提供了这两样东西。

您指出，批评者质疑许多读书俱乐部的严肃性，尤其是那些由名人领导的。我们的参与者并不缺乏严肃性。他们是我认识的最坚定的读者之一，尽管——也可能正因为——他们在获取一本书时面临着重重障碍。

莉兹·罗宾逊

首席执行官

Charmaghz

伦敦

SpaceX“是自由市场的奇迹”和“资本主义最卓越的体现”，您在关于这家火箭公司即将进行的首次公开募股的社论中如此说道（“星舰企业”，5月23日）。这忽略了政府在让SpaceX起步方面所起的关键作用。2008年，这家初创公司濒临破产，直到美国国家航空航天局（NASA）授予它一份16亿美元的合同，从而提供了改变发展轨迹的收入流。美国纳税人承担了私人投资者不愿承担的早期风险。SpaceX的成功令人印象深刻，但它更是国家支持型资本主义的胜利，而非自由市场的奇迹。

T. 迈克尔·斯宾塞

华盛顿特区

您关于《星球大战》如何从电影盛事沦为连续剧式填充内容的描述，值得更广泛的诊断（“尤达经济学”，5月23日）。我们文化时代的悖论在于，制造新奇感的手段从未如此丰富（生成工具、分发平台等），然而文化产业却从未如此胆怯。迪士尼从塔图因星球撤退到电视屏幕并非特立独行，而是有征兆性的。

数据驱动的项目绿灯制奖励的是可读的过去而非推测性的未来。算法推荐将品味坍缩到少数几个安全吸引子上。资本市场对用户流失感到焦虑，更倾向于扩展已知宇宙而非资助未知宇宙。结果是形成了一个生态系统，在这个系统中，失败的成本变得难以承受，而生产成本却已暴跌：一种无限混合有限想法的经济。

生成式人工智能只会加剧这一矛盾。一种在过去的资料上训练出来的技术，可以以极低的成本产生对现有事物更为精妙的变体。风险不在于《星球大战》变成肥皂剧，而在于一切都会变成肥皂剧。一旦观众能够自己缝制，他们是否还会继续为怀旧的装饰付费，这才是迪士尼新任老板乔什·达马罗桌面上的真正问题。

皮埃尔·路易吉·萨科

生物行为经济学教授

加布里埃尔·邓南遮大学

基耶蒂-佩斯卡拉

意大利

item.content:encoded:
Why the World Cup produces an ugly version of the beautiful game

By Invitation | Pass, pass, cross, yawn


DURING THIS year’s World Cup, three outcomes are guaranteed. First, fans of one country will experience nirvana, while those in 47 others (up from 31 previously) will be heartbroken. Second, there will be moments of everlasting genius and infamy. There could be a goal as mesmerising as Diego Maradona’s solo dribble against England, a touch as sumptuous as Johan Cruyff’s turn against Sweden or a save as improbable as Gordon Banks’s against Pelé; a penalty miss as agonising as Roberto Baggio’s against Brazil, a handball as blatant as Luis Suárez’s against Ghana or a headbutt as shocking as Zinedine Zidane’s against Italy.

The third certainty is plenty of stodgy matches which few people remember fondly. That is because the World Cup—for all the fervour about sweepstakes, sticker albums and occasional screamers—typically produces an ugly version of the beautiful game. One way to measure this is in goals: in the past three editions, there have been only 2.6 per game in normal time, falling to just 2.3 in the quarter-finals, semi-finals and final. During that time, the rate in the English Premier League, the world’s richest domestic competition, has been 2.8. Notably, the moments of brilliance and ignominy mentioned above happened in otherwise cagey games. In only one did a team score multiple goals, and that was because Maradona punched one in with the “Hand of God”.

This attritional nature shows up in other statistics. Compared with the preceding season of the Premier League, the last World Cup had 16% fewer shots per 90 minutes and 17% more fouls. One match featured 18 yellow cards and a red. This is partly because players are exhausted after an extended campaign. (The heatwaves expected in the upcoming matches will not help.) They also rarely train with international teammates, causing disjointed play. Tension is a factor, too, as eternal glory looms.

Another reason for humdrum football is that, for middle- and lower-tier countries, it works. Since the World Cup expanded to 32 teams in 1998, six ranked outside the top third by bookmakers have reached the semi-finals: Croatia (1998 and 2022), South Korea (2002), Turkey (2002), Uruguay (2010) and Morocco (2022). Their runs to the semis had an average score of 1.1 versus 0.7 in normal time. New Zealand, ranked last by bookies in 2010, were the only unbeaten team that year, scoring twice across three draws. Put simply, for countries outside the elite, it pays to “park the bus” and pray—a logic that will apply even more strongly with 48 teams. There might be more goals in group-stage drubbings, but also more Davids hacking down Goliath in the knockouts.

The possibility of winning the World Cup is so intoxicating that every game could be scoreless and billions would still watch. But football is competing in a global market for eyeballs, in which the governing bodies of other sports are trying to make their “product” more appealing. Sometimes that means making matches snappier, as Major League Baseball has done by introducing a 15-second limit for pitchers. Often it means making them higher-scoring, as both codes of rugby have done by refereeing the “ruck” more favourably to the attack, and the Indian Premier League has in cricket by adding a 12th “impact player”. Meanwhile, Formula One has increased unpredictability by changing several rules for constructors: this season Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen, champions in ten of the past 12 seasons, have yet to win a race.

There is a long history of administrators making such tweaks. America’s National Basketball Association introduced a shot clock to force more attacking play in the 1950s, when matches averaged 160 points (it is now 230). But today the rate of experimentation is accelerating, amid fears that broadcast deals have peaked and that younger audiences are watching more highlights and fewer matches. In truth, teams in most sports play conservatively in play-offs, so organisers who do not innovate are risking an anti-climax as other leagues reach a crescendo. Some governing bodies even use external analysts to model how changes in gameplay and the behaviour of fans might affect their businesses.

Football has historically been less open to this. The laws are largely untouched from 30 years ago—with changes few in number and mostly minor—though they are enforced more strictly: today you’ll get a red card for raking someone’s shin, with the video assistant referee (VAR) adding extra scrutiny to every decision. Recently, however, FIFA, world football’s governing body, has realised that it too might need to innovate, to maintain the sport’s share of the attention economy—and, perhaps, to grow it in America, which will host 78 of this year’s 104 matches. Arsène Wenger, a venerated former manager who now works for FIFA, has suggested relaxing the offside law to apply only when there is “clear daylight” between the attacker and defender. This is being trialled in the Canadian league. The idea is to reinstate many goals that are currently being chalked off by VAR (though officials will still have to draw a line somewhere, so the debate over whether someone’s shoelace was offside will never end).

Given how much fans dislike VAR—in a recent survey of British fans, 72% said it makes watching football less enjoyable—fixing it ought to be top of FIFA’s agenda. Using it solely when teams make “challenges”, with each given a limited number, as is common in other sports, should mean that only howlers get checked, while shifting some blame to the teams if something gets missed. That change, in tandem with Mr Wenger’s offside tweak, could mean more goals and fewer refereeing delays. For fans in the 47 eliminated countries that won’t lift the World Cup trophy, that would be a victory to celebrate. ■

James Tozer is a co-founder of Prospect, a sports analytics firm that works with governing bodies, teams, coaches and others. He was a data journalist with The Economist from 2014 to 2022.

item.title: The pain to come in private credit
item.description:
By Invitation

TO UNDERSTAND TODAY’S private-credit market, broadly defined as loans to private mid-size companies made by investment funds, you must start with a simple truth: the current environment was shaped by a decade of very low interest rates and abundant liquidity, which flattered leverage and suppressed ...
item.content:encoded:
The pain to come in private credit

By Invitation | Roll over and groan


TO UNDERSTAND TODAY’S private-credit market, broadly defined as loans to private mid-size companies made by investment funds, you must start with a simple truth: the current environment was shaped by a decade of very low interest rates and abundant liquidity, which flattered leverage and suppressed risk. Those conditions are unwinding, with implications that extend well beyond credit markets, to portfolio allocation, valuation methodology and risk-pricing across asset classes.

The sector has grown from around $500bn in 2015 to an estimated $2trn or more today by promising investors—including pension plans, insurance companies and increasingly individual investors—an attractive, stable yield with downside protection. Low interest rates and the hunt for yield fuelled investment in private markets and encouraged capital structures optimised for cheap money and seamless exits. That dynamic has now been fundamentally disrupted.

Higher interest rates have reset the cost of capital. Private equity, long the engine of deal flow and liquidity, has slowed, with exit paths such as mergers, acquisitions and initial public offerings narrowing and holding periods stretching well beyond historical norms. Capital is, in effect, trapped. Refinancing has become more difficult.

Layer onto this numerous structural pressures: a looming maturity wall as low-cost debt rolls into a higher-rate environment, the retreat of traditional bank lenders and sector-level disruptions, from AI-driven repricing in software to structurally higher energy costs, particularly in Europe.

And then there’s the geo-economic context. The long benign period in which debt-laden businesses were supported by globalisation has given way to an increasingly fragmented world, with its higher costs of doing business.

What does pain look like in this context? Many borrowers will face a financial shock, as the cost of debt resets to two or three times the levels before 2022, when markets began repricing risk after the long party. Some companies will adapt, preserving earnings power and restructuring their balance-sheets. Others will find that refinancing cannot restore sustainability. The dividing line will be the underlying resilience of each business.

Software is likely to be the first industry of many where these pressures erupt. Investors thought they were allocating to diversified, defensive, even “boring” private credit. Instead they were buying leveraged, highly concentrated exposure to a single sector with relatively low recovery rates in a downturn. We will look back on software’s go-go years as a major risk-management blind spot.

Many software firms took on piles of debt during the low-rate years, helping the industry to expand from about $8bn in 2015 to $500bn by the end of 2025. But the debt was often underwritten to aggressive growth assumptions rather than durable cash generation. Now the industry’s business and financing models are under heavy strain. AI is lowering barriers to entry, enabling competitors to quickly and cheaply replicate unique capabilities and workflows. Higher financing costs are exposing fragile capital structures built on optimistic expectations.

There will be winners, particularly firms able to integrate AI effectively. However, for many lenders, returns are likely to come under heavy pressure. Software businesses typically lack hard assets, limiting recoveries in downturns. When equity value is impaired, retaining senior engineers can also become difficult. These dynamics can compound in a restructuring. Recoveries for lenders may fall below historical averages, and in weaker cases could drop well below 50 cents on the dollar.

Signs of this shift are already visible in public credit markets, where software firms seeking leveraged loans are struggling to attract demand at a cost of capital they can afford. In private markets these pressures are taking longer to surface, with lenders amending loans and deferring interest to extend timelines. Default rates are still artificially low.

The recent benign period encouraged a belief that risk had been structurally reduced. In reality, it had often merely been deferred. This is hardly new in finance—and, indeed, the current transition follows a familiar pattern: as conditions normalise, overconfidence is corrected; and that adjustment forces a repricing of risk and a more disciplined use of capital.

Despite the portfolio-construction and underwriting mistakes of the decade following the global financial crisis, private credit does not present a systemic risk to the financial system. Unlike in 2008, this debt is not concentrated on the balance-sheets of highly leveraged banks. In that sense, much of the post-crisis regulation has worked as intended. The repricing will take years rather than months, and managing underperforming loans will soak up plenty of time and resources, limiting private-credit firms’ ability to adapt in a fast-changing market. But the risk of widespread contagion appears limited.

Nevertheless, the underwriting assumptions of the past decade, built on cheap capital, stable growth and predictable exits, can now be discarded. The new environment requires a far more forensic assessment of resilience, not just growth. It is a private-credit market defined less by outright distress and more by widening dispersion between winners and losers. There will still be opportunities. For investors able to distinguish between temporary dislocation and lasting impairment, the goal will be to deploy capital at more attractive entry points and to work through capital structures to restore sustainability.

The story of private credit today is not about excess giving way to crisis. It is about a structural transition from an era of abundant, undifferentiated capital to one in which liquidity is conditional, underwriting must be granular and outcomes will be increasingly unequal. The adjustment will not spark a broader financial meltdown, but expect it to inflict a good deal of pain—while, as always, giving those best placed to navigate choppier waters a chance to dig for treasure.■

Hamza Lemssouguer is the founder and chief investment officer of Arini, a credit investment firm with $20bn under management.

item.title: India’s population will soon be falling—probably quite fast
item.description:
Briefing

IN THE SPRAWLING slum in Delhi where Parul Gayen lived in the 1970s, children were everywhere. It was not unusual then that her mother had been one of six, or her grandfather one of 11. Swapan, the handsome boy whom she often saw cycling to work, and later married at 16, had six siblings—the seventh...
item.content:encoded:
India’s population will soon be falling—probably quite fast

Briefing | Demographic dive


IN THE SPRAWLING slum in Delhi where Parul Gayen lived in the 1970s, children were everywhere. It was not unusual then that her mother had been one of six, or her grandfather one of 11. Swapan, the handsome boy whom she often saw cycling to work, and later married at 16, had six siblings—the seventh did not survive infancy. But times have changed, says Ms Gayen, who is now 58 and lives with Swapan in a one-bedroom flat nearby. Of the couple’s three grown-up kids, only two decided to have children of their own. Both stopped at one. “One child feels lonely,” she says.

In 1950 India’s population was 360m. The average woman had six children—roughly the same as an American woman a century earlier. Today, with a population of 1.45bn, India accounts for a sixth of humanity. It surpassed China as the world’s most populous country in 2023 and has kept growing. But its total fertility rate (TFR), the number of births a typical woman has over her lifetime, has fallen to 1.9 (see chart 1), below the level needed to keep the population stable in the long run. Although the population will keep growing for a spell, as the generation that are currently children themselves become parents, a future contraction is inevitable unless the fertility rate rises back above 2.15. In practice, it is likely to keep falling, accelerating the impending shrinkage. In Delhi, for instance, the TFR is 1.2.

The rich world and many middle-income countries are awash with anxiety about declining fertility, shrinking workforces and impending or intensifying falls in population. Politicians often badger or bribe parents to have more children, with little success. Now India, once a source of angst about exponential population growth, is joining the same club. New school textbooks, to be published this summer, will warn of the perils of too few, rather than too many, children. In May Chandrababu Naidu, the chief minister of Andhra Pradesh, a southern state of about 55m, announced a 30,000 rupee ($315) payout for couples who have a third child.

As recently as 2019 Narendra Modi, the prime minister, warned of a “population explosion”. But the government’s thinking has flipped, says Sanjeev Sanyal, an adviser to Mr Modi. Today officials worry that India is on a similar path to China, whose population has been shrinking since 2021. Fertility has fallen much further and faster than expected, says Neelkanth Mishra, chief economist of Axis Bank. In both Tamil Nadu, a state of roughly 77m, and West Bengal (100m) the TFR stands at 1.3, the same as in Finland (see chart 2). The average for urban India is 1.5. For a long time demographers thought poor northern states would delay India’s demographic transition. Now they seem to be converging with wealthier, less teeming parts of the country.

Some might see a shrinking population as a blessing. After all, India’s infrastructure often seems inadequate: think of commuters cramming themselves into Mumbai’s local trains, for instance. Yet the prospect of an India with fewer children is not an entirely comforting one, either. It would get old before it gets rich, making for a difficult demographic transition. The effects would ripple through its society, its economy and its politics.

India’s extraordinarily fertile land and largely reliable monsoon help explain why it accounts for 2.4% of the world’s land mass but 18% of its people. Its population was given a further boost by the medical advances of the late 20th century. In 1950 a quarter of children did not survive to their fifth birthday; by 2000 only a tenth died young. India went through this transition in mortality at an unusually early stage of development, when its birth rates remained very high, says Sonalde Desai of the University of Maryland.

That combination made India exhibit A for population alarmists. It was a visit to a “hellish” slum in Delhi in the 1960s that inspired Paul Ehrlich, an American biologist, to write “The Population Bomb”. He warned that the battle to feed humanity was lost and that India was bound to starve. He was completely wrong, but extremely influential. His work informed a shameful drive in the 1970s to curb population growth, in which Indira Gandhi’s government forcibly sterilised some 10m men.

Subsequent governments, whether led by Gandhi’s party, Congress, or the Hindu nationalists of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), have largely enacted policies that enable family planning and reproductive choice, says Poonam Muttreja of the Population Foundation of India, a think-tank. In the 1990s the decline in fertility accelerated, as more girls went to school and the country got richer. Kerala, a southern state of 36m where the TFR is 1.3, has been closing schools and importing workers for decades. Other places are catching up.

The UN still forecasts that India’s population will keep growing until the 2060s and then fall slowly. This is based on a giant assumption: that fertility rates will stabilise, starting tomorrow. But there are only a handful of countries in the world in which fertility has fallen and then rebounded. “There is nothing natural or inevitable about a rate of two,” says Dean Spears, an economist. “There is no sign of stabilisation yet,” notes Rukmini S. of Data for India, a think-tank.

Demographers at the University of Washington’s Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) have produced a more plausible forecast. It shows India’s population peaking in 21 years and then falling as sharply as it has risen. By the end of the century India’s population would be just over a billion—a contraction of nearly half a billion. (The UN also produces high- and low-growth forecasts; the low one is similar.) Another model, by S. Irudaya Rajan, an Indian demographer, foresees India’s population peaking in the 2050s—a little later than IHME, but much sooner than the UN—before declining rapidly.

Few experts anticipated this, for several reasons. One is a paucity of data. The last full census was carried out in 2011. A follow-up is now belatedly under way, but the wait has forced demographers to patch together data from other surveys, which may have obscured the speed of the decline.

Another factor befuddling demographers is India’s relative poverty. Its GDP per person at purchasing power parity was only $7,000 in 2020 when fertility fell to the replacement rate, the level at which the population will stop growing in the long run. That is much lower than in most countries that have passed the threshold (see chart 3). “In the past in demography 101 we used to teach that countries reach a certain per-capita income, women get educated and join the labour force, then you get low fertility,” says Jesús Fernández-Villaverde of the University of Pennsylvania. But fertility is now low in many poorer countries, too.

In some ways India’s trajectory reflects what the evidence has long shown: by far the most important factor for fertility is whether girls go to school, says Lant Pritchett of the London School of Economics. Those with at least some education have a greater degree of autonomy, and over time this leads to fewer children. Falling fertility in India now reflects a surge in girls’ enrolment in school since the 1990s. If a country is able to provide schooling for girls at an earlier stage of development than is typical, it seems, fertility will start falling earlier, too.

But India’s experience also flies in the face of some conventional wisdom about fertility. Conservatives in Western countries often blame falling fertility there on the decline of marriage and the high proportion of women who work. It is true that many Western women complain that they end up having fewer children than they would have liked, because the difficulty of balancing family and career (or of finding a suitable partner) means they start having children relatively late in life.

Yet India, where more than 90% of women get married and only 33% work, is seeing fertility slump, too. Although childbearing happens a little later than in Ms Gayen’s day, the average Indian woman still ties the knot at 19 and has her first baby at 21 (see chart 4). In other words, age and career cannot be at fault, at least in India’s case. In fact, even as fertility has fallen, surveys suggest that Indian women would like even fewer babies. In many states desired fertility is around 1.5 children. The majority of women get sterilised once they have finished having kids, which suggests they are not hankering for more.

For women across the country, having fewer children has become a powerful cultural norm. A traditional Indian wedding blessing goes, “May you be the mother of a hundred sons.” But the attitude of modern Indian parents can be likened to an old story from the Mahabharata, a Hindu epic. The sage Agastya asks his wife Lopamudra whether she wants ten good sons or one super-son with the combined heroism of ten. Lopamudra chooses the super-son.

Three factors explain this shift. First is a change in the aspirations of modern Indian parents. A typical explanation comes from Sanjini Raman, a 42-year-old mother in Chennai. She says she and her husband decided, “All our resources should go to one because if it’s two it gets divided.” It costs around 3.5 lakh rupees ($3,650) to send her daughter to a private school and to pay for extra tutoring.

Demographers call this the “quantity-quality trade-off”, and it dominates conversations between Indian spouses. Ms Raman says that most of her daughter’s classmates are from one-child families, which is common in southern India. The proportion of Indian children in fee-paying schools rose from 31.7% in 2015 to 38.8% in 2025. This trend is not confined to richer states. Surveys in Bihar (one of India’s poorest states, with 130m people) and Uttar Pradesh (the most populous, with 240m) suggest that many poor parents are choosing to have just one child so that they can afford at least some private tuition.

A second factor discouraging lots of children is the waning of the tradition of living in an extended family. As recently as 2001 around half of Indian families lived in houses with several generations—grandparents, parents, children, aunts, uncles, cousins—under one roof. Now 70% or so live in nuclear families, according to government data, owing to urbanisation and changes in the labour market. This makes child care a bigger burden and creates an incentive to limit family size. But most Indian men do not seem to have noticed. “My husband sometimes washes his own plate,” says Kavitha Kannan, a farmer and mother of two from Tamil Nadu.

In the past, as the old blessing suggests, another consideration motivated couples: a strong preference for boys. That helped to keep fertility higher, because couples would keep having children until they had a boy. But “boy preference” has fallen dramatically: the data show that many Indian parents are content with a girl.

Third, even if education and family structures shape parents’ thinking, it is reinforced by culture. Having fewer children has become aspirational, and that is being shaped by changes in technology and access to information. A study has found that the spread of cable television to villages in the 2000s led to a fall in the number of pregnancies, which the author put down to soap operas depicting urban, middle-class women with small families.

It is possible that smartphones—which are becoming ubiquitous, even in poor villages—are having a similar compounding effect. There is as yet scant evidence that their spread has accelerated fertility’s fall. But it is likely that smartphones help disseminate cultural norms more rapidly. In Nagepur, a village in Uttar Pradesh, women say they see lots of videos that depict small families and discuss how hard it is for youngsters to find jobs. Mr Rajan likens low fertility to a “contagion”: “What happens in Kerala ends up in Bihar,” he says.

That all this is already leading to smaller families and paving the way for a contraction in population is beyond dispute. The only question is how far fertility will fall. Some demographers suggest that strong marriage and childbearing norms will act as a floor, sparing India a baby drought as severe as, say, South Korea’s. Others flip this on its head, arguing that it is remarkable that fertility has already fallen so low despite such norms. They speculate that in the coming decades more Indian women will opt out of marriage and childbearing altogether.

Even if India does not become South Korea, the speed of its demographic transition will have far-reaching consequences. Most obviously, it will get old before it gets rich. In Kerala, where almost a fifth of the population is over 60, the government has just created a department for ageing. The state has the most comprehensive social-safety net in India but, even so, only 19.4% of the workforce belong to any kind of pension scheme (the national figure is 12%). Providing for the growing ranks of elderly Indians seems a remote prospect.

Yet the decline of the extended family undermines the assumption that children will care for parents in their old age. In south India rich-world-style care homes are popping up. In rural places more basic forms of care for the elderly are appearing, centred around yoga and gossip. But families unable to find or afford care, particularly for those with serious illnesses such as dementia, may be forced back together. Cases of elderly relatives abandoned at mass gatherings, such as the Kumbh Mela, a Hindu pilgrimage, are on the rise.

The strains on family ties are exacerbated by another trend, a boom in internal migration. Southern states have long relied on labour from the North and East, particularly in hotels and restaurants. But the flows of migrants are increasing, to provide workers for factories and care homes, among other jobs. At the Athulya care facility in Chennai, the capital of Tamil Nadu, the staff are almost all young women from the state of Odisha. The pull of migration will see more elderly Indians left behind in the village. Some aggrieved parents are already taking to social media to castigate their absent children.

A more rapid demographic transition means that the share of India’s population that is of working age could peak as soon as 2030. India’s workforce can continue to grow even as its population ages because many working-age people are under-employed. In the long run the economy will need to make better use of women in particular, says Mr Mishra of Axis Bank.

Demographic concerns already infuse politics. Mr Modi’s BJP likes to stoke fears that Hindus (around 80% of the population) will be overrun by Muslims (around 15%). Although fertility among Muslims is indeed higher, it too is falling fast and the difference is mainly because Muslims are poorer. Nonetheless in February Mohan Bhagwat, the leader of the RSS, a huge Hindu-nationalist social organisation, exhorted patriotic Indians to have three children to help with “population stabilisation”.

Southern states, meanwhile, worry that Mr Modi will “punish” them for their lower birth rates by trimming their seats in parliament. There may also be tensions between internal migrants and their adoptive states. Most southern politicians realise that migrants boost the economy, but there is some griping about an influx of outsiders who do not speak the local language. It is easy to imagine the north-south divide becoming more fraught.

For now, expect politicians of all stripes to cast around for policies to promote baby-making, like Mr Naidu. Yet evidence from around the world suggests that exhortations and bungs will not work. Fertility seems to be driven by forces too powerful for states or religious leaders to control very easily. Mr Rajan points out that India’s fertility has been declining for 70 years. The odds of a sudden reversal are slim. ■

item.title: America’s Social Security trust fund is disappearing
item.description:
United States

AMERICA’S SOCIAL Security trust fund for the country’s elderly citizens is now more than old enough to be drawing a pension itself. When the programme launched in 1940, its future must have seemed assured. Lots of money went in and little came out: for each retired person drawing benefits, more than...
item.content:encoded:
America’s Social Security trust fund is disappearing

United States | Project 2032


AMERICA’S SOCIAL Security trust fund for the country’s elderly citizens is now more than old enough to be drawing a pension itself. When the programme launched in 1940, its future must have seemed assured. Lots of money went in and little came out: for each retired person drawing benefits, more than 150 workers were contributing to the fund, which invested in Treasury securities.

Today, after years of demographic transformation—lower birth rates bringing fewer workers to the labour force, and longer lifespans for the fortunate recipients—the ratio of workers to recipients is less than three to one. In 2017 the reserves held in the trust fund peaked at $2.8trn. Since then, the fund’s size has dropped by $400bn, with more money leaving it in payments to retirees than has entered it in the form of contributions. Outflows are accelerating, and some time around the end of the next presidential term, in late 2032 or early 2033, the fund will run dry.

Washington has a little more than six years to find a remedy, which means that senators elected in November may still be serving their term when the fund runs out. If nothing is done, the immediate consequences for pensioners will be dire. Payments will drop by around 23%, and will slide further in the following decades. The gap between the fund’s revenue and payments last year is estimated to have been around $209bn, about 0.7% of GDP, a gap which would have to be covered by borrowing. The system has been in a similar position before, but that was then.

Big amendments to Social Security have been secured in different political contexts: in 1965 Lyndon Johnson harnessed a supermajority in both houses of Congress to ram through changes that expanded the programme. He created America’s federal health-insurance schemes at the same time. In 1983, when the fund was months away from depletion, Democrats and Republicans inked an agreement that steadily increased the retirement age from 65 to 67 and broadened the tax base.

The changes required need not be drastic if they are made soon. Research published last year by Wendell Primus and Tara Watson of the Brookings Institution and Jack Smalligan of the Urban Institute suggests a series of fixes. They would raise payroll taxes fractionally, from 12.4% to 12.6%, and add some workers in local and state governments who do not currently pay into Social Security. At the same time, they suggest increasing retirement ages for better-paid workers from 67 to 70 and taxing their benefits more.

But getting the policy right is not the problem. The politics of Social Security and partisanship are both far more thorny than they once were. “A bipartisan group of people could pencil it out and we’d have a reform done, but that’s completely different to the political calculus,” says Daniel Bunn, president of the Tax Foundation, a fiscal think-tank. 

Imagining a repeat of the aisle-crossing deal that fixed the system in 1983 is now extremely hard. Based on data from Voteview, a research project cataloguing every American congressional vote for almost the past century and a half, legislative polarisation has never been as high as it is today. What’s more, President Donald Trump has shifted the Republican Party’s position on Social Security, an area where the Democrats have tended to command more public trust. During the 2024 presidential campaign all discussion of reform to the system was avoided, and Mr Trump’s platform promised no cuts and no increases to the retirement age.

It is not just Washington inertia that makes reforms tough. In polling conducted by YouGov for The Economist, 71% of respondents believe Social Security spending should be increased, more than for any other category of government spending. In the same poll, 45% say it should be increased a lot. The proportion who wish it to be reduced is just 5%, slightly less than the share of Americans who believe that covid-19 vaccinations were used to microchip the population.

A small clutch of politicians have more inventive proposals. Senators Tim Kaine, a Democrat, and Bill Cassidy, a Republican, want the federal government to borrow a huge sum, $1.5trn, to invest in risky assets like stocks. The proposal meets one of the long-held criticisms of the fund: that it has been much too conservative. Given its long-term liabilities, they argue, the fund could have taken far greater risk and reaped greater returns.

But the proposal offers nothing to improve the finances of Social Security in the short, medium or even quite long term: Mr Cassidy and Mr Kaine propose that the new $1.5trn investment compound and grow in size over 75 years, after which its returns can offset the borrowing needed to keep Social Security running in the interim. The Centre for Retirement Research at Boston College estimates that would require the government to borrow $25trn.

America’s public spending on old-age welfare, at 7.3% of GDP, is below the average in the rich world, and far lower than the double-digit figures in many European countries. But the American budget deficit is unusually large by rich-world standards, at almost 7% of GDP in 2025, compared with a little more than 2% among the other advanced economies.

Some analysts are less worried about the exhaustion of the account. Not only has the regime been rescued before, but in some ways it is an accounting trick. Had the federal government decided to finance Social Security payments from general taxation in 1940, rather than hypothecating American payroll taxes for the purpose, the government might have run smaller budget deficits in the past (when the trust fund was growing) and will run larger ones in the future (after its depletion). The net effect, they argue, is basically a wash.

There is some truth to the fact that the fund is a book-keeping oddity: the trust is money the government owes to itself. But if the fund is an accounting fiction, it is nevertheless a legally binding one. When the fund is spent, payments will fall automatically. The politicians who control Congress between now and then will determine its future generosity, funding model and fiscal sustainability.

The existence of the trust, and the hypothecated taxes which pay for it, provide some fiscal discipline. A direct connection between taxes paid by today’s workers and benefits received by today’s pensioners helps to ensure some element of intergenerational balance, so endless liabilities are not passed down to younger generations. But acting early to tackle well-known problems before they reach a crisis moment is not how Washington works. In the absence of that, expect yet more borrowing. ■

Correction (June 3rd): An earlier version of this article slightly misquoted Daniel Bunn; he said a proposed reform was “different”, not “difficult”, to the political calculus. Sorry.

On election night Xavier Becerra seemed to admit that his success in the primary to become California’s next governor was a surprise. “Here in Hollywood’s hometown, we love a good underdog story,” he told supporters in Los Angeles on June 2nd. The location of his celebration was apt: the Plaza de Cu...
item.content:encoded:
California is on the cusp of its “Becerra era”

United States | After Newsom


On election night Xavier Becerra seemed to admit that his success in the primary to become California’s next governor was a surprise. “Here in Hollywood’s hometown, we love a good underdog story,” he told supporters in Los Angeles on June 2nd. The location of his celebration was apt: the Plaza de Cultura y Artes, near where Los Angeles was founded as a Spanish pueblo in 1781. If current trends hold, Mr Becerra could become the first Latino elected governor of California.

The top two finishers in the primary, regardless of party, will face off in November’s general election. As The Economist went to press, votes were still being counted. California accepts mail-in ballots postmarked by election day, so the process can take days, sometimes weeks. This year many undecided Democrats held on to their ballots until the final days of voting, perhaps prolonging the count further. As of June 4th it appeared that Mr Becerra and Steve Hilton, a Republican and former adviser to David Cameron, a former British prime minister, would advance. (Tom Steyer, the progressive billionaire running in third place, had yet to concede.) Because Democrats outnumber Republicans in California nearly two to one, Mr Becerra is overwhelmingly likely to defeat Mr Hilton in the general election.

Early in the campaign Mr Becerra—a former congressman, state attorney-general and cabinet secretary—was a non-factor. A rather milquetoast establishment Democrat, he got lost in a field that included presidential and Senate wannabes (Eric Swalwell and Katie Porter), a billionaire activist (Mr Steyer), a has-been (Antonio Villaraigosa) and an upstart (Matt Mahan). Three factors explain his ascent.

First is the downfall of Mr Swalwell. The Democratic congressman seemed on the cusp of pulling away from the pack in April when credible allegations of sexual misconduct annihilated his campaign and ended his congressional career. Around the same time, left-leaning voters grew anxious that the crowded Democratic field would split the vote, allowing two Republicans to advance to the general election. Polling suggests many of those voters then coalesced around the candidate they regarded as the safest choice: Mr Becerra. In the weeks since, his campaign has somehow turned affable cringe into an asset. “Competence is cool,” Mr Becerra told one reporter. “Having experience is hot.” (Some former Biden administration colleagues might observe that competence and experience are not the same.)

Second, it probably helped Mr Becerra that his main Democratic rival was Mr Steyer, a former hedge-fund manager who spent more than $200m of his own money on his campaign. If these primaries offer a lesson, it may be that Californians remain wary of wealthy candidates trying to buy their way into office. (Saikat Chakrabarti, a tech millionaire, also failed to advance in the race to succeed Nancy Pelosi as San Francisco’s representative in Congress.)

Last is California’s changing political geography. For decades San Francisco’s political machine dominated Democratic politics in the state and beyond. It nurtured the careers of Nancy Pelosi, Gavin Newsom and Kamala Harris, among others. But its grip on the Golden State has weakened in recent years as political power has shifted south, to a younger and more Latino electorate. The old guard either stayed out of the governor’s race or offered only tepid endorsements. Before Willie Brown, the former mayor of San Francisco and one of the city’s remaining kingmakers, endorsed Mr Steyer, he expressed dismay at the field. “They are boring people,” he told your correspondent earlier this year. “That’s the problem. There’s no life!”

What kind of governor would Mr Becerra be? He doesn’t seem to know yet. His speeches consist largely of vague platitudes. On plugging health-care funding gaps, he says: “We’re going to move forward.” On keeping film production in California: “We have to fight tooth and nail.” When your correspondent asked what accountability should look like for cities and counties trying to tackle homelessness, Mr Becerra replied: “You can see it with your eyes.” Some voters don’t mind his equivocating. “It’s unrealistic to expect a lot of specifics,” said Susan, an Angeleno who attended a rally for Mr Becerra in Los Angeles last month. His experience, she said, “is enough for me”.

When Mr Becerra has ventured into specifics, he has sometimes displayed a shaky grasp of the state’s problems. Asked during a debate how he would stop home insurers from fleeing California’s dysfunctional insurance market, he suggested freezing premiums. Insurers, though, are leaving in large part because a ballot measure passed in 1988 limits their ability to raise rates. Perhaps over the next five months Mr Becerra will unveil a proper agenda for tackling California’s problems, many of them self-inflicted. So far voters have rewarded him for his CV; they may eventually want to know his plans. ■

Stay on top of American politics with The US in brief, our daily newsletter with fast analysis of the most important political news, and Checks and Balance, a weekly note that examines the state of American democracy and the issues that matter to voters.

The family were turned away from a restaurant because black people were not allowed to sit indoors. Be...
item.content:encoded:
欢迎来到埃文斯顿，觉醒文化从未消亡

美国 | 过去与现在

77岁的拉莫娜·伯顿是芝加哥郊区埃文斯顿的居民，她记得自己第一次遭遇赤裸裸的种族歧视。那时她六七岁，去圣路易斯看望叔叔。一家人被餐厅拒之门外，因为黑人不能坐在室内用餐。伯顿女士说，在此之前，“我并不知道什么是偏见，因为我既有黑人朋友也有白人朋友。”之后，她开始注意到这一点。她说，在学校里，老师对待黑人孩子的方式不同。埃文斯顿的黑人家庭居住在一个更拥挤、更破败的社区。“这里有些不对劲，”她记得自己曾这样想。

2022年，伯顿女士成为该市2019年设立的“赔偿”计划的首批受益者之一，该计划旨在向种族主义受害者支付赔偿。她获得了25,000美元，用于翻新房屋。她说这笔钱令人兴奋。“能够修缮房屋，我感觉很好。”但她接着说，这远不足以补偿她的种族在美国几个世纪以来所遭受的苦难。“在我看来，这并非40英亩土地和一头骡子”——这是内战末联邦军将军威廉·谢尔曼对获得自由的黑奴许下的承诺。

自1989年以来，三位不同的黑人国会议员提出了HR40法案，旨在成立一个委员会来探索联邦赔偿计划。五个州和一些城市也启动了各自的委员会。然而，埃文斯顿——一个多元文化且深度自由派的地方，也是西北大学的所在地——是唯一一个实际支付了款项的计划。其支持者希望它能激发更大规模的行动。随着唐纳德·特朗普攻击DEI（多元化、公平与包容）以及最高法院削弱《投票权法案》，这似乎显得异想天开。

自该计划启动以来，已有127人收到了款项。在早期阶段，受助人只能将这笔钱用于房屋修缮。最近，款项已以现金形式支付。今年夏天，将从465名申请者中通过抽签选出的另外44人将成为下一批受益者。总计将有2000万美元被指定用于发放。埃文斯顿11000名黑人中，大多数人并不符合条件。

出于法律原因，该计划仅赔偿受到20世纪上半叶埃文斯顿市划红线政策和其他种族主义政策伤害的人。但制定该计划的罗宾·鲁·西蒙斯表示，目标更大。她说，这关乎“对人类最严重的罪行，即奴隶制度及其遗留影响”。一半资金来自房产转让税，其余来自大麻销售税。

鲁·西蒙斯女士现在经营着一个更广泛倡导赔偿的慈善机构，她仍然认为全国性的计划是可能的，并且对于美国实现自由和机会平等的承诺是必要的。然而，埃文斯顿的计划进展不顺。大麻税收收入仅为预期的零头。在3月市议会赔偿委员会的一次会议上，主席克里西·哈里斯报告称，对该项目的“反抗”是大麻购买者回避该市药房的部分原因。右翼团体司法观察正代表白人居民在法庭上挑战该计划，认为基于宪法理由，政府不能基于种族进行歧视。

西蒙斯女士表示，赔偿不仅就其本身而言是必要的，还将有助于保护黑人文化。年长居民......（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

BILL PULTE, a 38-year-old Floridian, has run America’s Federal Housing Finance Agency for little over a year, mostly in blessed obscurity. Now he is America’s top spy. This might sound like the plot of a screwball comedy. Unfortunately it is not.

On June 2nd Donald Trump appointed Mr Pulte, whose p...
item.content:encoded:
美国情报协调员影响力日减

美国 | 谁需要情报？

38岁的佛罗里达人比尔·普尔特掌管美国联邦住房金融局刚过一年，期间大多默默无闻。现在他成了美国最高情报官员。这听起来像是荒诞喜剧的情节。不幸的是，并非如此。

6月2日，唐纳德·特朗普任命普尔特先生（此前曾在房屋建筑和私募股权领域任职）担任代理国家情报总监（DNI）。普尔特先生将接替因丈夫健康问题于5月22日辞职的前众议员图尔西·加巴德。长期反战的加巴德女士在大多数重要外交政策辩论中被边缘化，包括对委内瑞拉和伊朗的打击决定。

普尔特先生没有加巴德女士那样的意识形态包袱，后者对叙利亚、俄罗斯和伊朗的看法使她在共和党内成为异类。但他仍然极不称职。国家情报总监一职设立于21年前的9/11袭击之后，旨在协调美国庞大情报机构的工作，这些机构的组成部门曾相互之间不善分享机密。

设立国家情报总监办公室（ODNI）的法律规定，任何被提名领导该职位的人“应具备广泛的国家安全专业知识”。此前每一任国家情报总监要么是前情报官员、军官，要么是民选官员。普尔特先生三者皆非。他担任这一角色的主要资格只有在“让美国再次伟大”的圈子里才有意义。

总统尚未表示是否打算长期提名普尔特先生担任该职务。这需要参议院的确认，可能会很困难。2019年，特朗普选择时任众议员约翰·拉特克利夫担任国家情报总监。拉特克利夫先生曾在多个国家安全委员会任职，包括众议院常设特别情报委员会。然而，在拉特克利夫先生的资格受到质疑后，特朗普撤回了提名。（他后来获得了该职位，现为中央情报局局长。）与拉特克利夫先生相比，普尔特先生是情报新手。

缺乏资格并非参议院确认的唯一障碍。普尔特先生似乎渴望利用其接触机密信息的权限来针对激怒特朗普的人物。去年，他指控美联储委员会成员丽莎·库克、民主党参议员亚当·希夫和纽约州总检察长利蒂希娅·詹姆斯犯有抵押贷款欺诈罪，并将案件提交司法部。他还针对美联储主席杰罗姆·鲍威尔，当时特朗普正试图罢免后者。

普尔特先生愿意将职权武器化，在本届政府中并不罕见。国家情报总监办公室的政治化也越来越普遍。加巴德女士今年早些时候出席联邦调查局对佐治亚州一个选举中心的突袭时引起了强烈抗议，该中心是特朗普谎称2020年选举被窃取的焦点。她还执行了特朗普的指令，成立了一个“武器化工作组”来协调针对邪恶的拜登政府的投诉。

普尔特先生监督美国情报机构的前景已引起一些参议员的警觉。参议院情报委员会副主席、民主党人马克·沃纳指责特朗普选择了“一位不仅表现出愿意而且渴望利用政府权力来......（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

item.title: 认识一下“摩天监狱”
item.description:
United States

CHARLES DICKENS was no stranger to grim prisons. When he was 12 his father was sent to a debtors’ jail. The writer would later visit London prisons for research. Yet in 1842, when he went inside a New York City jail, he was horrified. “Such indecent and disgusting dungeons”, Dickens wrote, “would br...
item.content:encoded:
认识一下“摩天监狱”

美国 | 摩天监狱

查尔斯·狄更斯对阴森的监狱并不陌生。他12岁时，父亲被送进了债务人监狱。这位作家后来为了研究曾参观过伦敦的监狱。然而在1842年，当他走进纽约市的一座监狱时，他感到震惊。“如此不堪入目、令人作呕的地牢，”狄更斯写道，“会给世界上最专制的帝国带来耻辱！”黑暗、拥挤、容易积水，它得了个绰号“坟墓”。该地后续的监狱也继承了这一绰号。今年1月，下一代“坟墓”监狱破土动工。但它不像地牢，这座容纳1000名囚犯的监狱将直冲云霄。它高达335英尺（102米），比自由女神像还高。

这是纽约市为取代东河上狄更斯式的雷克斯岛监狱综合设施而新建的四座垂直监狱之一。该计划于2019年由市议会批准，耗资160亿美元，已落后原计划五年。为方便出入，新监狱将靠近曼哈顿、皇后区、布鲁克林和布朗克斯的法院，位于各行政区的市中心核心地段。这要求建筑师采用纽约经典的解决方案：向上建造。尽管此前已建造过垂直监狱，但此番的造价和野心是前所未有的。

目前，雷克斯岛关押着纽约市6700名囚犯中的大部分，其中约85%处于审前拘留状态。该监狱长期以来存在暴力和疏忽问题：2015年，当暴力程度高到被认为违宪时，一个联邦监察小组被派驻该岛。此后十年间，情况只会更糟。“如果我们能回到（当时的）暴力水平，那简直是梦想，”时任市长比尔·德布拉西奥治下领导纽约市刑事司法办公室的利兹·格拉泽说。监狱中武力使用率增加了一倍多，死亡率按人口比例上升了82%。去年，一名法官将监狱置于联邦任命的独立管理者控制之下。

用靠近法院的垂直监狱取代雷克斯岛将带来自身的问题。“这完全前所未有，百分之百独特，”智库曼哈顿研究所的拉斐尔·曼瓜尔说。“这将带来我认为没人能预见的挑战。”住在工地附近的居民，尤其是曼哈顿唐人街的居民，感到愤怒。尽管最初计划设定在2027年前建成新监狱并关闭雷克斯岛，但最新估计预计建设要到2032年才能完成。

除了在纽约施工的常规挑战，以及将通常用于办公楼或公寓楼的形态融入围栏、运动场和岗哨的新奇挑战外，建筑师们希望他们的设计更加公正。新监狱的最新草图看起来更像是大学院系而非混凝土堡垒。低楼层设有公共大厅、探视区和医疗设施。较高楼层是带有大露台的居住单元，配有篮球架和种植床。这不是“一点点光线和空气，”建筑师兼项目经理贝弗莉·普赖尔说。“你会感受到热度，你会看到阳光。”露台被网罩包裹，既能防止人们出去（或进来），也能让囚犯仰望天空，而不是俯视街上的人（网罩也......（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

Of all the jokes President Donald Trump has told at his aides’ expense, none has been more demeaning than his remark in late May about his civilian leader of the armed forces, Pete Hegseth. “He loves war,” Mr Trump said during a cabinet meeting, grinning as he patted Mr Hegseth on the arm. Mr Hegset...
item.content:encoded:
唐纳德·特朗普说皮特·赫格塞斯热爱战争。这应该让他失去资格

美国 | 列克星敦

在唐纳德·特朗普总统拿他的助手们开的所有玩笑中，最贬低人的莫过于他5月底关于其武装力量文职领导人皮特·赫格塞斯的言论。“他热爱战争，”特朗普在一次内阁会议上说，咧嘴笑着拍了拍赫格塞斯的胳膊。赫格塞斯谄媚地跟着笑。如果赫格塞斯对自己常说的美国需要恢复武士精神的话当真，他本该皱眉。在美国最伟大将领的准则中，对战争的憎恨与对备战必要性的清醒认识一样是基础性的。

“战争是人类最悲惨、最愚蠢的愚蠢行为，”德怀特·艾森豪威尔将军在1947年对美国军事学院西点军校的毕业生说。15年后，道格拉斯·麦克阿瑟将军——没人认为他是和平主义者——告诫学员不要成为战争贩子。“恰恰相反，”他说，“军人比任何人都更祈求和平。”

特朗普可能只是像以前一样在取笑赫格塞斯，因为他早期主张对伊朗开战，而这场战争陷入了代价高昂的僵局。然而，总统凭借其揭示令人不安真相的才能，指出了他的“战争部长”（他和赫格塞斯偏好的头衔）身上一个令人不安的特质。过去的军事领导人视暴力为悲剧性的必要，而赫格塞斯则将其颂扬为正义甚至激动人心。他最喜欢的词——听起来确实很酷——是“ lethality（杀伤力）”。当他在5月23日的毕业典礼上获得对西点军校学员讲话的机会时，他用了五次这个词，还不算两次使用了“ lethal（致命的）”。相比之下，“和平”他只提到一次，用以衬托他对凶猛的看法：“你们在暴力中感到舒适，”他教导学员，“这样我们的同胞才能和平地生活。杀伤力是你们的名片。”

赫格塞斯信息的核心在过去的军事领导人看来是常规的：部队必须准备好战斗并赢得胜利。凭借他在国民警卫队的多年经验，赫格塞斯对装备不足暴露在外的恐惧挥之不去。在他2024年出版的《战士之战》一书中，他两次提到反复出现的“赤身裸体站在全班面前的噩梦”关于执行任务。“我焦虑不安，”他写道。“我的武器在哪里？我找不到我的步枪。我希望没人注意到。”（好吧，弗洛伊德可能会说，有时步枪只是步枪。）

但是，就像紧握步枪一样，在需要时做好杀戮准备，在美国最伟大的战士眼中传统上只是基本要求。他们通常对崛起的军事领导人提出更高要求。当艾森豪威尔作为总统再次在西点军校毕业典礼上讲话时（1955年），他反思了自己40年前毕业时的自满。变化的速度、灾难性强力新武器的出现，此后加剧了“对智慧以及智慧所强加的谨慎的需求”。学员不仅要准备指挥，还要理解其他民族的经济、政治和精神诉求：“你们的整个生命可能并且应当像为战争任务做准备一样，严肃地致力于引领和平。”至于麦克阿瑟，他敦促学员要有“真正智慧的开放心态，真正力量的谦逊”。由于学员们必定知道哈里·杜鲁门总统在1951年因麦克阿瑟抵制朝鲜停火而解雇了他，他关于......（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

To celebrate the Brazilian system’s 30th anniversary in May, the country’s Superior Electoral Court (TSE), which oversees general elections, launched a mascot, Pilili, a friendly-looking voting machine with big round ey...
item.content:encoded:
巴西的高科技投票系统正在失去选民的信任

美洲 | 博索纳罗效应

这是世界上唯一一个所有选举完全电子化的国家。为庆祝巴西系统运行30周年，今年5月负责普选的巴西最高选举法院（TSE）推出了一个吉祥物——皮利利，一个长着圆圆大眼睛的和蔼可亲的投票机。然而，皮利利和法院对巴西人的广泛宣传并未能提振人们对投票系统日益下降的信任。

2009年，民调机构拉丁晴雨表有45%的受访者认为选举是干净的，而47%的人认为存在舞弊。到2024年，只有32%的人信任选举，61%的人怀疑存在欺诈（见图表）。对投票机的看法也在变化。最近一项民调中，43%的人表示不能信任投票机。同一公司在2022年的调查中，只有22%的人表示对机器没有信心。正是在那一年，右翼民粹主义者雅伊尔·博索纳罗在竞选连任总统失败后，用关于投票机的虚假信息充斥了互联网。这些说法助长了2023年1月8日的叛乱，当时数千人冲击了政府大楼。博索纳罗因试图推翻选举结果正在服刑。

他只是巴西对投票系统信任度下降的最极端表现，这种趋势在世界各地都有出现。他的儿子、参议员弗拉维奥正在参加10月的总统选举。今年3月，在达拉斯举行的右翼集会保守政治行动会议上，弗拉维奥声称如果选举“自由公正”他就会赢，暗示任何其他结果都表明选举不公正。在场的许多其他MAGA（让美国再次伟大）类型的人也煽动了关于投票机可疑的虚假谣言。尽管弗拉维奥的竞选活动在泄露信息将他与一个腐败银行家联系起来后受挫，但博索纳罗效应依然存在：相当一部分巴西右翼人士正在质疑投票机，尤其是在社交媒体上。候选人曾在2014年、2018年和2022年质疑普选结果。如果今年结果势均力敌，落选者可能再次指责舞弊。

对选举制度的不信任是由两极分化和网络虚假信息引发的，而非已被证实的欺诈。但其技术性质有助于关于该系统的虚假信息传播。当选民进入投票间时，机器通过指纹识别他们。然后他们输入所选候选人的两位数ID。选票不按时间顺序记录，而是随机记录，以保持投票保密。下午5点投票结束时，会打印出计票结果并张贴在投票站供公众查看，这是唯一的纸质选票记录。

投票官员随后从每台机器中取出内存条，并通过虚拟专用网络将加密的电子计票记录发送到TSE总部。执行此操作的软件由TSE自行编写，并使用与银行交易类似的安全协议。每台机器都有一个唯一的数字签名，用于传输给TSE的电子记录。如果一批选票上的签名与TSE的记录不符，该机器将被禁止进入网络。按照设计，这些机器缺乏连接互联网或蓝牙的硬件。内存条也带有签名，因此机器会拒绝任何不匹配的。

“即使TSE中有一个或几个恶意行为者，安全层数也太多，他们无法影响系统......（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

item.title: Protesters have controlled Bolivia’s capital for a month
item.description:
The Americas

For a month protesters have blocked the roads into Bolivia’s seat of g...
item.content:encoded:
Protesters have controlled Bolivia’s capital for a month

The Americas | Peasant power


When Túpac Katari, an indigenous leader, laid siege to La Paz for more than 100 days in 1781, the city folk were reduced to eating cats and dogs. La Paz today is not there yet. But its people are becoming increasingly desperate.

For a month protesters have blocked the roads into Bolivia’s seat of government. They are demanding that President Rodrigo Paz resign. The price of fresh food has doubled. Petrol stations have run dry. Businesses are closing. Hospitals are running out of oxygen. But the blockaders have refused even to sit down with the government. The calls for Mr Paz to impose order are growing.

Mr Paz came to power seven months ago, ending 20 years of almost uninterrupted rule by the Movement to Socialism (MAS). Voters ejected that party because of economic mismanagement that led to biting inflation and fuel shortages. Many former MAS voters were wooed by Mr Paz’s promise of gradual reform. But the economic problems have persisted. And those voters accuse Mr Paz of ignoring them since he took office.

As The Economist was published there were more than 80 blockades across the country. They are manned by the general workers’ union, peasant federations and followers of Evo Morales, a former president and a founding member of the MAS. Blockades are a controversial political tradition in Bolivia. The blockaders inflict pain on everyone to make themselves heard. And they have mechanisms that help them keep going. “They’re experts at cycling people in and out,” says María Teresa Zegada, a political analyst.

If Mr Paz can convince them to talk, he might make concessions. But he has little room for manoeuvre. Offering cabinet posts to their organisations would anger the middle class, who would see it as a return to the old ways of the MAS. Wage rises would add to the fiscal deficit, which is set to hit 9% of GDP this year. Bolivians fear a repeat of the 1980s, when the government printed money to meet union demands, triggering hyperinflation. “The dilemma is between inflation and governability,” says Gonzalo Chávez, an economist.

But at least the more radical protesters are refusing to engage in dialogue. At a meeting on June 2nd in El Alto, the largely working-class city adjacent to La Paz, their leaders slammed those suggesting negotiations as “traitors”, saying that the blockades would continue until Mr Paz resigns.

Exasperated citizens are starting to demand that Mr Paz use force. Some have taken it upon themselves to remove blockades, raising the possibility of street battles. Mr Paz sent police to clear the blockades around La Paz two weeks ago, but they were back the following day. The next move could be to declare a state of emergency and send in the army. The defence minister resigned on June 2nd without providing an official statement.

But there are unhappy precedents for breaking blockades with military force. When President Gonzalo Sánchez de Lozada sent soldiers to clear blockades in El Alto in 2003 and dozens of civilians were killed, it sparked a general strike that led to his resignation and exile. That is surely on Mr Paz’s mind. “They must have doubts,” says Gonzalo Colque, an economist. “Because the resistance of the people in the blockades would likely be iron.” ■

item.title: Abelardo de la Espriella is now the front-runner in Colombia
item.description:
The Americas

PITY THE traditional centrist politician in Latin America. Time and again they campaign claiming that voters are tired of extremes. And time and again, from Argentina to Chile and now in Colombia, they get hammered. In the first round of Colombia’s presidential election on May 31st nearly 85% of vot...
item.content:encoded:
Abelardo de la Espriella is now the front-runner in Colombia

The Americas | Colombia’s next president


PITY THE traditional centrist politician in Latin America. Time and again they campaign claiming that voters are tired of extremes. And time and again, from Argentina to Chile and now in Colombia, they get hammered. In the first round of Colombia’s presidential election on May 31st nearly 85% of voters chose either the right-wing populist Abelardo de la Espriella or the deeply leftist Iván Cepeda. Mr de la Espriella is now the favourite to win the run-off on June 21st. He surprised pollsters by winning almost three percentage points more of the vote than Mr Cepeda, who had been leading in the polls. The establishment centre-right candidate, Paloma Valencia, who was polling close to Mr de la Espriella a few weeks ago, crashed out, taking less than 7% of the ballot. Far from being tired of extremes, Colombians seem tired of the traditional centre.

Ms Valencia and her centrist ilk deserve much of the blame. Across Latin America they have spent years in power but have made little progress in solving the problems that most worry voters. Violence, insecurity and drug-trafficking are a scourge, and getting worse. Centrist failings have opened a gaping window for right-wingers inspired, as Mr de la Espriella is, by Nayib Bukele, the authoritarian president of El Salvador. (He has crushed gang violence by locking up a staggering 2% of the adult population.) Centrists have also done little to reduce the region’s vast inequality, a gift to the hard left. And economic growth has been woefully slow: real GDP growth per person in Latin America in the decade to 2024 was just 4%—in total, not per year. Politicians of the extreme and populist variety have seized upon all these failures with exaggerations, sweeping denunciations and tall promises.

Colombia exemplifies much of this. It is one of the world’s most unequal countries, marred by the violence of rebel groups. It produces about two-thirds of the world’s cocaine. Colombians now have a stark choice in the run-off. Mr Cepeda promises left-wing economics, which is unlikely to solve Colombia’s fiscal woes, and to double down on the policy of Paz Total, an effort to negotiate with all rebel groups at once. It has been failing under Gustavo Petro, the outgoing leftist president. Mr de la Espriella promises free markets, but has worryingly populist economic policies. He also plans a heavily militarised response to the rebels and to build ten mega-prisons in the jungle in the style of Mr Bukele.

Election night witnessed deep polarisation. Shamefully, Mr Cepeda and his ally Mr Petro both cast doubt on the results without providing evidence. Mr Petro claimed that “hundreds of thousands of votes were added” at some polling stations. Mr Cepeda warned of an alleged discrepancy involving 885,000 people and “atypical voting patterns”. Mr de la Espriella was typically hot-headed in response. He called Mr Petro a coup plotter and said that Mr Cepeda was “disabled”. He promised to defend democracy “by reason or force”, adding that he is willing to “be killed for Colombia” if necessary. On June 1st Mr Cepeda changed his tune and said there had been “no irregularities big enough to speak of fraud.”

The short run-off campaign ahead will probably be nasty. Both sides will try to convince voters the other is an existential danger to Colombia while trying to persuade the small pool of centrist voters that they can be trusted. Mr Cepeda will relentlessly highlight Mr de la Espriella’s past as a criminal-defence lawyer who has associated with former paramilitary leaders and defended a man who ran a notorious pyramid scheme in Colombia.

On election night Mr Cepeda said his rival represented “mafia-style fascism”. Mr Petro, who has already been pumping up the economy to try to help his ally, will probably splurge even more. Mr de la Espriella will continue to puff his claims that Mr Cepeda is a threat to democracy who wants to take Colombia on the same path as Cuba and Venezuela, calling him the candidate of drug-traffickers and rebels.

Mr de la Espriella is now the firm favourite. This has cheered markets nervous of Mr Cepeda. Colombian shares surged on the news of Mr de la Espriella’s win. But the run-off could be tight. Mr Cepeda also outperformed recent opinion polls and won slightly more of the first-round vote than Mr Petro did four years ago. Back then Mr Petro went on to win the run-off, in part by boosting turnout.

But most expect Mr de la Espriella to buck that precedent. The latest polling gives him an eight-point lead in the run-off. Donald Trump has interfered in order to endorse him. If Mr de la Espriella wins he will have to deal with a congress where the left has a lot of influence. That confrontation could make his campaign look like an easy prelude. ■
