item.title: Nigeria’s Christian groups scramble to win over Trump’s America
item.description:
Middle East & Africa

A BILL currently being considered by America’s House of Representatives would attach new conditions to financial aid sent to Nigeria. Republicans in Congress say they want Nigeria’s government to do more about the violence in the northern and “Middle Belt” states of the country. Specifically, they w...
item.content:encoded:
Nigeria’s Christian groups scramble to win over Trump’s America

Middle East & Africa | MAGA missionaries


A BILL currently being considered by America’s House of Representatives would attach new conditions to financial aid sent to Nigeria. Republicans in Congress say they want Nigeria’s government to do more about the violence in the northern and “Middle Belt” states of the country. Specifically, they want it to ensure better protection of Nigerian Christians against “brutal persecution”.

The bill would be a pain for Nigeria’s government, which might have a harder time getting American aid if it passes. But it would be a victory of sorts for the country’s Christian pressure groups, which have been lobbying Donald Trump’s administration since the president’s second term began last year. While Nigeria’s government stresses the complexity of the country’s security crisis, Christian activists are finding it useful to follow American evangelicals in framing the violence in religious terms. Some even allege that a “genocide” of Nigerian Christians is under way.

Thousands of people, both Christians and Muslims, are killed in attacks in Nigeria every year, mostly in the north, where the state is weakest. The violence stems from jihadism, banditry and conflicts between herders and farmers. Only a small fraction of incidents involve Christians being directly targeted for their faith.

Yet pressure groups claim that Christians are systematically persecuted and demand American intervention. “If international attention is what is required to spur decisive governmental action, then the Christian community in Nigeria welcomes it,” says Archbishop Daniel Okoh, who leads the Christian Association of Nigeria.

The archbishop and others echo a narrative forged in America that resonates with officials in the Trump administration. MAGA-friendly missionary groups argue that “mainstream media” underplay the threat to Nigerian Christians. To counter this, the groups package violent scenes into videos for social media to show “the truth” about persecution. “Not every video we see is doctored or manipulated,” says Ebenezer Obadare of the Council on Foreign Relations, an American think-tank, “but at some point, you find it impossible to tell the difference.”

One source of viral content is Equipping the Persecuted, an Iowa-based missionary group that runs a website called Truth Nigeria. The site says it reports on violence in Nigeria “with fearless honesty”. But it pursues a clear narrative of Christian victims and Muslim perpetrators, mixing reports of attacks in Nigeria with MAGA-minded content such as reports on supposed mass vigils in Africa for Charlie Kirk, an American right-wing activist who was murdered last year.

Christian activists approve of the country’s re-designation by America late last year as a “country of particular concern” for religious freedom. They have also welcomed American air strikes against terrorist groups in northern Nigeria and the dispatch of American soldiers to help the army fight militants.

Other benefits may come in the form of money and power. The bill making its way through the House recommends that some funds be dispensed to “faith-based organisations”. Nigerian groups may get a slice of this pie, as well as a bump in donations from sympathetic American Christians. They may also hope for America to boost their influence vis-à-vis prominent Muslim politicians from northern Nigeria.

Yet their focus on the persecution of Christians is poisoning Nigerian politics. The president’s national security adviser faces baseless accusations that he is in league with terrorists because he is Muslim and Fulani (a majority-Muslim ethnic group whose members are often stigmatised as jihadists and criminals). Mr Obadare warns that as next year’s presidential election approaches, “there will be more killings, because those who want to use this issue as a cudgel to beat [the president] are going to try and stoke more tension.” In Abuja, the capital, several people interviewed said they did not feel safe discussing the killing of Christians.

Even so, those wishing to draw American attention to security problems or political threats in Africa increasingly speak in terms of Christians’ rights. In Tanzania, the repression of religious leaders who denounced election-time violence is being framed as a threat to Christians. Even the Rapid Support Forces, a party in Sudan’s civil war that has itself been designated by America as a danger to religious freedom, is appealing to the Trump administration by stressing its army foes’ ties to Islamists. The strategy looks likely to spread. ■

Sign up to the Analysing Africa, a weekly newsletter that keeps you in the loop about the world’s youngest—and least understood—continent.

item.title: The parable of the tshukudu, Goma’s quintessential transport
item.description:
Middle East & Africa

For many outsiders the symbol of Goma is a young man with an automatic rifle. Last year the city in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo was captured by M23, rebels backed by next-door Rwanda. It remains occupied or, according to M23, “liberated”. Recently its name may also have evoked images of hea...
item.content:encoded:
The parable of the tshukudu, Goma’s quintessential transport

Middle East & Africa | It’s alright, Goma (I’m only wheeling)


For many outsiders the symbol of Goma is a young man with an automatic rifle. Last year the city in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo was captured by M23, rebels backed by next-door Rwanda. It remains occupied or, according to M23, “liberated”. Recently its name may also have evoked images of health workers in hazmat suits, because of the Ebola outbreak that has spread from the province to the north.

The true symbol of Goma, however, is an idiosyncratic, man-powered wooden scooter known as a tshukudu. It looks as if it has been drawn by a child, with its simple, angled frame and two-metre-long deck. Yet as a way of carrying cargo in this chaotic city, it has proved perfect. It is narrow enough to zigzag through busy markets. Rubber strips around the wheels and a spring beneath the cow-horn handlebars help absorb the shock of potholes. It can bear more weight than a bicycle: riders brag about carrying loads of more than 500kg on a single tshukudu. At $200, with no petrol costs, it is cheaper than a motorcycle.

The tshukudu was apparently invented in the 1970s by farmers on the mountain slopes around Goma to take produce downhill. To this day tshukudus allow young men to make ends meet. “The tshukudu is good because we don’t have jobs,” says Sadiki, a 26-year-old whose heaviest load was 50 cans of petrol and who says he once carried a cow. “It was not alive,” he clarifies.

The war between Congo and M23 is hurting business. Banks remain closed. Farmers have fled their land. Many aid workers have left. Sadiki says that shoppers who once bought 20kg of rice buy just 5kg at a time, so they need him less. Meanwhile cheap motorised cargo tricycles from India and China—known as “three hills” after the number of wheels—are competing for the remaining heavy loads. “The three-hill drivers are taking our market,” sighs Bahati, 23.

Yet the city’s emblem will endure. The UN peacekeeping mission that has been in Goma for 30 years once sponsored a tshukudu race; the winner painted his white with blue UN letters. Souvenir sellers flog little wooden versions. In the centre of town is a statue of a man on his tshukudu. (In a very Goma twist, the sculptor was an army colonel.)

As a small crowd waits to take selfies, a local guide watches and says: “When you go to Paris, you take a photo of the Eiffel Tower. When you come to Goma, you must take one of the tshukudu.” ■

Sign up to the Analysing Africa, a weekly newsletter that keeps you in the loop about the world’s youngest—and least understood—continent.

item.title: Ukraine is now Europe’s war. Survival can’t be the only aim
item.description:
Europe

“This is a moment of truth for Europe,” declared Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, when Vladimir Putin’s tanks rolled into Ukraine in 2022. Now, after years of dallying, Europe might finally mean it. European Union members, plus other European countries such as Britain, are...
item.content:encoded:
Ukraine is now Europe’s war. Survival can’t be the only aim

Europe | Vision quest


“This is a moment of truth for Europe,” declared Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, when Vladimir Putin’s tanks rolled into Ukraine in 2022. Now, after years of dallying, Europe might finally mean it. European Union members, plus other European countries such as Britain, are today responsible for almost all aid to Ukraine (see chart). Military integration is moving ahead, and a Franco-British initiative to police a notional ceasefire has been set up. A €90bn ($105bn) loan to Ukraine will start flowing this month. Sanctions on Russia are growing tougher.

Meanwhile Ukraine’s recent battlefield advances have revived a sense of diplomatic possibility. Europe wants to take over where American efforts have fizzled. “We will be part of the solution, and we should be part of the discussion,” said Emmanuel Macron, France’s president, in February. For the first time, such words sound descriptive rather than pleading.

Europe’s support, says Katarina Mathernova, the EU’s ambassador to Ukraine, “has been more resilient than we could have dared imagine.” Yet although Europe’s takeover gives it leverage, ministers and officials acknowledge that their governments are still groping towards a strategy that goes beyond maintaining Ukraine’s survival. In recent weeks policymakers have prematurely debated sending an envoy to negotiate with Mr Putin (the array of names floated included Angela Merkel and Mario Draghi), without a clear sense of what Europeans hope to achieve. On May 28th Kaja Kallas, the EU’s foreign-policy co-ordinator, deemed it wise to play down the speculation.

European officials agree that Mr Putin is in a tight spot. Yet few see any sign that he is willing to row back on his demands. That limits the potential for meaningful talks. One official says Europe will have nothing to offer Mr Putin except a gradual slowing of further sanctions. “We are not against negotiations if they are real,” says Margus Tsahkna, Estonia’s foreign minister. “But there is nothing to talk about yet.”

The confusion reflects differing aims. Some European governments want to sound out Russia’s red lines via “mediation” efforts, which could involve individual go-betweens rather than governments, or non-EU states such as Turkey. A serious negotiation with Mr Putin, in which Europe would sit on Ukraine’s side, still appears to be a way off. “I think we need both,” says one foreign minister. Some of the most intensive discussions about potential talks are taking place among the E3: Britain, France and Germany. That could revive fears among eastern European countries such as Poland that western countries might seek a “reset” with Russia over their heads. Ukraine is also sceptical.

Should Mr Putin grow willing to compromise, a ceasefire would probably require Ukraine to accept a loss of territory in the eastern Donbas region. Beyond providing as-yet-vague security guarantees, Europe’s best way of sugaring that pill is to speed up Ukraine’s bid to join the EU, something Ukrainians have craved since the Maidan revolution of 2014. Last year suggestions emerged—during peace talks led by America—that Ukraine could join the EU as soon as 2027. But although Mrs von der Leyen and others are pushing to keep Ukraine’s dream alive, that date is utterly implausible for a large, partly corrupt country with an income per person roughly one-third of Bulgaria’s. Officials believe Ukraine would be lucky to join in a decade.

That leaves a growing gulf between Ukraine’s sky-high hopes and many EU governments’ willingness to let the topic slide. To arrest that, Friedrich Merz, Germany’s chancellor, recently proposed an “associate membership” that would see Ukraine granted access to various EU institutions with limited or no voting rights, subsidies or single-market access. This is probably “as good as it’s going to get for Ukraine”, says Alexander Gabuev, the Berlin-based director of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Centre, a think-tank. But the proposal has flopped among Ukrainians, who hear it as code for sitting in indefinite limbo. Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukraine’s president, immediately dismissed Mr Merz’s suggestion as “unfair”.

One or more negotiating “clusters” may be opened at an EU summit this month. But, as one European official says, “the accession discussion is hypocritical on both sides.” Europeans think Mr Zelensky’s failure to rein in expectations is irresponsible. They also worry that making an exception for Ukraine would upset aspirants in the Balkans. Meanwhile, among Ukrainians a new mood of scepticism towards the West is emerging. New polling finds that nearly three-quarters of Ukrainians still back EU membership—but that support has fallen most quickly among the young.

As the country has taken on a growing share of responsibility for its own defence, including the manufacture of arms and drone technology sought by partners across the world, it wants recognition of the shifting balance of power. “I see a deep change in Ukraine’s identity,” says Jana Kobzova, a Ukraine-watcher at the European Council on Foreign Relations. “Where they once saw the EU as a saviour, now it’s about self-reliance. Many say, ‘We are protecting you now.’”

Reformers in Ukraine still hope to use the EU’s money and political pledges as a barrier against authoritarian drift. “EU accession is like a light in the tunnel for Ukraine,” says Lana Zerkal, a Ukrainian diplomat. Conditions have been attached to the €90bn package, to Mr Zelensky’s chagrin. The first stage of the accession process requires rule-of-law reforms by 2027 before funding is released. Yet the slow pace of reform in Ukraine frustrates European officials. “We need to see more effort in Kyiv,” says one. “They need to help us advocate for them.”

Time is short. Although Ukraine’s “long-range sanctions”, as Mr Zelensky calls its drone and missile strikes inside Russian territory, have lifted spirits, no one knows how long that will last. Russia is escalating its attacks on Kyiv and other cities, and further attacks on power and water infrastructure could make next winter even harder than the last. For now, European arms and money keep Ukraine in the game. Last week Mr Zelensky struck a deal with Sweden for fighter jets that could help stop cruise missiles. But Europe cannot yet provide the anti-ballistic missiles needed to protect Ukraine’s cities. Last week Mr Zelensky also sent a letter to Donald Trump appealing for Patriot interceptors.

Meanwhile Europe’s own clock is ticking. Next year brings elections in most of its bigger countries, starting with France in April. Foreign-policy analysts worry that if the populist-right National Rally secures the presidency it would try to pull the plug on some of Europe’s commitments, including fundraising. It would certainly oppose Ukraine’s EU bid. “The French farmers have not woken up to this yet,” says Fabrice Pothier, a former NATO official now at Rasmussen Global, a consultancy. “We have not started the hard part.”

Intensifying discussions over aid, diplomacy and accession show that Europe is taking responsibility for the war on its eastern flank. But much of its plan still rests on hope: that Ukrainian resolve will not be broken, that Mr Trump can somehow be persuaded to turn against Russia or that Mr Putin can be forced to negotiate. “This is clearly Europe’s war now,” says Mr Pothier. “The question is whether it can be Europe’s peace.” ■

item.title: Why France is uneasy about German rearmament
item.description:

item.content:encoded:
Why France is uneasy about German rearmament

Europe | Who’s afraid of the Bundeswehr?


When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 France and Germany spent nearly the same amount on defence. By 2029 Germany’s defence budget is expected to swell to at least €150bn ($174bn)—roughly double France’s. For European security, German rearmament is plainly welcome. Yet in Paris the prospect also prompts discomfort. The risk, General Fabien Mandon, head of the armed forces, told a Senate hearing last month, is that in five years France “falls behind” its neighbour in the field it has hitherto dominated.

The Franco-German link was forged around an implicit equilibrium: France carries the military burden, while Germany provides economic might. As the EU’s only nuclear power, and with a strong expeditionary and strategic culture, France is used to taking the lead. For example, Emmanuel Macron, the president, has partnered with Britain to set up a “coalition of the willing” for Ukraine to be deployed in the event of a ceasefire. Germany has signed up, but Friedrich Merz, the chancellor, is reluctant to commit ground troops. Indeed French military types are dismissive about Germany’s low appetite for risk, and its tendency to need American reassurance. “We have to be able to think about waging war differently, and without America, but they are absolutely not ready to think about this,” says a French military official. On most defence matters, the French still find that they are far more in tune with the British.

Across Europe Mr Merz’s promise to make the Bundeswehr “the strongest conventional army in Europe”, with a 40% increase in troops by 2035, is broadly applauded. Mr Macron has long argued for greater European “strategic autonomy”. A bigger German contribution could help achieve that ambition. Poland and the Baltics are reassured by the prospect, as is Italy. A poll last year suggested that 48% of Poles think a reinforced Bundeswehr would improve Poland’s security, with just 25% disagreeing. Yet, behind closed doors, the French are uneasy—and not only out of frustration that they do not have the fiscal space to spend as much. “It’s the elephant in the room,” says a top French military figure. That Germany might have the biggest army in Europe is “unthinkable for us”.

Germany has invaded France three times, but nobody in the French establishment seriously thinks it might pose a threat to its NATO allies. The popularity of the populist-right Alternative for Germany stirs concern, but mainly due to its pro-Russian tilt. Yet a desire to embed German power in larger organisations, the EU and NATO, has long guided French geopolitical thinking. “Beneath the relief”, suggested Franziska Brantner, co-head of Germany’s Greens, in a speech about rearmament last month, “[allies] also feel something they are too polite to say loudly: a quiet, persistent, historically rooted unease at the prospect of a continent in which the dominant military power, by a considerable margin, is once again Germany.”

One genuine worry is industrial rivalry. France has leading defence firms such as Dassault, Thales, Safran and Naval Group, which have won big recent export contracts. But in other sectors, such as the manufacture of combat tanks, the two countries compete for exports. If Germany’s extra spending goes on improving technology and more efficient production, this could leave France behind. As it is, infighting between Dassault (a French aircraft-maker) and the German division of Airbus over the joint Future Combat Air System—a pet project of Mr Macron’s which includes a next-generation fighter jet—threatens the project’s survival.

For France, any future imbalance in conventional forces will be countered by its nuclear deterrent. In March Mr Macron proposed a new doctrine of “forward deterrence”, an arrangement with other European countries in which Germany will be the “key” partner. The idea is that European conventional forces should help “shoulder” the French deterrent, in exercises or deployments of France’s nuclear-capable fighter jets. Indeed, Michel Duclos, of the Institut Montaigne, a think-tank, suggests that “forward deterrence” could be seen as a further way to bind an expanding German conventional force into a broader European project.

In the short run the political consequences of the spending gap may be limited, argues François Heisbourg of the Foundation for Strategic Research in Paris, notably because of France’s deterrent. But were France to elect the populist-right National Rally (RN) in next year’s presidential election, this would bring fresh tension. Jordan Bardella, a possible RN candidate, says France’s nuclear deterrent should be extended only to allies who buy French, not American, fighter jets. Other European nationalists also want to attach strings: Poland’s want German rearmament to be accompanied by war reparations.

For now, German leadership within the EU is likely to continue to lean heavily on its economic clout. Its strategic credibility remains to be earned. Yet General Mandon argues that France cannot be complacent even on this point. “In five years’ time, the argument that we have operational experience and a certain culture will no longer hold,” he told the Senate. “For the Americans, Germany is little by little becoming the European benchmark.” ■

item.title: 佩德罗·桑切斯还能撑多久？
item.description:

The prompt was the conviction for corruption of former officials in Mr Rajoy’s centre-right People’s Party (PP). Now Span...
item.content:encoded:
佩德罗·桑切斯还能撑多久？

欧洲 | 争取时间八年前的这个月，佩德罗·桑切斯组织并赢得了一场针对保守派现任首相马里亚诺·拉霍伊的议会不信任动议，从而成为西班牙首相。触发这一动议的导火索是拉霍伊所在的中右翼人民党（PP）前官员因腐败被定罪。如今西班牙政治几乎回到了原点。桑切斯曾承诺复兴西班牙民主，如今却因自己所在的社会党高层人物卷入丑闻而实力受损。他面临着举行大选的呼声，民调显示右翼将胜出。但他坚持自己领导的中左翼政府将持续到本届议会任期结束（2027年7月）“甚至更久”。桑切斯在党内最亲近的两名助手，何塞·路易斯·阿瓦洛斯和桑托斯·塞尔丹，分别在2024年和2025年因操纵公共合同被起诉。首相声称遭到背叛，道歉并誓言继续执政。但如果说有变化，最新打击甚至更为严重。上月，一名高等法院法官将前社会党首相何塞·路易斯·罗德里格斯·萨帕特罗列为涉嫌操纵影响力的犯罪团伙头目，萨帕特罗曾被一些人誉为该党当前价值观的守护者。司法调查聚焦于萨帕特罗与委内瑞拉独裁政权有争议的关系，特别是桑切斯政府在大流行期间向委内瑞拉-西班牙合资航空Plus Ultra提供的5300万欧元（6200万美元）纾困金。法官声称，向萨帕特罗及其女儿支付的约200万欧元咨询费，主要是安排纾困的佣金。与其他成为司法调查目标的社会党人一样，萨帕特罗否认有不法行为。桑切斯从未明确解释为何只有四架飞机的Plus Ultra能获得原本针对具有战略经济重要性的西班牙企业的纾困金。几天后，另一名高等法院法官下令警方搜查社会党在马德里的总部。这是他对塞尔丹等人涉嫌诽谤或贿赂参与其他调查的警方和检察官的指控进行侦查的一部分。桑切斯承认该党犯了错误。但他的几名助手声称，这些调查是旨在通过不公平手段推翻政府的协同企图。他们抱怨遭受迫害以及双重标准：针对社会党的案件比涉及人民党的案件处理得更快。他们的说法有一定道理。桑切斯的兄弟和妻子分别在低级法院面临刑事指控，涉及的行为只是看起来不道德，并非违法：前者接受地方政府一份明显的挂名职位，后者为一所大学教席筹集资金。相比之下，拉霍伊政府前内政部长2013年涉嫌滥用权力一案直到现在才开庭审理。但领导最新调查的两位高等法院法官均享有无可指责的声誉。对萨帕特罗的调查始于法国和瑞士检察官。而迫害的指控带来的回报越来越低。社会学家、前社会党议员伊格纳西奥·乌尔基苏指出，一项未公布的民调显示，只有大约一半的社会党选民相信这些指控。最新丑闻促使政府的两名议会盟友——巴斯克和加泰罗尼亚民族主义政党——呼吁提前举行大选。但他们不愿通过支持不信任动议来实现这一点，因为那样会……（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

item.title: 意大利追踪到了科萨·诺斯特拉的财富
item.description:
Europe

It began with a suspicious bank employee in Andorra, a mini-state between France and Spain. She wanted to know more about the €12m ($14m) in the accounts of a client, an Italian woman whose son claimed she had inherited it from her late husband. A tip-off reached an officer at the Italian embassy in...
item.content:encoded:
意大利追踪到了科萨·诺斯特拉的财富

欧洲 | 非法掠夺之财一切始于安道尔（法国和西班牙之间的迷你国）一名可疑的银行职员。她想知道一名客户账户中1200万欧元（1400万美元）的更多信息，这位客户是一名意大利女性，其子声称她从已故丈夫那里继承了这笔钱。一条线报传到意大利驻马德里大使馆的一名官员那里，引发了一场持续近三年的全球调查。5月28日，调查达到高潮，这名女子、她的儿子以及前夫贾科莫·坦布雷洛被捕，坦布雷洛此前因贩毒被判有罪，实际上一直活着并在西西里岛软禁。这次行动还导致了意大利执法部门有史以来协调的最大规模资产扣押之一：至少2亿欧元，分布于九个司法管辖区。根据长达226页的逮捕令，这些资产代表的不仅仅是国际毒枭的财富。逮捕令称，65岁的坦布雷洛先生、他的前妻和他们的儿子卢卡，是黑手党一个派系积累的流动资产的保管人，该派系在1990年代向意大利国家宣战。这些来自西西里小镇科莱奥内的科莱奥内西人，由萨尔瓦托雷·“托托”·里纳领导，暗杀了两名反黑手党检察官乔瓦尼·法尔科内和保罗·博尔塞利诺，并在罗马、佛罗伦萨和米兰放置炸弹，给意大利本土带来了恐怖。意大利首席反黑手党检察官乔瓦尼·梅利略将最新的逮捕和扣押与西西里黑手党科萨·诺斯特拉试图卷土重来的企图联系起来。自1993年里纳被捕（他于2017年在狱中去世）以来，科萨·诺斯特拉一直将地盘输给卡拉布里亚的恩德朗盖塔、那不勒斯的卡莫拉以及外国犯罪集团。梅利略先生说，除了扣押该团伙的非法所得，“我们还挫败了科萨·诺斯特拉试图通过一个统一组织重新装备自己的企图”。这显然是指一个名为“库波拉”的组织，该组织协调科萨·诺斯特拉的活动，据信由里纳担任主席。所有这些尚未在法庭上得到证实；三名嫌疑人否认有不法行为。检方部分依赖于pentiti（悔过者），即意大利语中指与检方合作的证人。根据一名证人的说法，坦布雷洛先生自1983年起就与科莱奥内西人的主要同伙马泰奥·梅西纳·德纳罗有生意往来，后者于2023年被捕并于同年晚些时候去世。逮捕令中还包含一段里纳在监狱院子里与另一名囚犯的对话片段，其中他说他已将财富托付给梅西纳·德纳罗，一些人认为后者是里纳作为“所有老大中的老大”的继任者。梅西纳·德纳罗在可再生能源、超市、建筑和旅游业有投资。调查人员称，到他去世时，他的身价约为40亿欧元。从坦布雷洛家族扣押的资产包括分散在从加勒比海到地中海地区的40多个账户中的现金、12公斤金条、通过一家在开曼群岛注册的公司持有的黎巴嫩银行股份、六辆汽车以及在西班牙马贝拉及其周边的22处房产，坦布雷洛先生的儿子卢卡在那里是一位受人尊敬的商人。卢卡在金融领域工作过，曾就职于纽约的法国兴业银行和伦敦的摩根士丹利，之后定居在太阳海岸。直到最近，他还是沃伦·巴菲特创立的投资公司旗下房地产部门伯克希尔哈撒韦家居服务公司（BHHS）马贝拉分部的管理合伙人。一位BHHS发言人表示，他自20……（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

item.title: 欧洲无需暴力手段就减少了非法移民
item.description:
Europe

Given its oft-proclaimed calling as a peace project, the European Union can sound oddly bellicose when it sets about crafting policy. There are trade and fiscal “bazookas” to blast away crises, “silver bullet” solutions for every problem, and “nuclear options” to be used as a last resort. Yet in the...
item.content:encoded:
欧洲无需暴力手段就减少了非法移民

欧洲 | 查尔斯曼专栏鉴于欧盟常常宣称自己是一个和平项目，它在制定政策时听起来却出奇地好战。有贸易和财政“火箭筒”来炸掉危机，有解决所有问题的“银弹”，还有作为最后手段的“核选项”。然而，由于没有欧盟军队甚至警察部队，笔杆子上的欧盟官僚很少能接触到任何看起来像真武器的东西。唯一例外——值得注意的是——是该俱乐部的边境巡逻机构。自2005年成立以来的十多年里，Frontex的特工们在使用哨子和警告帮助国家当局阻止移民时，几乎没别的工具。如今，他们还携带类似FBI的格洛克9毫米手枪。在一个旨在让战争不可想象的联盟中，第一件超国家武器并非用于防御军队，而是用于阻止手无寸铁的人进入。无论是由于格洛克手枪，还是更可能因为近年来的大量新措施，最近进入欧盟的非正常移民明显减少。Frontex发现的非法越境在过去几年中下降了一半以上。欧盟国家的庇护申请也大幅下降。尽管移民可能以不可预测的节奏起伏——2015年和2016年，一百万叙利亚人和阿富汗人涌入欧洲，而这距离他们各自国家爆发冲突已有多年——但最近欧盟外部边境有一种奇怪的平静感。6月12日，一套最初在十年前危机最严重时期构思的“移民方案”措施将生效，收紧边境管制并进一步减少非正常移民。也许，可能，可以想象，欧洲已经解决了新移民涌入其海岸的问题。唉，已经在欧洲的移民（通常融合状况不佳）这个政治上有毒的问题依然存在。可以说，欧洲解决了一半移民问题的一半。尽管如此，内政部官员们首次出现了类似乐观的情绪。非法移民是每个欧盟领导人都知道如果处理不当会让他们丢掉工作的一个议题。因此，布鲁塞尔的官员们想出了切实可行的方法来扼制不受欢迎的移民。最有效的手段是向突尼斯和埃及等“中转”国家提供大量现金，如果它们阻止来自更远地方的移民继续前往欧洲的话。2016年与土耳其达成的类似协议帮助遏制了危机；此后该协议已扩大。欧盟现在与移民来源地合作更加紧密，即使这意味着与塔利班这样的讨厌政权对话。对于潜在的移民来说，情况将变得更加严峻。从本月下旬开始，任何非正常抵达欧盟且获得难民保护机会渺茫的人（因为他们来自被视为安全的国家，如孟加拉国），将在边境拘留营中等待其申请评估。那些不符合庇护资格的人——目前占绝大多数——曾经可能会在欧洲国家的影子经济中工作数年，等待被驱逐出境。但这种情况将不复存在。根据6月1日达成的一项协议，任何庇护申请失败的人可能会被送到乌干达或乌兹别克斯坦等遥远国家的“遣返中心”，同时欧盟安排将他们遣返回原籍国。希望是潜在的移民选择不踏上这段旅……（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

Mr Nowak’s murderer, Vickrum Digwa, had lied to o...
item.content:encoded:
这是英国的乔治·弗洛伊德时刻吗？

英国 | 亨利·诺瓦克亨利·诺瓦克生命的最后时刻必然是难以想象的痛苦。这名18岁的学生躺在地上，因刀伤内出血，却被警方铐上手铐，警方对他声称被刺伤表示怀疑。诺瓦克先生的凶手维克鲁姆·迪格瓦向警方撒谎，称这名青少年对他进行了种族辱骂并造成他受伤。迪格瓦先生是一名印度裔锡克教英国人，他声称诺瓦克先生打掉了其作为信仰象征所佩戴的头巾，并称他为“Paki”（对巴基斯坦裔的侮辱性称呼）。事实上，根据判处迪格瓦先生至少21年监禁的法官的说法，发生的事情是受害者“也许有点无礼地”评论了凶手佩戴的大匕首（另一个宗教象征，尽管大多数虔诚的锡克教信徒会携带藏在衣服下的小得多的刀）。作为回应，迪格瓦先生抢走了诺瓦克先生的手机，引发了一场扭打，最终他拔出21厘米长的刀，刺了这名学生数次。即使在被捕后，迪格瓦先生也没有被戴上手铐。这起犯罪发生在去年12月，地点在南海岸的南安普顿。但直到本周，在迪格瓦先生被判刑以及令人痛心的视频片段显示警察在诺瓦克先生无助地躺在地上时给他戴上手铐之后，这些事件才在政治上引发爆炸性影响。首相基尔·斯塔默爵士表示，他观看视频时“感到恶心”。内政大臣莎巴娜·马哈茂德称其“令人不安”，但坚称应让警察监管机构——警察行为独立办公室——完成对所涉警察行为的调查（在他们到达之前，据说一次紧急电话提到可能发生了刺伤）。总检察长正在考虑是否审查最低刑期是否“过于宽大”。民粹主义右翼的奈杰尔·法拉奇和他的改革英国党同僚则没有那么克制。法拉奇先生在6月2日播发了一段“紧急讲话”，呼吁公众以“纯粹的、冰冷的愤怒”回应，并宣称：“白人的命也重要。”他的经济发言人罗伯特·詹里克说：“这个国家存在反白人种族主义问题。”当以反觉醒身份为傲的保守党领袖凯米·巴德诺赫指责法拉奇试图通过将自己标榜为白人的捍卫者来煽动分裂时，改革党咄咄逼人的内政发言人齐亚·优素福可耻地反驳道：“凯米和保守党不关心白人。”这种言论对英国政治来说是新的——也是危险的。主要政党基本上在种族团结的立场上达成一致，并避免鼓励白人多数群体心怀不满。尽管法拉奇先生在其整个职业生涯中倾向于从白人选民中获得不成比例的支持——2015年他的英国独立党（UKIP）获得了14%自认为是白人的选民的支持，而少数族裔选民中只有2%——但他一直推动一种“色盲”政治愿景。他为自己加速了公开种族主义的英国国家党的衰落而自豪，该党在2000年代末一度受欢迎后被UKIP实际上取代。这一策略取得了成功。现在有12%的非白人选民支持改革党。法拉奇先生一些最知名的同事，如优素福先生和前保守党内政大臣苏埃拉·布雷弗曼，都来自少数族裔背景。那么，他为什么接受了一种新的、更丑陋的……（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

item.content:encoded:
绿党限制CEO薪酬的政策考虑不周

英国 | 为了惩罚保罗而抢劫彼得抨击肥猫是英国左派的试金石。1998年，彼得·曼德尔森未能通过这一考验，当时作为工党大臣，他说“对于人们变得极其富有，只要他们纳税，我完全放心”。对英国的社会主义者来说，这是黑暗之主的原罪；他与被定罪的儿童性犯罪者杰弗里·爱泼斯坦的联系，仅仅证实了他是个坏蛋。绿党领袖扎克·波兰斯基之所以成为左派的宠儿，部分原因在于他对高收入者毫不留情的追究。绿党的解决方案是，将任何公共或私营组织中最高收入者的薪酬限制在最低收入者的十倍。这个想法很受欢迎：根据YouGov的民意调查，65%的公众支持它。该党议会领袖埃莉·乔恩斯声称，“这样的比例将结束贪婪CEO们过高的薪水，同时提高组织中最低收入者的工资。”确实，这项政策会降低高管薪酬。但低收入者的情况则不那么乐观。波兰斯基先生认为收入差距已经扩大，这是正确的。根据学者亚历山大·佩珀的估计，20世纪70年代，富时100公司CEO的中位数薪酬仅为英国工人中位数薪酬的20倍（见图表）。在2024-25年度，这一比例超过120倍。博彩公司Bet365的创始人丹尼斯·科茨去年赚了2.8亿英镑（3.77亿美元），超过了马绍尔群岛（人口38,000）的GDP。企业薪酬差距在20世纪80年代开始扩大，当时工会权力衰弱，边际税率下降激励高管要求更多现金。美国发放了越来越大的绩效相关薪酬。英国很快效仿，尽管其薪酬差距从未达到美国水平，但明显高于欧洲大陆。一些人认为，明星CEO可以创造与其薪酬相形见绌的回报。但实证证据尚不清楚。怀疑论者表示，天价薪酬反映的不是运作良好的人才市场，而是公司治理的失败，高薪带来的好处并不足以证明其造成的不平等是合理的。然而，即使有理由让工资更加平等，波兰斯基先生提出的方法也糟糕得惊人。最接近的先例是旧金山，那里通过向支付CEO薪酬超过普通工人中位数薪酬100倍的公司征税，推动了富人的外流。美国民粹主义左翼参议员伯尼·桑德斯提出，对违反50比1薪酬比率的公司征收高达五个百分点的全国公司税附加费。但这两项政策与绿党的提议相比都只是小儿科。波兰斯基先生声称这会提高最低工资者的收入。数学计算表明，这种好处将微乎其微。以该国最大的连锁超市乐购为例，该公司在英国雇佣了26万人。其CEO在2024-25年度的总薪酬为920万英镑，而最低工资工人每小时挣12.02英镑（全职每年不到24,000英镑）。即使假设波兰斯基先生的上限涵盖所有报酬而不仅仅是工资，通过降低CEO的薪酬也只能节省900万英镑。这几乎无法为每名工人每年加薪34英镑。再加上其他高管的节省，可支配的金额会多一点——但不会很多，因为高管层以下的薪酬下降很快。更重要的是，……（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

Fury at the Labour Party for its handling of the issue ha...
item.content:encoded:
英国政治已越过巴勒斯坦议题的顶峰

英国 | 绿党与红党“首先，他们对加沙的种族灭绝非常共谋，”曼彻斯特的一名年轻穆斯林伊山在被问及工党政府时说道。“这是一件大事。”随着加沙冲突持续，英国人对以色列的看法变得强硬。工党在处理这一问题上的愤怒，推动了亲加沙的独立议员在穆斯林聚居选区的崛起，以及绿党在其他地区的崛起。但尽管围绕这一议题情绪高涨，相对较少的选民将以色列或巴勒斯坦列为他们最关心的问题。有迹象表明，这场战争开始从人们的脑海中淡去。尽管如此，对加沙的支持已经催生了一群（通常是年轻的）左翼民粹主义选民。英国并非特例。在皮尤研究中心2025年3月调查的24个国家的中位数中，62%的人对以色列持负面看法，29%持正面看法。在英国，这一数字分别为61%和30%。同样，YouGov在2025年5月发现，32%的英国人更同情巴勒斯坦而非以色列，而德国为18%，法国为24%，意大利为31%，西班牙为33%。即便如此，该议题在英国尤为棘手的原因也有几个。尽管英国对以色列的武器进口贡献不到1%，但活动人士抓住了英国政府支持以色列战争的想法。英国在该地区的历史也无助于解决问题。工党屡次失策。在2023年10月7日之后几周——当时哈马斯突破以色列边境围栏，杀害并绑架以色列人——时任反对党领袖的基尔·斯塔默爵士笨拙地为以色列的回应辩护。为了避免被指控反犹太主义，斯塔默爵士多次拒绝呼吁停火，引发了自己议员的反叛。执政后，工党转向了亲巴勒斯坦立场，暂停了对以色列的部分武器出口，正式承认巴勒斯坦国，同时对一些抗议者采取了强硬路线。英国的穆斯林占总人口的6%，他们尤其活跃。2024年5月，Savanta的一项民调发现，21%的穆斯林表示，在决定如何投票参加当年大选时，以色列-巴勒斯坦冲突是最重要的问题（而英国整体为3%，包括18至24岁人群中的9%）。随着工党以压倒性优势赢得大选，亲加沙的独立议员成功夺取了四个穆斯林人口众多的原工党安全席位。在5月的地方选举中，加沙独立人士未能赢得他们瞄准的四个议会（尽管穆斯林领导的Aspire党在塔村连任）。相反，许多穆斯林转向绿党。工党附属智库Think Labour最近的一项民调发现，绿党在穆斯林中的支持率为30%，而工党为44%，独立人士为10%。只有极少数非穆斯林选民表示加沙战争是他们最关心的问题。英国选举研究给受访者提供了一个开放式文本框，让他们写下最重要的问题。在2024年5月至6月，不到0.5%的受访者在回答中写了“加沙”、“巴勒斯坦”、“以色列”、“种族灭绝”或“战争罪”等词。到2025年5月，这一数字下降了一半。2026年5月，英国关于战争的谷歌搜索降至2023年以来的最低水平。尽管加沙只是少数不断缩小的边缘人群的主要议题，但它仍在塑造英国政治。仔细审视2025年5月对英国选举研究做出回应的人……（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

item.title: 英国政府更倾向于签证禁令而非言论自由

In the most recent example his home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, banned Cenk Uygur and Hasan Piker, two left-wing American commentators,...
item.content:encoded:
英国政府更倾向于签证禁令而非言论自由

英国 | 禁止入境基尔·斯塔默爵士并不以果断著称。但有一件事他的工党政府以一反常态的积极性来处理：言论自由。最近的一个例子是，内政大臣沙巴纳·马哈茂德禁止了两名左翼美国评论员岑克·乌伊古尔和哈桑·皮克进入英国，而他们原定几天后在伦敦的一个节日上发表演讲。两人均声称他们被禁是因为批评以色列。也可能是因为他们曾发表可能被解读为支持恐怖组织的言论（皮克先生曾表示，如果必须在投票支持以色列或哈马斯之间做出选择，他会投票给哈马斯）。无论原因如何，马哈茂德女士认为他们的入境“可能不利于公共利益”。这一表述源于1971年《移民法》，该法案赋予内政大臣权力，否决此类个人的签证申请（并在不经审判的情况下驱逐他们）。最初，该法案用于排除疑似俄罗斯间谍，实际上往往意味着具有共产主义倾向的活动家。在1991年海湾战争期间，该法案被用于以国家安全为由驱逐伊拉克国民。2005年7月7日伦敦恐怖爆炸事件后，法律背景发生了变化。此后，托尼·布莱尔爵士的政府公布了一份可能导致驱逐出境的“不可接受行为”官方清单。其中包括：表达“为恐怖暴力辩护或美化”的观点，以及可能“煽动仇恨”或“导致社区间暴力”的观点。此后几年，该权力主要用于阻止极端伊斯兰传教士在英国活动。此类禁令的数量实际上一直在下降。2019年，英国禁止了37人入境。2024年（有数据可查的最近一年），仅排除了15人。但自那以后，政府似乎找到了一个喜欢按下的按钮。今年4月，有反犹太主义历史的说唱歌手坎耶·韦斯特在音乐节演出前被吊销了签证。一个月后，极右翼活动家汤米·罗宾逊看到他的几名盟友被禁止参加他在伦敦举行的“团结王国”集会。英国并非唯一基于模糊判断排除入境者的国家。澳大利亚经常以“品格理由”拒绝或取消签证。特朗普政府指示移民官员在准移民的社交媒体上寻找“反美”态度。2025年，它取消了至少六名被指控庆祝保守派活动家查理·柯克被谋杀的人的签证。不同之处在于，英国似乎不成比例地针对最知名的政治活动家和名人。韦斯特先生（人称Ye）是世界上最有影响力的音乐家之一；皮克先生是最受关注的流媒体主播之一。这并非巧合。对英国而言不同寻常的是，拒绝签证的过程可能毫不官僚。在大多数其他国家，这完全由公务员处理，他们进行预先确定的检查并得出安静的结论。在英国，这也是内政大臣根据其个人自由裁量权行使的一项权力。这使反恐工具变成了美德信号工具。正是公众的愤怒导致当时的工党内政大臣约翰·里德在2007年因希思罗机场斗殴事件禁止美国说唱歌手史努比狗狗入境英国。2015年，当保守党内政大臣特蕾莎·梅禁止另一位美国说唱歌手泰勒·克里特时……（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

item.title: 英国私校征税的影响开始显现
item.description:

In mid-May it announced that, unless it can find a big cash injection, it will close in July. The school has blamed years of rising costs—worsened by...
item.content:encoded:
英国私校征税的影响开始显现

英国 | 紧缩的课程超过500名儿童就读于雷丁的圣约瑟夫学院，这是一所私立学校，以提供其所在地区“性价比最高”的教育而自豪。5月中旬，该校宣布，除非能获得大笔资金注入，否则将于7月关闭。学校将原因归咎于多年来成本上升——工党政府决定让私立学校开始全额缴纳商业税率，并对学费征收增值税，这加剧了成本上升。马丁·库克是数百名正在为孩子寻找新学校的家长之一；作为服役20年的军官，他有摆脱困境的经验。“但当你有问题，你的孩子难过时，情感上很难熬。”工党改革实施18个月后，许多私立学校发现日子不好过。政府6月4日公布的数据显示，今年英格兰主流独立学校的学生人数下降了5%（约27,000名学生）。此前2024-25学年（工党上台后的第一年）已下降了2.8%。下降主要来自加入私立学校的新生减少，而非现有学生大量流失。下降在伦敦以外最为显著——可能是因为在较贫困地区，家长为支付私校学费而承受的压力最大。这些下滑在多大程度上是由工党政策驱动的，尚有疑问。部分原因无疑是由于英国学龄儿童总数在下降（去年英格兰约为1.2%）。而在工党执政之前，生活成本上升早已迫使许多家长仔细考虑开支。但即使考虑到这一点，改革对入学率的影响似乎比预测的要大。早在2024年，政府预测征收增值税将使该行业到2030年代学生人数比原本情况减少6%。实际可能造成更大的萎缩。一个激烈的争论是，这些下滑是否已开始推动许多学校破产。政府坚持认为没有：事实上，它称自其增值税政策实施以来，开办的独立学校多于关闭的。这是事实，但有误导性。新开办的学校大多是为残疾儿童服务的小型“特殊”学校，对此类学校的需求激增。这些机构的学生学费主要由地方当局支付（地方当局可以申请退还增值税）。只关注“主流”私立学校，则会呈现一幅更加模糊的景象。人们仍在开办此类学校（自2025年初以来开办的18所中有7所列其宗教精神为“伊斯兰”）。但长期趋势是整合：2016年至2025年间，英格兰的主流学校数量下降了11%，而接受教育的学生人数仅略有下降。2025年有近60所学校关闭（共1,600所）。这比2024年多，但与工党当选前的2023年大致相同。追踪今年迄今已宣布或威胁关闭的情况，目前还没有迹象表明2026年肯定会更糟。然而，最近的一个变化非常引人注目。倒闭学校的平均规模似乎在急剧上升。长期以来，最常倒闭的是小规模学校，学生人数少至50人。但自2025年1月以来，至少有十几所拥有200多名学生的学校已关闭或宣布可能关闭——这大约相当于过去八年……（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

item.title: 打造一位首相
item.description:
Britain

Ask a typical British voter to design a prime minister and they might pick one with a distinguished career in public service. They would probably prefer someone pragmatic over an ideologue. And they would certainly prefer someone serious (if boring) rather than a showman. Out of a line-up, they migh...
item.content:encoded:
打造一位首相

英国 | 白芝浩让一个典型的英国选民设计一位首相，他们可能会选择一个在公共服务领域有卓越职业生涯的人。他们可能更倾向于务实者而非空想家。当然，他们肯定更喜欢严肃（即使无聊）的人而非表演者。在一排候选人中，他们可能会选择一个穿着西装、长相适中的中年男子。不仅仅是基尔·斯塔默爵士的形象可以由民调受访者设计。他的政府也严格遵循了典型选民的民调优先事项。公众赞成他对私人房东的严格新规、扩大就业权利以及对昂贵住房征收高额税。铁路国有化和提高最低工资在调查中获得了强烈支持。当政府偏离轨道时（例如削减养老金领取者的冬季燃料补贴），就会迅速调头。选民想要，选民得到。基于焦点小组的治理实验也延伸到了社会政策。应民众要求，内政大臣沙巴纳·马哈茂德将净移民降至多年来最低水平。政府禁止了对争议性抗议团体“巴勒斯坦行动”的支持，并永久禁止对跨性别儿童使用青春期阻断剂，这符合公众的社会保守本能。基尔·斯塔默爵士在塑造自己和政策以适应英国选民的愿望方面达到了令人毛骨悚然的程度。然而他们讨厌他。他的支持率是有记录以来首相中最低的之一，接近利兹·特拉斯的灾难性水平。“打造首相”——这种基于焦点小组的治理方式根本行不通。你可能会争辩说，这是无能的后果，或者是在困难时期执政的代价。但基尔·斯塔默爵士甚至在掌权之前就已经有了负面评价。2024年，工党在一场与后特拉斯时期摇摇欲坠的保守党竞选的对决中，仅获得了34%的选票。引人注目的是，民调显示，那些本应从工党政策中获益的选民是最急于抛弃它的。低收入者比高收入者离开得更快；私人租房者涌向了绿党；工会成员背弃了本世代最亲工会的政府。净移民降至2012年以来的最低水平（排除疫情年份），这并未削弱奈杰尔·法拉奇及其右翼民粹主义改革英国党的崛起。选民得到了，选民不说谢谢。相反，基尔·斯塔默爵士加入了众多迷失在寻找选举版黄金国的政客行列。许多西方民主国家的民调显示，大多数选民在经济上左倾、在社会问题上不自由。这个象限里选民众多，却几乎没有政客代表。那些试图填补空白的人往往失败。这种方法的倡导者曾称赞长期执政的丹麦社会民主党，该党持怀疑移民的中左立场，据称压制了极右翼。但尴尬的是，社会民主党在3月赢得了一个多世纪以来最低的得票率，而反移民的丹麦人民党则取得了进展。基尔·斯塔默爵士抵达了黄金国，却发现那里没有黄金。追逐民调是糟糕（因而最终不受欢迎）政府的秘诀。原因之一是，通常不应只看民调的表面价值。例如，询问选民对移民的偏好，他们会……（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

item.title: 国债市场的特殊角色岌岌可危
item.description:
Special report

IT IS THE nightmare scenario for any market: everyone rushes for the exits at the same time and trading seizes up. That kind of crunch was not thought to be possible in the most liquid market in the world. But in early 2020, as the covid-19 pandemic took hold and the global economy faltered, many co...
item.content:encoded:
国债市场的特殊角色岌岌可危

特别报道 | 32万亿美元的问题这是所有市场的噩梦情景：所有人同时涌向出口，交易停滞。这种崩溃在世界上流动性最强的市场被认为是不可能的。但在2020年初，随着新冠疫情蔓延、全球经济步履蹒跚，许多公司、政府和个人在常规收入枯竭时发现自己急需现金。最容易出售的资产，正是由于该市场假定的流动性，就是美国国债。尽管国债价格通常在风险市场突然承压时上涨，但这次它们反而开始下跌，抛售浪潮的另一边买家寥寥。大银行——通常是国债的最大交易商——自身也感到了压力，因此没有介入以促成“现金争夺”。突然间，一种被视为终极安全资产、全球许多其他金融资产以其定价的投资变得难以出售。为了防止市场完全冻结，美联储不得不开始购买，最终收购了数万亿美元的美国政府债务。这一事件与亚历山大·汉密尔顿在1790年设想的情况完全相反。当时，作为美国第一任财政部长，他说服持怀疑态度的同事，联邦政府应承担新国家13个州的战争债务。美国如期发行了年利率6%的开放式证券——第一批真正的国债。当时，英国政府债券是世界上交易最方便的金融资产，汉密尔顿嫉妒地注视着伦敦的债务市场。他认为，公共债务必须是安全且可转让的。他辩称，这样的市场能吸引投资者，从而降低所有人的利率，而不仅仅是政府的利率。用现代术语来说，汉密尔顿梦想的是流动性。当投资者能够在任何他们想要的时候，安全且廉价地以已知的当前价格买卖资产时，这个市场就是流动的。在正常情况下，世界上没有哪个市场比美国国债市场承诺更多的流动性。它是一个近32万亿美元的庞然大物——远大于任何其他主权债务市场。这些债券不仅美国视为安全资产，更是世界的安全资产。关于如何为风险定价的讨论始于与国债市场的比较。它是全球金融体系的指路星。鉴于其崇高地位，国债市场变化之快令人震惊。过去三年，未偿国债价值平均每年增长8%（见图表）。二十年前，美国占七国集团（世界上最富裕经济体俱乐部）政府债务的38%。现在，这一比例达到60%。不到十年，国债市场预计将增长到50万亿美元，比今天大60%以上。随着市场膨胀，参与者也在改变。最可靠的投资者——为满足监管要求而购买的银行、为货币危机建立储备的外国央行，或者美联储本身——持有的国债不到三分之一，这是30年来的最低水平。它们已被寻求回报而非安全性的买家所取代。对冲基金利用国债借款，将微小的套利机会转化为更大的收益。保险公司和养老基金也是大买家，但它们的兴趣取决于收益率……（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

item.title: 外国对美国国债的需求正变得愈发不可靠
item.description:
Special report

In 1974, soon after the first oil shock, William Simon, America’s treasury secretary, flew to Jeddah to sign a secret deal with the king of Saudi Arabia. Among other things, he promised the Saudi government preferential access to American Treasury bonds. In exchange, the regime agreed to invest some...
item.content:encoded:
外国对美国国债的需求正变得愈发不可靠

特别报道 | 不再特殊

1974年，第一次石油危机过后不久，美国财政部长威廉·西蒙（William Simon）飞往吉达，与沙特国王签署了一项秘密协议。其中，他承诺沙特政府享有购买美国国债（Treasury bonds）的优先权。作为交换，该政权同意将其部分巨额石油收入投资于美国公共债务。

三年前，理查德·尼克松（Richard Nixon）结束了美元与黄金的兑换，开启了浮动汇率时代。各国央行发现自己不得不管理汇率。外国政府大量囤购美国国债，部分是为了防止本币对美元升值。美国政府也需要外国买家：其债务的客户越多，所需支付的利息就越低。

美国的金融官僚们提供了一项优惠交易：在私人拍卖中投标购买国债的机会，并享受优惠的税收待遇。尽管沙特从未成为大买家，但在21世纪初，由于货币危机尤其使亚洲政府确信需要储备美元计价资产，外国政府购买了2.3万亿美元的美国国债，使其持有量达到2.9万亿美元。逻辑是，如果本币开始下跌，它们可以通过出售美国国债来购买国内资产，从而阻止跌势。

最大的储备在中国，其在2013年峰值时持有1.3万亿美元的美国国债。这些债券主要由中国人民银行持有，该行通过买卖美国政府债券来管理人民币价值。许多其他国家也是如此。2008年，外国政府持有的美国联邦债务比例达到峰值38%。

这些购买是一大福音。对其影响的最大估计来自智库安德森研究所（Andersen Institute）的拉沙德·艾哈迈德（Rashad Ahmed）和约翰·霍普金斯大学（Johns Hopkins University）的亚历山德罗·雷布奇（Alessandro Rebucci）。他们认为，外国政府意外投资1000亿美元，可使十年期国债收益率在投资发生时下降一个百分点，一年后降至约半个百分点。

此外，外国政府投资美国国债总体上并非为了赚钱。它们需要美元资产仅仅作为一种预防措施，以便在必要时帮助捍卫本币。这使得它们成为令人羡慕的稳定、可靠的资金来源。

然而，近20年来，外国政府在美国国债市场中的作用一直在缓慢萎缩。它们目前仅持有13%的美国国债，为30年来最低水平。部分原因在于央行的多元化。美元在全球外汇储备中的份额已从2001年的71%下滑至去年的大约57%。部分降幅源于美元的长期强势，因为央行倾向于在美元便宜时买入、昂贵时卖出，以保持本币不会升值或贬值过多。但这一下降也是央行现在持有更广泛货币的结果。如今，除了欧元、日元和英镑储备外，它们的囤积中还包含了更多的瑞士法郎和加拿大元。

在目睹俄罗斯央行外国资产因俄罗斯入侵乌克兰而被冻结后，外国央行对投资美国国债也变得更加犹豫。“这是一条已经跨过的卢比孔河，”美国财政部借款咨询委员会（Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee）的一名成员表示，该委员会是向财政部提供建议的私营部门小组。“他们害怕……”

item.title: 无论喜欢与否，对冲基金已是美国国债市场的永久组成部分
item.description:
Special report

THE SCALE of the Treasury market is mind-boggling. Some $1trn in securities change hands each day. Trillions more are used as collateral for short-term loans. Financial institutions of all stripes are involved: banks, central banks, high-speed traders, insurers, endowments, pension funds, hedge fund...
item.content:encoded:
无论喜欢与否，对冲基金已是美国国债市场的永久组成部分

特别报道 | 基差交易（basis trade）

美国国债市场的规模令人难以置信。每天有约1万亿美元的证券易手。还有数万亿美元被用作短期贷款的抵押品。各类金融机构都参与其中：银行、央行、高频交易商、保险公司、捐赠基金、养老基金、对冲基金等等。

过去，银行是这一切的主要推动者，为其他金融公司充当“做市商”（market-makers）。就在2009年，一年期及以上期限的美国国债中，约有一半是由投资银行的经纪部门在拍卖中购买，然后再转售。但金融危机后出台的新规定削弱了银行在美国国债市场中作为中介的角色，要求它们用更多资本为这类普通交易提供资金。现在，交易商银行在拍卖中仅购买12%的一年期以上美国国债。

另一个高产买家帮助填补了空白：对冲基金（hedge funds）。它们试图通过多种方式从美国国债中获利，但一种称为相对价值（relative value）的策略尤其引起恐慌。该策略利用类似资产价格之间的微小差异，这些差异会随时间收敛。由于价格差异微乎其微，利润也很小。为了使此类交易值得进行，对冲基金使用借入资金以巨大规模进行交易。为此，它们持有2.4万亿美元美国国债的多头敞口（即押注债券价值上涨），形式包括证券本身和衍生品（见图表）。

最常见的相对价值策略称为基差交易（basis trade）。它试图从美国国债期货（在固定日期买入或卖出美国国债的合约）与标的美国国债本身之间微小的价格差异中获利。资产管理公司对国债期货需求巨大，因为持有它们比购买债券涉及的繁琐手续更少。这意味着，某一特定美国国债的交易价格通常略低于类似的期货合约。Citadel、ExodusPoint等对冲基金卖出期货合约，用所得资金以略低的价格购买相关美国国债，然后在合约到期时赚取差价。

这两种资产在到期时价格将会收敛，这是确定的，因此交易本身不涉及风险。但为了让交易有利可图，这些公司通过大量借贷来放大投资，这带来了巨大风险。它们通常以美国国债作为抵押品。如果美国国债价格下跌，贷款人可能会要求更多保护。如果下跌幅度足够大，借款人可能被迫清算资产以偿还贷款。

这种动态可能加剧美国国债市场的波动幅度。在“现金争夺”（dash for cash）期间，对冲基金估计卖出了1720亿美元的美国国债，加剧了市场失灵。自那以来，为基差交易借入的美国国债数量增长了160%。如果再次发生危机，基差交易只会使情况更糟。

一些监管机构担心对冲基金在美国国债市场中日益增长的影响力。2023年，时任美国证券交易委员会（SEC，负责美国国债市场的多个监管机构之一）主席加里·根斯勒（Gary Gensler）建议，对冲基金应像银行的交易部门一样受到监管。这引发了Citadel创始人兼首席执行官肯·格里芬（Ken Griffin）等人的强烈反对。“这是一种幻觉，认为它是安全、最深……”

item.title: 主要合作伙伴：美联储与财政部的新关系
item.description:
Special report

NO FINANCIAL institution or government agency matters more to the Treasury market than does the Federal Reserve. The central bank’s responsibility for financial stability and monetary policy has made it a mammoth buyer of Treasuries in this century, snapping up trillions of dollars’ worth after the ...
item.content:encoded:
主要合作伙伴：美联储与财政部的新关系

特别报道 | 平衡之举（Balancing Act）

对美国国债市场而言，没有哪个金融机构或政府机构比美联储（Federal Reserve）更重要。央行对金融稳定和货币政策的责任，使其在本世纪成为美国国债的庞大买家，在2007-09年全球金融危机后以及新冠疫情期间都抢购了数万亿美元的国债。结果，美联储的资产负债表比以往大得多：20年前其资产不足1万亿美元，而现在约为6.7万亿美元。

今年5月成为美联储主席的凯文·沃什（Kevin Warsh）认为这是一种不健康的失常。他指出，美联储资产负债表的扩张主要使已经富有的人受益（因为当美联储在金融市场上撒钱时，个人持有的资产价格会上涨）。也许更令人担忧的是，他说，美联储的反复干预扰乱了重要的市场信号，使投资者更难区分信用良好的借款人和风险借款人。他梦想着一个在金融市场中作用远小于现在的美联储。

在财政部长斯科特·贝森特（Scott Bessent）身上，沃什找到了观点相似的伙伴。贝森特去年曾表示，美联储的资产负债表扩张已经越界，进入了通常由民选决策者保留的领域——比如向债券市场上最大的公司施予恩惠，同时可能使小公司更难找到扩张所需的信贷。贝森特可以采取一种既能限制美联储在市场中的作用，又能减少美国日益增长的利息支出的策略。贝森特目前希望财政部发行更多短期债务（即国库券，bills），因为财政部对此类债券支付的利息通常较低。这可能有助于减少利息支出，但会使美国债务更容易受到利率变化的影响，即所谓的“展期风险”（rollover risk）。

如果美联储希望看起来不那么干预市场，自然的做法是重新调整其持仓，使其与美国国债未偿总额的期限结构相匹配。这将使其持有更少的长期债务和更多的国库券。从长期债券撤出可能会产生与购买狂潮相反的效果：此类债券的利率将不得不上升，以说服私人投资者接盘。美联储在美国国债市场中的份额已经在下降，从2022年的26%降至如今的仅12%。（美联储的资产负债表也在收缩，因为它让持有的债券到期而不替换，同时联邦债务却激增。）

如果政府的借贷成本上升，那么所有以美元贷款的人的借贷成本也会上升。堪萨斯城联储（Kansas City Fed）的安德鲁·李·史密斯（Andrew Lee Smith）和达拉斯德克萨斯大学（University of Texas at Dallas）的维克多·瓦尔卡塞尔（Victor Valcarcel）等研究人员已经表明，美联储减持美国国债导致长期利率上升，因为投资者面临流动性较低的国债市场和对未来的确定性降低。这种上升似乎是通过期限溢价（term premium）产生的，这是一个难以衡量的残差，用于补偿持有长期债券的各种不确定性。

如果美联储作为不太活跃的买家，当国债市场出现抛售恐慌时，也会增加金融稳定风险。2019年9月，融资市场陷入停滞，导致大型金融机构之间隔夜贷款的利率（即所谓的……）

item.title: 银行和稳定币都无法拯救美国国债市场
item.description:
Special report

“YOUR PIPELINE”, according to a popular saying in the sales industry, “is your lifeline.” The debt managers responsible for issuing Treasuries might not like to associate themselves with cold-callers. But with some once-reliable buyers of Treasuries no longer behaving so reliably, the task of search...
item.content:encoded:
银行和稳定币都无法拯救美国国债市场

特别报道 | 新玩家（New players）

销售行业有句流行谚语：“你的管道就是你的生命线。”负责发行美国国债的债务管理者可能不愿将自己与电话推销员相提并论。但随着一些曾经可靠的美国国债买家不再那么可靠，寻找替代客户的任务日益重要。

特朗普政府中的乐观支持者希望两种类型的人能更加活跃：穿卡其短裤的加密货币爱好者（crypto-bros）和穿细条纹西装的银行家。两者都有助于增加对美国国债的需求，并可能使市场运行得更好——尽管它们都不会以改变世界的规模实现这一点。

先来看加密货币爱好者，他们带来了稳定币（stablecoins）。稳定币是与特定价值挂钩的加密资产——通常与美元一比一挂钩。去年国会通过的《GENIUS法案》规定了谁可以发行它们以及它们可以用于什么用途。关键在于，该法律要求稳定币必须由完全匹配的短期美国国债（期限短于94天）作为支持。

这类资产迅速崛起，在过去两年中规模翻了一番多，达到3250亿美元（见图表）。最大的稳定币Tether持有1170亿美元的美国国债；如果它是一个国家，它将是美国债务的第18大国家持有者，排名介于韩国和阿联酋之间。一些政策制定者，尤其是财政部长斯科特·贝森特（Scott Bessent），认为持续快速增长可能使稳定币成为美国国债需求的重要来源。去年11月，贝森特表示，到本十年末，稳定币市场可能增长十倍，从而推动对国库券的需求。

渣打银行（Standard Chartered）更为乐观，预测市场将在不到两年内增长至2万亿美元。这种增长将刺激约1万亿美元的对国库券的额外需求（不是2万亿美元，因为对稳定币的部分热情可能会蚕食其他需求来源，比如货币市场基金）。再加上美联储可能更大的胃口（见前一篇文章），将使财政部能够将其债务的更大比例作为国库券发行，减少长期债券的发行，从而降低平均收益率。

但有充分理由持怀疑态度。另一家银行摩根大通（JPMorgan Chase）认为稳定币增长将慢得多。它认为到2027年底，市场规模在5000亿至7500亿美元之间更为合理。事实上，自10月底以来，稳定币的增长几乎停滞，增幅不到5%。这与比特币等风险较高的加密资产的下跌同时发生。2022年至2024年间也出现了类似模式，当时稳定币市场在加密货币价格另一次下跌中实际上规模缩小——强化了稳定币仅仅是加密货币投资工具的看法。实际上，如果没有加密货币价格的复苏，即使对稳定币的悲观预测（到明年年底翻一番）也可能过于乐观。

银行是久经考验的美国国债需求来源，正在卷土重来。自全球金融危机后不久，它们作为美国国债市场参与者的地位一直在下降，当时国会和监管机构急于防止更多银行倒闭，使它们更难扩张业务——包括交易或使用美国政府债务进行贷款。现在政策制定者感叹，这类规则将系统性风险转移到了其他地方……

item.title: 有什么能取代美国国债市场吗？
item.description:
Special report

There is no iron law dictating that the world’s reserve asset be Treasury bonds. For centuries British gilts held that crown, until they were dethroned after the second world war. But there is no successor to Treasuries. The potential heirs lack size and other crucial features.

Since its constructi...
item.content:encoded:
有什么能取代美国国债市场吗？

特别报道 | 别无选择（No other option）

没有铁律规定世界的储备资产必须是美国国债。几个世纪以来，英国金边债券（British gilts）一直占据这一地位，直到二战后被取代。但美国国债没有继任者。潜在的继承者缺乏规模和其他关键特征。

自1999年建立以来，欧元区一直是最有可能的竞争者。但2010年代初的欧洲主权债务危机炸毁了希腊、意大利和西班牙等国的长期债券收益率。

最近，欧盟委员会开始发行债券。但这些债券甚至尚未满足欧洲投资者的需求，更不用说全球了。首先，市场太小了。欧盟委员会计划在今年上半年发行1000亿欧元（合1160亿美元）的长期债务，而财政部计划发行2.2万亿美元。

更重要的是，这些债券的行为不像是由欧洲超级大国联合实力支持的资产，而是由一个没有征税权的超国家机构发行、由一群主权债权人支持的债券。结果，十年期欧盟委员会债券的收益率约为3.5%，意味着投资者认为其风险高于该地区信用最好的政府（德国政府债券收益率为3%）。市场尚未准备好接受欧洲政治统一的故事。

美国国债市场现在规模大得令人担忧，但其他市场太小，无法竞争。目前有九个国家的国债被三大评级机构均授予AAA评级。名单包括德国和少数节俭的北欧欧元区成员国、澳大利亚、加拿大、新加坡和瑞士。它们合计的政府债务总额约为7万亿美元，不到美国国债市场的四分之一（见图表）。

黄金是恐慌央行的首选资产，但它几乎不具备美国国债中如此宝贵的特性。投资者无法从金条中获得利息收入，这意味着贵金属无法扮演生产性无风险证券的角色。即使在黄金支持货币的时代，当货币理论上可以兑换黄金时，政府债券仍被优先作为安全资产，因为它们为投资者提供了收益，而不仅仅是存放资金的场所。

随着中国经济实力的增长，分析人士猜测中国是否也能接过全球金融超级大国的衣钵。但中国的资本管制限制了资金进出，因此无法想象中国能发行真正流动的国际安全资产。在危机中，闸门会落下，外国买家将无法将资金汇回国内。

一些评级最高的公司债券、大型金融机构之间的短期贷款安排，以及以看似稳定资产为抵押的债务，通常被视为接近安全，其价格与美国国债的交易如此接近，以至于大部分时间它们似乎以几乎相同的方式运作。

但这只在一切正常时才成立。在2007-09年全球金融危机期间，依赖近乎安全的资产（如高评级抵押贷款债券）来获得巨额杠杆的投资者发现，近乎安全与安全是完全不同的两回事。

并没有任何说法表明美国国债的潜在继任者不能齐心协力，为世界提供安全可靠的……

item.title: Imagining a world without a safe asset
item.description:
Special report

Around THE time The Beatles were setting the standard for pop music, a group of academics—many of them future rock stars of investment—were doing the same in finance. They developed the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM), which estimates the return investors should expect for taking on risks.

To wo...
item.content:encoded:
Imagining a world without a safe asset

Special report | Debts of despair


Around THE time The Beatles were setting the standard for pop music, a group of academics—many of them future rock stars of investment—were doing the same in finance. They developed the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM), which estimates the return investors should expect for taking on risks.

To work out that return on risk, they realised, investors would need to know what a riskless investment earned. An economist named William Sharpe aimed to find a “pure interest rate”. Six decades later the CAPM drives trillions of dollars of investment decisions; the “Sharpe ratio”, measuring risk-adjusted performance, is still used everywhere in finance. The supposedly riskless asset underlying these influential calculations is almost always a Treasury security.

What happens, then, if Treasuries are no longer deemed riskless? A lot more than the theory underpinning portfolio construction would be in jeopardy. Treasury-market prices are to investors like water to a fish. The assets are so fundamental to global finance that it is tough to imagine a world without them. It would be a world with higher interest rates, greater uncertainty and more risk. It would be more dangerous and difficult to navigate for investors and taxpayers not just in America, but in the rest of the world, too.

The world’s safest assets encourage much risk-taking. If investors own an asset that they know will benefit during a sudden market spasm, a sell-off or a recession, they will be happy to take greater risk elsewhere. “If you don’t have a safe asset”, says Markus Brunnermeier, an economist at Princeton University, “it leads to less lending to risky projects, to a supply shock.”

The privileges of being judged risk-free are visible across the economy. Banks have to hold far less capital against Treasuries than against other assets. The bonds can be used as collateral for loans in the enormous repo market, or to hedge risk in currencies and interest rates. The yields on any other dollar-denominated bond, issued by a firm, a foreign government or an American state or city are judged by their spread—how much higher they are than on Treasury bonds.

But wobbliness is beginning to show. Recently one of the most valuable attributes of Treasury bonds went up in smoke. For the first two decades of the 21st century, Treasuries tended to rally when equity markets slumped. Investors could protect themselves against turmoil in risky assets by holding American debt.

That negative correlation made Treasuries even better ballast than they had been in diversified portfolios—now they could, in theory, offset losses in equities. New investment strategies emerged. So-called risk-parity funds, which borrowed to raise their exposure to bonds and did well when stocks and bonds moved in opposite directions, boomed in size.

But high inflation in 2021 and 2022, then a spike in interest rates, ended that. Bonds and stocks sold off at the same time, burning the fingers of investors who thought they had diversified their risk (see chart).

Another new risk for Treasuries is that many market-shaking moments are coming from policymakers in Washington instead of from external economic shocks. Early in 2025, as word of steep new tariffs rattled markets, Treasuries offered no safe harbour: ten-year yields climbed by around half a percentage point over the course of a week, as investors rejected American assets indiscriminately. Gone was their “convenience yield”, the dividend of seeming safe and liquid.

A diminished Treasury market would have dismal knock-on effects. Research published in 2024 by Jason Choi of the University of Toronto and colleagues suggests that America’s unique status as the issuer of safe assets saves the government more than half a percent of GDP each year in interest payments.

What is more, between 1994 and 2019, the rising share of Treasuries held by foreign central banks reduced America’s neutral interest rate—the rate at which the country can sustain full employment and low, stable inflation—by 0.5 percentage points, by one estimate. The benefits of that accrue to businesses, homeowners, states and cities across the country.

Pricing the risk of corporate bonds is getting more difficult, too. The spread between AAA-rated corporate bonds and Treasuries of the same maturity has dropped to just 0.34 percentage points on average since the beginning of 2024, compared with an average of 0.64 percentage points from 2010-19. In September two bonds issued by Microsoft offered lower yields than Treasuries of the same maturity.

Such performance is common where debt is seen as high and risky, and it is likely to become more common in America. JPMorgan Chase, a bank, reckons the coming increase in federal debt—from 100% to 120% of GDP by 2040—may reduce spreads with the most creditworthy firms by half a percentage point.

Some on America’s political right welcome a decline in the Treasury market. The Coalition for a Prosperous America, a pro-tariff lobbying group, want a “market access charge”, or a tax on many American financial assets. That would, they say, reduce demand for dollars, weakening the currency and making domestic manufacturing more competitive. In November 2024 hedge-funder Stephen Miran suggested a “user fee” be charged on foreign holdings of Treasuries; Mr Trump put him on the Fed board (he has since left).

Investors saw last year what a political attack on foreign holders of American assets might look like. An early version of Mr Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act gave the White House the authority to withhold investment income owed to foreigners in retaliation for putatively unfair taxes on American firms overseas. The threat did not apply to holders of Treasury bonds specifically, but it was a worrying portent.

A self-sabotage of Treasuries might seem crazy. But issuers of the world’s reserve assets have changed the rules before. The American government devalued the dollar against gold in 1934 and 1971, and the British government did the same with sterling, in 1931 and 1949. In each case foreign bondholders were sacrificed for the sake of domestic financial security.

If the Treasury market were to lose its special status, the consequences would be more extreme for much of the rest of the world than they would be for America. Foreign investors have relied on Treasuries as a safe asset in their portfolios, where their alternatives were far more volatile government bonds at home. They have nothing to replace Treasuries with.

The interwar period holds a troubling precedent. Britain’s position as the world’s supplier of safe assets snapped under the fiscal pressure of the first world war and the bursts of inflation that followed. But the Treasury market was not yet ready to take on the role. The era was marked by repeated financial panics, a downturn in the global economy and a fragmenting of global trade. Not having a single reliably deep reserve to turn to made all of that worse. A world where Treasuries are no longer reliable safe assets will be a world in which there are no plausible replacements at all.

The Treasury Department provides the world with something close to a public good. Mercantilist politics, nervous investors and a surge in American government debt are eroding its status. Global finance is in danger of losing its lodestar, making the job of keeping markets and economies on course a more treacherous and difficult one at home and abroad. ■

item.title: Texas is America Inc’s new centre of gravity
item.description:
Business

“Just when I thought I got him to fall in love with Tennessee, I shoulda known better than to take him back to Abilene.” So laments Ella Langley in “Choosin’ Texas”, a song that has ranked near the top of America’s music charts throughout 2026. Some of those listens may be coming from policymakers e...
item.content:encoded:
Texas is America Inc’s new centre of gravity

Business | Rodeo capitalism


“Just when I thought I got him to fall in love with Tennessee, I shoulda known better than to take him back to Abilene.” So laments Ella Langley in “Choosin’ Texas”, a song that has ranked near the top of America’s music charts throughout 2026. Some of those listens may be coming from policymakers elsewhere in the country. Much like Ms Langley, they are losing to Texas.

On May 27th ExxonMobil’s shareholders approved a plan to cut the oil giant’s ties with New Jersey and reincorporate in Texas, where it has long had its headquarters. It is not alone. According to CBRE, a property firm, at least 184 companies shifted their headquarters to Austin, Dallas or Houston between 2020 and 2025, among them Tesla, a car company, and Caterpillar, a maker of construction equipment (see chart 1).

Texas is steadily establishing itself as America Inc’s new centre of gravity. No state receives more business investment or is adding more people to its population. From 2020 to 2025 it created roughly a fifth of all net new jobs in the country.

In the early 2020s Texas was luring in remote workers fleeing high taxes, exorbitant house prices and bad policies in America’s coastal metropolises, while benefiting from the Biden administration’s subsidies for green energy and chipmaking facilities. Now the state’s dominance in energy has made it a major beneficiary of the data-centre boom. Meanwhile, its technology and finance ecosystems have been deepening. This summer it will ring in its first standalone bourse, the Texas Stock Exchange, joining outposts of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) and Nasdaq already operating in the state. (Donald Trump has called the NYSE’s new branch an “UNBELIEVABLY BAD THING” for his hometown of New York, even if his social-media venture was the first business to list on it.) The state’s appeal to yuppies is also growing with every stream of a country song. It seems there is no part of America with which Texas is not competing.

To understand its ascendancy, start in Houston, heart of the Texan energy industry. Its oil-and-gas barons have been raking in profits as a result of the Iran war. But over the past few years the state has also become a hub for green energy (see chart 2). This year it is expected to build two-fifths of all new utility-scale solar in America, a technology for which its wide-open flatlands are ideal. (One project, Tehuacana Creek, is adding 837 megawatts, making it the largest that will come online in America this year.)

This investment bonanza has caused some hiccups along the way. In 2021 Texas’s grid suffered a series of critical failures during a winter storm. But the episode led to modernisation efforts—including big investments in battery storage—that state officials hope will position the system to deal with soaring demand better than many other parts of the country. So far the signs are positive. Despite huge increases in power consumption, Texas’s retail energy prices are middling among American states. Since the crisis its grid has had only one emergency alert, notes Judd Messer of the Advanced Power Alliance, a green-energy lobbying group.

What is more, many of the data centres being built in Texas are powered off-grid, meaning they do not need to wait for an interconnection. That includes the gas-fuelled mega-project in Shackelford County commissioned by OpenAI, maker of ChatGPT, and Oracle, a wannabe hyperscaler. About half of the off-grid energy projects in America are based in Texas, says David Brown of Wood Mackenzie, a research firm.

Loose planning rules help. Most of Texas’s counties have limited control over development on land outside city limits, such as the Grimes County site where Mr Musk plans to build Terafab, a semiconductor facility the size of a European microstate. A sales-tax exemption for data centres, introduced in 2013, has further added to the appeal of building them in the state. JLL, another property firm, reckons that Texas may overtake Virginia, currently the state with the largest data-centre capacity, as soon as 2030.

Abundant energy and the freedom to build have also fuelled Austin’s rise as a hub for advanced hardware. Its “Silicon Hills” are home both to established businesses, such as Dell, a computer-maker, and to buzzy startups, such as Apptronik, a robotics firm. Venture-capital (VC) investment in Austin reached a record $7.4bn last year, according to PitchBook, a data provider (see chart 3). The city is now America’s fifth-most active for VC investment, up from tenth a decade ago. One floor of its largest startup incubator, Capital Factory, also hosts an outpost of the American army’s innovation unit.

The investment wave in Texas has helped lure the financial sector to Dallas’s “Y’all Street”. Goldman Sachs is building a $500m campus in the city with room for 5,000 employees. JPMorgan Chase, America’s biggest bank, now has more staff in Texas than in New York. There is plenty for them to do. Nasdaq’s Texas branch, which opened in March, will host SpaceX, a rocketry firm, in conjunction with its sister exchange in New York.

Corporate lawyers in Dallas and other Texan cities will be just as busy. State officials are eager to supplant Delaware as America’s corporate-law hub. In 2024 they established the Texas Business Court, presided over by expert judges capable of handling even the most complex disputes. Last year the state also introduced a measure to allow firms to prevent shareholders with a stake of less than 3% from suing them, and another to let only large shareholders put forward proxy proposals.

Those changes, along with other drawcards such as low business taxes, are luring ever more companies to Texas. Bryan Hughes, a state senator and one of the architects of the business court, predicts that the reincorporation of a business of Exxon’s size will cause a rush southwards: “The ice is broken.”

On South Congress Avenue, one of Austin’s upmarket shopping streets, long lines stretch outside shops selling cowboy boots and shiny belt buckles. They reflect another of Texas’s less-appreciated assets: its growing soft power.

Kendra Scott, a jewellery firm last valued in 2016 at over $1bn, is but one example of the state’s growing list of successful brands. In 2023 it launched Yellow Rose, a cowboy-chic sub-brand that has been expanding rapidly as the ranch aesthetic has become trendy. (Even the Princess of Wales has recently donned cowboy boots.) Rodeo style is “not just a Texas thing” any longer, says Ms Scott, founder of the brand. She points out that Louis Vuitton now sells Western-themed products and singers such as Post Malone have begun making country music.

Ms Scott’s is not the only Texan brand with national ambitions. Companies such as Yeti, a maker of supersize water bottles, and Buc-ee’s, a roadside convenience store, are fast expanding outside the state. They serve as advertisements for the Texan way of life much as surf brands did for California or preppy retailers like Ralph Lauren did for the WASPy north-east.

Texas’s growing cultural appeal is making it easier for firms to convince workers to move there, notes Richard Florida of the University of Toronto. That matters, because securing skilled workers will be crucial to Texas’s continued ascent. Cultivating homegrown talent is a big part of Texas’s economic plan, but in the short term the state will need to lure superstars from elsewhere. Abundant housing and low personal taxes only go so far. Many workers are put off by parts of the state’s political agenda. Blue enclaves help. Showy displays of lib-owning, including those gleefully pursued by Texas’s attorney-general (and Republican senatorial candidate) Ken Paxton, do not.

Texas’s success should worry those in New York and California monitoring their tax take. At the same time it has spawned a number of imitators. Legislators in North Carolina have passed a plan to get rid of its corporate-income tax by 2030. Tennessee has copied Texas’s strategy of offering firms shovel-ready mega-sites. Nevada is trying to launch its own business court. But none is close to competing with the Lone Star State, argues Michael Sury of the University of Texas at Austin. “Texas had the seeds already planted, but as we’ve started to attract more capital and firms, we’re at an inflection point.” ■

To track the trends shaping commerce, industry and technology, sign up to “The Bottom Line”, our weekly subscriber-only newsletter on global business.

item.title: BYD is losing its spark
item.description:
Business

For years visitors to the Shenzhen headquarters of BYD, the world’s largest maker of electric vehicles (EVs), have been treated to an explosive safety demonstration. As they peer into a chamber made with thick protective glass, a drill bores into a conventional EV battery, which erupts into flames. ...
item.content:encoded:
BYD is losing its spark

Business | Engine problems


For years visitors to the Shenzhen headquarters of BYD, the world’s largest maker of electric vehicles (EVs), have been treated to an explosive safety demonstration. As they peer into a chamber made with thick protective glass, a drill bores into a conventional EV battery, which erupts into flames. Then one of BYD’s signature “blade” batteries is similarly pierced—without the subsequent blast.

BYD was built around batteries. And its founder, Wang Chuanfu, created his car empire using the same rigid vertical integration that made them successful. That entails everything from running its own lithium-processing plants to training its own artificial-intelligence models. On May 28th Mr Wang unveiled a semiconductor, designed in-house, that he claimed was the world’s most powerful for self-driving.

With far fewer middlemen to deal with, BYD has managed to control costs even as they have surged for others, turning out ultra-cheap, high-quality models such as the Seagull, a compact EV that sells in China for around $10,000. Vertical integration is also credited with speeding up innovation, as engineers from different divisions collaborate on common problems. When supply bottlenecks have held rivals back, BYD has been able to step on the accelerator. It churns out new models faster than most, with several brands at different price points, some with captivating, quirky add-ons. Models from its luxury Yangwang brand can float in water or jump over potholes. One from Denza, another upmarket marque, can “crabwalk” sideways into parking spots. (It uses the brand “BYD” for its mass-market range.)

The company’s strategy has served it well. Revenue has increased ten-fold in the past decade, to $116bn last year. In 2025 it sold more cars than Elon Musk’s Tesla. Mr Wang is thought to be worth around $25bn. But the model is showing signs of weakness. Operating profit fell for the first time in four years in 2025 (see chart). In April sales fell, year on year, for the eighth month running. In the first two months of 2026, Geely ended BYD’s run of more than three years as China’s leading EV-seller, though BYD has since reclaimed top spot.

China’s EV industry as a whole has been battered by a ferocious price war that has crushed margins. Yet BYD is also starting to look out of place as the market focuses far more on software and entertainment. Young would-be customers often inspect the large entertainment display panels on the dashboard before anything else. Several challengers, such as Xpeng and Li Auto, were founded by internet bosses.

Other carmakers have been forging partnerships with tech firms. Volkswagen has bought system know-how from Xpeng. A division of Huawei, a Chinese tech giant, is selling software and entertainment systems to no fewer than five carmakers. It has helped JAC, a stodgy state-owned firm, launch a luxury EV brand called Maextro that sells for more than $100,000. Geely has been inking deals left and right, for instance with StepFun, an AI startup, for autonomous driving and with iFlytek, another AI business, for voice recognition. In September it launched a computing platform for AI models with Thundersoft, a Chinese software developer.

By contrast, BYD is keeping things in-house. Max Zhang, a member of the team developing its autonomous driving system, points out that other carmakers are at the whim of their third-party suppliers for upgrades. Keeping that control is still the most important thing for BYD, he says.

But autonomous driving is one area where the risks of BYD’s vertical integration have become clear. Missteps are more difficult to correct. BYD has been quick to deploy its system in several models, including cheaper ones, even before the technology was mature. This has drawn rare direct criticism from competitors. Yu Chengdong, a Huawei executive, has said that “so-called ‘good enough’ and ‘safe’ intelligent driving are two completely different levels.” Such remarks may explain why Mr Wang said on May 28th that BYD would be the world’s first company to cover losses from autonomous-driving accidents. Visitors to its headquarters this year are treated to a new demonstration: a sporty model spins donuts in the car park while the driver takes his hands off the wheel.

BYD still hopes its batteries will set it apart. Its latest charging technology gets its EVs near to capacity in around ten minutes. An installation at its headquarters freezes an EV at -30°C to show off its resilience. Although competitors such as CATL, the world’s biggest battery-maker, are reproducing many of its achievements, BYD believes it can stay one step ahead. Even so, it is getting ever harder to maintain an advantage from batteries alone. ■

To track the trends shaping commerce, industry and technology, sign up to “The Bottom Line”, our weekly subscriber-only newsletter on global business.

item.title: A new defence champion is rising from the Gulf

item.content:encoded:
A new defence champion is rising from the Gulf

Business | Sheikh, rattle and roll


THE PETRO-MONARCHIES of the Gulf are celebrated big spenders—not least by the West’s defence industry. Their oil wealth pays for about a fifth of global arms imports, with a shopping list ranging from fighter jets to frigates. In a noisy, volatile neighbourhood, safety comes at a price.

Now the rich rulers are nurturing their own defence industries, hoping to reduce their reliance on the West. Not surprisingly, the Iran war has hardened this ambition. Saudi Arabia intends that by 2030 half its arms budget will be spent at home, up from a quarter today, and that Saudi Arabia Military Industries (SAMI) will be in the world’s top 25 defence firms by revenue. Yet so far the state-owned enterprise, which has joint ventures with Boeing, an American aerospace giant, among others, mainly produces spare parts for American fighter jets and a few lines of armoured vehicles. Qatar’s Barzan Holdings is likewise ambitious but small.

It is in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) where momentum is strongest. In 2019 around 25 Emirati companies were merged to form the EDGE Group, a national defence champion. It has since bought majority stakes in several foreign firms, and in May agreed to acquire 80% of Costruzioni Motori Diesel, an Italian engine-maker. It has stakes of 51% in ventures with two other Italian firms, Leonardo (in a range of areas) and Fincantieri (in shipbuilding), and a partnership with Germany’s Rheinmetall (in air defence). In November it formed a joint venture with Anduril, a fast-rising American defence-tech firm, to make drones for the UAE and its allies.

Last year EDGE’s revenue topped $5bn, with “healthy” profit margins. Orders of about $8bn brought the total outstanding to more than $20bn. Hamad al-Marar, the company’s chief executive, estimates revenue will rise by a fifth over the next two years as these are fulfilled. Already it is among the world’s top three makers of precision-guided munitions.

EDGE does not aim to localise everything and anything; rather, it prioritises systems and components deemed critical or whose supply chains might prove insecure. At the same time, its ambition is growing. The firm was already focused on owning IP. Now, says an executive, it is increasingly intent on producing it, too.

EDGE’s expansion has led to a reduction in the UAE’s share of global arms imports, to 2.7% in 2021-25 from 3.5% in 2016-20, according to SIPRI, a Swedish think-tank. But the company is not only producing for its home market. In fact it exports close to three-quarters of what it makes, to countries in Latin America, Africa and Asia. Even as regional competition rises, the state of geopolitics means there will be more places to export to, Mr Marar says. In January his company signed a joint-venture deal with Barzan, and it has licensed its vehicle technology to SAMI.

The UAE’s growing defence prowess has stood it in good stead in the war. Iran has struck at the Emirates far more often than at Saudi Arabia or Qatar. About 80% of Iran’s incoming Shahed drones were tackled by Emirati products, officials say. EDGE’s electronic-warfare systems kicked into action, spotting incoming missiles and drones, and setting off jamming and spoofing, working in concert with American anti-ballistic-missile systems.

The upside is that EDGE’s technology is now combat-tested, says Mr Marar. Of course, the war has created challenges as well: supplies stuck in the blocked Strait of Hormuz, for instance, are bound to delay production plans. Still, the Emiratis’ efforts over the past few years to indigenise defence production now look farsighted. Even with powerful allies and brotherly neighbours, greater self-sufficiency is valuable. The UAE’s defence champion might just give it the edge it needs. ■

item.title: Lego, Pokémon and the future of fun
item.description:
Business

Lego executives tried valiantly to present their latest products on June 2nd amid a din of chirping, croaking and snoring. The toy giant’s newest range is part of a collaboration with Pokémon, a Japanese brand that has evolved from video game to multi-media phenomenon. Built-in chips let the creatur...
item.content:encoded:
Lego, Pokémon and the future of fun

Business | Gotta build ’em all


Lego executives tried valiantly to present their latest products on June 2nd amid a din of chirping, croaking and snoring. The toy giant’s newest range is part of a collaboration with Pokémon, a Japanese brand that has evolved from video game to multi-media phenomenon. Built-in chips let the creatures train, battle and noisily chat when put near each other.

Pokémon is the latest in a growing line of Lego tie-ups with media brands. Since the success of a Star Wars set in 1999, the Danish firm has sought licences everywhere from gaming (Nintendo) and Hollywood (Harry Potter) to sport (Formula One). Generic pirates and spacemen are increasingly squeezed off store shelves by the likes of Super Mario. Toys based on licensed intellectual property (IP) provide more than half of Lego’s $13bn annual revenue, estimates Circana, a research firm.

The brickmaker is not the only example. Hasbro’s Monopoly has versions that license everything from James Bond to Barbie. Funko, which makes the wildly popular Pop! dolls, offers likenesses based on athletes, actors and much else. Its slogan—“Everyone is a fan of something”—sums up the idea. The share of global toy sales based on licensed IP has risen from 25% to 37% in the past seven years, says Frédérique Tutt of Circana.

Lego shows how the strategy can work. Tapping into another brand’s fanbase is less risky than investing in a new line of your own. It is also more agile: last year Lego went big on “Jurassic World” sets to coincide with a new movie; this year it will capitalise on Pokémon’s 30th anniversary. IP also attracts adults, who might not buy an ordinary Lego castle but could be tempted by a $650 replica of one from “Lord of the Rings”. Changing from a kids’ company into an all-ages pop-culture brand has helped to nearly double Lego’s annual revenue since 2020, to over twice that of Mattel, its nearest rival.

Working with partners isn’t easy. Pokémon staff made weekly trips to Lego’s headquarters in Billund. Twenty-five new types of brick were needed to get details like Pikachu’s arms and Jigglypuff’s ears right. And Lego has to send licensees a cut of sales—though the generally higher prices of its branded sets suggest it is passing some of the cost on to consumers.

Fast-moving online culture also presents challenges. Julia Goldin, Lego’s marketing and product chief, says that social media make it easier than ever to spot trends—but harder to know which will endure. Creating a new Lego range takes a good 18 months, longer than the lead-time for firms making card games or plush toys. Lego’s take on “KPop Demon Hunters”, a surprise blockbuster film last summer, will not be out until later this year.

The company emphasises that it still builds its own brands. Botanicals, a newish floral range aimed at adults, will probably be its best-selling line this year. But third-party IP seems to be what its customers crave. On Lego Ideas, a forum run by the company where fans suggest new themes, requests include a “Happy Days” diner and a “Scooby-Doo” haunted house. Time for children—and perhaps adults—to make more space on the toy shelf. ■

item.title: Two American tycoons are betting big on a casino revival
item.description:
Business

Chance plays a big role in Las Vegas. But two events in the space of a week seemed to be more than just coincidence. On May 28th Tilman Fertitta, a hospitality mogul, announced that he had agreed to buy Caesars Entertainment, a chain of more than 50 casino resorts, in a deal valuing the company at $...
item.content:encoded:
Two American tycoons are betting big on a casino revival

Business | Rolling the dice


Chance plays a big role in Las Vegas. But two events in the space of a week seemed to be more than just coincidence. On May 28th Tilman Fertitta, a hospitality mogul, announced that he had agreed to buy Caesars Entertainment, a chain of more than 50 casino resorts, in a deal valuing the company at $17.6bn. Four days later Barry Diller, the high-rolling owner of People Inc, a publishing business, upped the ante with a bid for MGM Resorts that valued the casino operator at over $18bn.

It may seem a surprising time to be betting on the gambling industry, which has been on a painful losing streak. Online gaming has been disrupted by the arrival of “prediction markets” run by firms like Kalshi and Polymarket, which allow punters to bet on anything from sports results to American invasion plans. Meanwhile, bricks-and-mortar casinos have struggled as consumers have grown anxious about the state of the economy. Las Vegas, where MGM and Caesars operate glittering casino-resorts along the Strip, received 10% fewer visitors last year than at its pre-pandemic peak.

Having been dealt such a bad hand, many investors have folded. In the five years up until last week, MGM’s share price had fallen by about 15%; that of Caesars, which is more leveraged and less diversified, had dropped by nearly three-quarters. Messrs Fertitta and Diller, however, seem to have concluded that the market has now reached the bottom.

Are they right? Many in Vegas—admittedly the world capital of optimism bias—believe that the industry is about to turn a corner. The city is “hitting an inflection point” in visitors’ perception of the value it offers, says Barry Jonas of Truist, a bank which recently upgraded MGM from “hold” to “buy”.

Some long-term trends in consumer behaviour also look to be playing out in casino operators’ favour. One is the growing demand for live entertainment, something on which casino-resorts have placed big wagers in recent years. In the early 1990s gambling accounted for nearly 60% of the revenue of resorts on the Las Vegas Strip. Today it accounts for just over a third, as visitors to Sin City splash more of their cash on concerts, sports and various other diversions.

And although online betting has introduced new competition, it also presents opportunities for the gambling industry. MGM and Caesars both have betting apps which they use to acquire new customers, with the ultimate aim of luring them to spend an expensive vacation at one of their resorts. Online gambling is also helping to popularise what was once considered a taboo pursuit. As many as one in six Americans placed a bet on a sporting event last year, twice as many as two years earlier, according to polling by Ipsos.

What will MGM and Caesars’ new owners do with the properties? Following Mr Diller’s offer of $48.30 a share for MGM, the price initially rose to over $51, suggesting the market believed he would have to offer more to clinch a deal (though the price has since fallen back). If he does succeed in taking control, he may keep things at MGM much as they are: Mr Diller’s firm already owns more than a quarter of the casino operator and he has a seat on its board. The media baron, who is busy restructuring the rest of his empire, is said to get along with MGM’s current management.

Mr Fertitta’s acquisition of Caesars, which seems like a surer bet to go ahead, may also bring more continuity than change. The buyers have already said that Caesars’ boss will stay in place. But there may be benefits from tying up with Mr Fertitta’s other properties, encompassing the Golden Nugget chain of casinos and his string of hotels and restaurants, including Morton’s steakhouses and the Bubba Gump Shrimp chain. Visitors to Caesar’s Palace might soon be able to celebrate their wins with a fillet steak—or drown their sorrows in a bowl of gumbo. ■
