item.title: Nvidia wants to supercharge your laptop
item.description:
Business

For the past few years, whenever Jensen Huang, boss of Nvidia, has taken the stage, he has followed a familiar script, unveiling ever more powerful semiconductors, software and systems for running artificial intelligence in data centres. No wonder: the AI boom has sparked a spending spree on giant s...
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia wants to supercharge your laptop

Business | Chip shot


For the past few years, whenever Jensen Huang, boss of Nvidia, has taken the stage, he has followed a familiar script, unveiling ever more powerful semiconductors, software and systems for running artificial intelligence in data centres. No wonder: the AI boom has sparked a spending spree on giant server farms, and much of that money has flowed straight to the giant chipmaker. In the past four years, annual revenue at Nvidia’s data-centre division has grown from $11bn to $194bn, pushing the firm’s market value past $5trn, more than any other company ever.

But on June 1st at Computex, an annual tech-industry jamboree in Taiwan, Mr Huang did more than refresh Nvidia’s data-centre wares. He unveiled RTX Spark, a chip to be launched later this year for personal computers (PCs), built in collaboration with Microsoft, whose software they will run. Nvidia is taking on Intel and AMD, the chipmakers that dominate the segment—and is betting that the next phase of AI will play out not just in data centres, but on devices at the edge.

In recent years PCs have been one of tech’s backwaters. Evercore, an investment bank, estimates that in the past decade unit sales of chips for desktop computers have fallen by 4% a year, while those for laptops have been roughly flat. What is drawing fresh interest is the rise of “agentic” AI, software that can carry out complex tasks on its own. As it spreads, the number of tokens (the chunks of text processed by AI models) is expected to rise sharply. Model-makers and cloud providers are already straining to keep up. Offloading some work from the cloud to local devices could be cheaper and more efficient.

Nvidia argues that this will require a different sort of machine. PCs rely on central processing units (CPUs), general-purpose chips that handle everything from word processing to web browsing. CPUs may co-ordinate the work of AI agents, but the models those agents rely on need another type of chip: graphics-processing units, or GPUs, the market for which Nvidia dominates. With RTX Spark, Nvidia is combining the two types into a “superchip”. The upshot, according to Mr Huang, is that the PC is being reinvented for the first time in 40 years, replacing the old model, in which humans did most of the clicking and typing, with one in which AI agents do much of the work.

Success is far from assured. Nvidia is not a stranger to PCs; before the AI boom, it made a big chunk of its money selling GPUs for gaming machines. But in CPUs for PCs, it is a newcomer. Intel and AMD together supply more than four-fifths of all CPUs sold for PCs. As for software, Nvidia says it has worked with Microsoft for over two and a half years on the new chip. Even so, some analysts remain sceptical that developers and users will quickly embrace a new class of AI-first PC.

Yet Nvidia has plenty of advantages. For a start, it has piles of money to invest; analysts expect the company to generate roughly $200bn in free cashflow this year. It also has the clout to draw in partners and a brand that may help catch the attention of consumers. A number of the biggest PC-makers, including HP, Lenovo and Acer, have already signed up to offer the new chip in their devices.

Nvidia’s move is another sign of how fiercely contested the chip business has become, with firms venturing ever further from their original turf. In March Arm, a British designer that licenses chip blueprints to others, announced its own CPU for AI data centres; RTX Spark uses Arm’s designs for its CPU. A day after Mr Huang spoke at Computex, Lip-Bu Tan, Intel’s boss, presented his own plans. Among them was an AI chip due later this year, aimed at running models in data centres. Intel, Mr Tan said, was “going to do really well”. Mr Huang is equally confident. ■

item.title: What to read to understand your next employer
item.description:
Business

Welcome to Ungoliant! As part of your onboarding process, we encourage you to read a few books before you actually start work. That will give you the best chance of understanding our unique culture.

If a reading list seems retro, it’s not. “The Little Prince” has a special place in Netflix lore: An...
item.content:encoded:
What to read to understand your next employer

Business | Bartleby


Welcome to Ungoliant! As part of your onboarding process, we encourage you to read a few books before you actually start work. That will give you the best chance of understanding our unique culture.

If a reading list seems retro, it’s not. “The Little Prince” has a special place in Netflix lore: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry is still quoted in the streaming firm’s culture guide. The US Marines have something called “The Commandant’s Professional Reading Programme”, a kind of book club with bullets; marines are expected to read five titles a year from a list of recommendations on topics such as strategy, warfare and decision-making. “The Looming Tower”, a history of the 9/11 attacks, and (more improbably) “Impro”, a guide to improvisational theatre, have both featured on lists for Palantir employees.

Other forms of entertainment can also provide clues to how bosses want you to think. As a child Howard Schultz, the man behind Starbucks, was a big fan of the Gene Wilder version of “Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory”. When he was planning the firm’s first roastery, a premium retail outlet built around coffee, he invited a bunch of executives to his house to watch the film and use it as a source of inspiration.

At Ungoliant, you will never ever be invited to watch the boss’s favourite childhood film. Willy Wonka is not a lodestar. But if you read these books instead, you will understand our values and how we like to work.

“The Trial” by Franz Kakfa. This tale of an ordinary person who is abruptly plunged into a nightmarish world of senseless bureaucracy is less a novel, more an employee handbook.

“Catch-22” by Joseph Heller. The title of Heller’s novel is about an impossible wartime dilemma: pleading insanity as a reason to avoid flying missions is itself clear proof of sanity. At Ungoliant, if you do good work, you will be asked to move into a role managing people. If you do bad work, you will be fired. There is absolutely no way to carry on doing what you actually enjoy.

“The Waves” by Virginia Woolf. Streams of consciousness, individuals blurring into each other, entire lifetimes passing and an overpowering sense of confusion. This is the perfect introduction to office life.

“Say Nothing” by Patrick Radden Keefe. It doesn’t matter what this book is about. It’s just very good advice.

“Tomorrow and Tomorrow and Tomorrow” by Gabrielle Zevin. None of us have actually read this one but we think it must be a primer on project management.

“1984” by George Orwell. Some people apparently regard this book as dystopian, and it is true that the Party is a bit keener on sticks than carrots. But there’s a lot to learn from its core messages: that harnessing data is a source of genuine competitive advantage and that it’s better to work together towards a common purpose than pursue your own selfish aims. Winston Smith is clearly not a team player and we can all see how well that worked out for him.

“The Island of Dr Moreau” by H.G. Wells. The one thing you can say about Dr Moreau is that he dared to dream. Yes, his dream was heavily based on vivisection, and some of the consequences were rather unfortunate. But no omelette is made without breaking a few eggs. To be clear, Ungoliant has no current plans to turn animals into beast folk. But thinking differently and failing is far, far better than accepting arbitrary boundaries. Further reading: “Frankenstein”, “Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde”.

“Emma” by Jane Austen. An inveterate meddler ends up getting everything she wants. Proof that micromanaging can really pay off.

“The Secret History” by Donna Tartt. An outsider joins a tight-knit group of people who are devoted to a single mentor figure and steadily loses all sense of morality. The fact that the characters wind up paying a heavy price for their behaviour is the only thing to quibble with in this book. In all other respects, it tells you just what you can expect from your time working here.

“Wolf Hall” by Hilary Mantel. A supremely capable operator scales the organisational ladder on merit but fails to remember that his fate is in the hands of a wildly capricious boss. All Ungoliantians matter, but only one of us has 85% of the voting rights.

If you read all of these and still turn up to your first day at work, you are just the kind of employee we want. We look forward to seeing you next month. ■

item.title: American capitalism has taken an apocalyptic turn
item.description:
Business

Charles Mackay’s “Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds” (1841) is reviled by historians and revered among traders. The book is best known for its colourful passages on tulip mania in the 17th century and the South Sea bubble in the 18th. But those wanting to understand business ...
item.content:encoded:
American capitalism has taken an apocalyptic turn

Business | Schumpeter


Charles Mackay’s “Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds” (1841) is reviled by historians and revered among traders. The book is best known for its colourful passages on tulip mania in the 17th century and the South Sea bubble in the 18th. But those wanting to understand business in the 21st should instead turn to Mackay’s chapter on the “epidemic terror of the end of the world”.

Apocalyptic thinking is the strongest impulse in American capitalism today. Elon Musk, a character who could be straight from Mackay’s pages, will soon float SpaceX, a rocket company whose professed mission is to avert existential threats to humanity by establishing a colony on Mars. Mr Musk is America’s richest capitalist in part because he is its loudest Cassandra.

Mr Musk is rushing to list before two other prophets with similarly millenarian worldviews. Anthropic filed paperwork for a public offering this week. Dario Amodei, its boss, has made much of the destructive potential of his firm’s Mythos model, which has thus far been kept from the public. OpenAI, run by Sam Altman, will probably file its paperwork soon. The lab recently published a utopian plan for the social contract after (or, rather, under) AI.

American business nowadays is best segmented not by industry but eschatology. The threat of war looms nearly as large in business as that of AI. Last year Alex Karp, the boss of Palantir, wrote a book arguing that the future of the West depends on high-tech defence companies such as his own. Palmer Luckey, the founder of Anduril, another defence-tech outfit, often talks up his expectation that China will try to invade Taiwan. Every firm selling critical minerals has a compelling story for why theirs would become painfully scarce in the event of such a conflict.

Much of Wall Street is in a fatalistic mood. Investor withdrawals from hitherto unknown private-credit funds recently shook faith in all private markets. The list of financial innovations central bankers say pose “systemic” risks to the economy is so long it’s hard to believe the system hasn’t collapsed under the weight of its own anxiety. One of these, cryptocurrency, is itself an intrinsically apocalyptic endeavour, since it claims to offer protection against government control and inflation caused by Uncle Sam’s spending—on, among other things, defence.

Dates of previous calamities assume almost superstitious significance. The most read book on Wall Street last year was called “1929”. A good bet for this year is “1873”. Traders describe the stockmarket in terms of previous catastrophes. “Will 1999 turn into 2000 or 1987? Or will the clock reset back to 1996?” wrote a strategist at Deutsche Bank this week. That’s before you even consider the prospect of a 1973. And surely a 1999 would increase the likelihood of another 2008?

A millenarian economy is necessarily a paranoid one. The appearance of comets has often foretold the end of the world. Nowadays a website tracks the private jets of the super-rich, supposedly because they would flee to safety in the event of a catastrophe. Economists anxiously examine America’s remarkably resilient economic data for the mark of “K”, the idea that the economy is unsustainably propped up by the super-rich while everybody else languishes.

Permitting disputes have become questions of national survival. “It’s over. We’re done, folks,” warned the governor of Utah if America were to cede ground to China in AI (his constituents are up in arms about a massive data centre in the state backed by Kevin O’Leary, a TV star best-known for appearing on “Shark Tank”). Issues of contract have assumed cosmic importance. “I apologise, but the fate of civilisation is at stake,” Mr Musk wrote to Mr Altman as they quarrelled over the governance of OpenAI.

Debates about regulating business have taken an evangelical turn. Peter Thiel, a tech investor, says AI will summon the Antichrist in the form of authoritarian rules. “Merely regulating it is insufficient,” wrote Pope Leo XIV in a 40,000-word essay on AI last month. “It must be disarmed.” A new tune by Charli XCX, a pop star, captures both the papal and the popular mood: “Spring, Summer ’26/When the world is gonna end, no hope for any of it/Yeah, we’re walkin’ on a runway that goes straight to hell.”

If things are so dire, why are American stocks so expensive? It is often said that American markets today are a triumph of greed over fear. But this gets things the wrong way round. Firms are raising capital in proportion to the intensity of their apocalyptic vision, and are rushing to do so before the impending market collapse many of them expect.

Fear of missing out has been replaced with something more hysterical. The instinct to accumulate capital is greater if you believes your labour will soon become worthless, as some hedge-fund types think. They are betting the house. But their portfolios are often indistinguishable from those who think that is nonsense. Other than tech stocks, what else can they buy? If AI does create a new economy, it will be a fast-growing one where bonds are worth less because of inflation and higher interest rates. If it doesn’t, it will wreck the existing economy and bonds will be worth even less. Every investor is an acolyte, whether they believe it or not.

It is possible for a country to worry itself into irrelevance. But America is an experiment in terrifying yourself to riches. Predictions of total and irreversible change certainly have their uses: there is no stronger pitch to investors than claiming your business will end the world as we know it. That said, an economy which combines widespread distrust of business with a growing elite millenarianism is also a combustible one. Perhaps the danger is not 2008, 1999, 1973 or even 1873, but 1789. ■

item.title: Gen-Z socialism, from Zohran to Zack and beyond
item.description:
Finance & economics

DIFFERENT TIMES inspire different sets of leftist ideas. After the second world war, especially in Europe, socialism drew strength from heavily unionised heavy industry. It aimed not to abolish capitalism but to manage it, by nationalising utilities and redistributing income widely. After the financ...
item.content:encoded:
Gen-Z socialism, from Zohran to Zack and beyond

Finance & economics | The left in front


DIFFERENT TIMES inspire different sets of leftist ideas. After the second world war, especially in Europe, socialism drew strength from heavily unionised heavy industry. It aimed not to abolish capitalism but to manage it, by nationalising utilities and redistributing income widely. After the financial crisis of 2007-09 “millennial socialists”, as The Economist dubbed them, argued that the post-war European model had created leaders too distant from ordinary workers and too complacent about climate change. Their solution was to put workers on company boards, create employee-owned co-operatives and subsidise green technology, all to create a more durable, fairer and greener capitalism.

Now the latest wave of socialism is swelling. It is propelled partly by outrage over the humanitarian crisis caused by Israel’s war in Gaza. But for many voters Gaza has come to stand for something larger: a sense that their governments lavish attention and money on things other than their citizens’ problems at home. They desire the 21st-century version of the “square deal” offered to Americans by Theodore Roosevelt in 1904.

Today this means taking on a broken system that enriches powerful interests, the argument goes, since the modern economy screws over anyone who is not on the Forbes list. GDP is larger than ever, and yet the rent is too high, lunch costs $28 and good work is hard to find.

The new socialists thus want the state to dictate the prices of many goods and services, especially essentials such as food and rent. Where money is required it will come, almost exclusively, by squeezing the very wealthiest. It is a form of retail politics that appeals not to notions of the common good, as in prior waves of socialism, but to people’s narrow self-interest. Lower my rent! Cut my bills! Give me free buses! Protect my job! The solutions are naive, and often unworkable. But the message is so simple, and so attractive, that this Gen-Z socialism is gaining adherents across the democratic world.

Zohran Mamdani, New York’s newish mayor, is one. Katie Wilson, a fellow traveller, runs Seattle. Far-left candidates such as Graham Platner in Maine and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan hope to become senators in November’s midterm elections. In Wisconsin, another left-winger, Francesca Hong, is surging in the polls for the governorship. Betting markets put Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a socialist congresswoman from New York, second only to Gavin Newsom as the most likely Democratic nominee for president in 2028.

In Canada, Avi Lewis, the husband of Naomi Klein, a radical-left author, recently became the leader of the New Democratic Party, the third-biggest national party. In Britain the Green Party, led by Zack Polanski, is surging. In Germany, Die Linke, a left-wing outfit, is polling at its highest level in years. In France, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, an ageing leftist with youth appeal, is eyeing next year’s presidential race.

Mr Mamdani wants to freeze rents on New York’s rent-stabilised apartments, open municipally owned grocery stores selling cheap staples and offer universal free child care until the age of five. Before a recent state election Die Linke promised the abolition of “all fees from day care to university”. Mr Polanski’s Greens would impose rent controls and make buses free for young people; the Australian Greens would like to make all public transport free. “Think Costco—but run as a public service,” says Mr Lewis of his plan to create public grocery stores across Canada.

Voters rejected millennial socialism. In 2019 Jeremy Corbyn, a baby-boomer beloved of young Britons, led the Labour Party to its worst result since 1935. Bernie Sanders, that movement’s even wrinklier American face, lost the Democratic presidential nomination in 2016 and 2020. In France, Mr Mélenchon didn’t make the presidential run-off. Socialists had to look for a new approach. The post-pandemic economy has provided the opening.

In the 2020s an unprecedented chasm has emerged between the economy on paper and the economy as lived experience. Even as the rich world enjoys low unemployment, record real household incomes and soaring stockmarkets, people have rarely been so gloomy.

Since 2022 American consumer confidence has hovered around an all-time low (see chart 1). During the pandemic, 20% of Europeans thought cost-of-living pressures or housing were one of the two biggest issues facing their country. Now 36% think this, even as concerns about climate change, unemployment and immigration fade away (see chart 2). James Meadway, a socialist thinker, sums up the left’s belief: economic growth “has become detached from improvements in living standards”.

People blame both businesses and the state for their predicament. A poll in 2024 by Navigator, a research firm, found that three in five Americans thought “corporate greed” was a “major cause” of inflation. This may be why they seem greedier themselves. The share of Britons who want the government to “increase taxes and spend more” on public services has dropped sharply (see chart 3), while the share who think that income tax is “unfair” or “very unfair” has doubled since 2019. The share of Americans who believe their federal income tax is “too high” is hovering around a two-decade high. In France the share who trust the central government to use public funds well fell from 33% in 2023 to 22% in 2025.

People also increasingly blame technology, and especially artificial intelligence. They fear that mushrooming data centres will push up electricity prices and that AI powered by these server farms will take their job. More than 60% of Americans, Britons and Canadians say that AI products and services make them “nervous”, compared with a global average of around 50%. A recent poll of young adults in America found that 59% thought AI was “a threat to their job prospects”.

And if you think today’s economy is a scam, Gen-Z socialists warn, just wait for the AI-powered economy of tomorrow. A tiny number of tycoons stand to gain unprecedented power and riches at the expense of everyone else. At a recent university ceremony, students booed Eric Schmidt, a former chief executive of Google, every time he mentioned the dreaded two letters.

So what do people want done about all this? Voters are, on paper, less socialist than a few years ago. After jumping to a peak of 5% in 2018-21, the share of Americans who described themselves as “extremely liberal” has fallen to 3.4%. Yet this is not because people have become more right-wing, but because they have lost interest in -isms. A poll by Harvard University’s Institute of Politics found that among young Americans, support for both capitalism and socialism fell sharply between 2020 and 2025 (see chart 4).

In place of ideology, people want someone to raise their incomes and cut their costs. Not since 1975 have so many Americans wanted government action to “improve the standard of living” of the poor, according to the General Social Survey, a long-running poll. They want someone to stop AI from wrecking society.

An influential group of socialist academics provides the intellectual ballast for these views. The work of Isabella Weber of the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, suggests that businesses’ pricing power means that the modern economy serves executives and shareholders better than it does ordinary people. In a paper last year Ms Weber and her colleagues analysed companies’ earnings calls, finding that many firms took advantage of inflation to “protect or even increase profits”.

Many economists point out that wage increases, not price gouging, have driven much recent inflation. Nonetheless Ms Weber’s ideas, along with associated ones such as the “K-shaped economy”, where the rich win and everyone else loses, have gained traction.

Others go further, suggesting that economic growth can never give people what they really need. Jason Hickel (an anthropologist) and Kohei Saito (a philosopher) argue, among other things, that GDP growth is socially destructive, forcing people to work too hard to make ends meet. Mr Saito’s “Slow Down: The Degrowth Manifesto” was a hit in Japan, selling more than 500,000 copies. Mr Hickel’s ideas are vague, but they are hip among European politicians; in 2023 Ursula von der Leyen, head of the European Commission, spoke at a “beyond growth” jamboree at the European Parliament.

In response to these political and intellectual developments, Gen-Z socialist politicians are trying out a new message. First, chuck out “woke” talking-points that, in a world of unprecedented anger about the economy and distaste for ideology, feel less urgent. No more talk of “structural racism” or DEI. The “climate crisis”, the ultimate collectivist problem, gets relatively little airtime—even among Mr Polanski’s Greens. Democrats have gone quiet about a “Green New Deal”. Mr Platner even vows to abolish federal taxes on petrol, something unthinkable for a climate-cuddling millennial-socialist politician. Traditional tax-and-spend, the bedrock of old socialist thought, is also out.

Gen-Z socialism is instead all about making life more affordable and jobs more secure, especially against AI. Proponents favour just about anything that provides immediate relief over long-term investment projects with uncertain returns. Some want free public transport. Most love rent controls. Virtually all pledge to make child care free. Until what appeared to be a narrow defeat in a primary on June 2nd, Tom Steyer campaigned for governor of California on “a jobs guarantee for the AI era”, promising “good-paying jobs and benefits for workers impacted by AI”. Mr Lewis would pause data-centre construction in Canada and opposes “any attempts to replace public servants with chatbots”.

The sharpest intellectual break between the Gen-Z socialists and their predecessors is in who pays for all these perks and protections. Leftists of yore envisaged broad-based tax increases. In the late 2010s Mr Sanders suggested levying a 4% surcharge on incomes over $29,000 a year (the vast majority of American households). To the extent that they propose tax rises, the new socialists focus entirely on the uber-rich. Mr Polanski wants an annual tax of 1% on wealth over £10m ($13m) and 2% over £1bn (Britain has just 100 or so billionaires). Mr Mamdani is implementing an annual surcharge on some luxury residential properties. Washington state is adopting a “millionaire’s tax” of 9.9% on earnings over $1m.

Additional money will, the theory goes, come from making government more efficient. Verdant, Mr Meadway’s think-tank, which is close to the Greens, has argued for a “DOGE of the left”, named after Elon Musk’s short-lived effort to eliminate wasteful federal spending under Donald Trump. On May 28th Mr Mamdani promised COGE—the Commission on Government Efficiency—for his city.

Most of these ideas are batty. Rent controls fail to make housing more affordable by discouraging investment in the sector, which in turn raises rents by constricting supply. Trying to stop AI will cause investment and jobs to move elsewhere. Efficiency savings are great on paper but hard to find in practice: just ask Mr Musk. And relying so heavily on taxing plutocrats is risky: there simply are not that many of them and they can move (as some have from California in anticipation of a potential extra tax on billionaires).

Regardless, plenty of non-socialists are entertaining policies to make Mr Mamdani proud. Middle-of-the-road Labourites are toying with price caps on groceries, centrist Democrats have proposed tax cuts for anyone outside the top few per cent of high earners and even MAGA Republicans are partial to pauses in data-centre construction. Whether or not more Gen-Z socialists succeed at the polls, Gen-Z socialism is not going away.■

item.title: 股市能否消化SpaceX、Anthropic和OpenAI？
item.description:
Finance & economics

They promise to be the biggest stockmarket debuts in history. On June 11th SpaceX reportedly hopes to raise $75bn from investors, by issuing shares that will begin trading on the Nasdaq exchange the next day. Elon Musk’s rocketry firm will probably soon be followed by two other mammoth listings. Ant...
item.content:encoded:
股市能否消化SpaceX、Anthropic和OpenAI？

财经 | 超级IPO这些公司有望成为历史上规模最大的股市首秀。据报道， SpaceX 希望于 6 月 11 日通过发行股票从投资者那里筹集 750 亿美元，这些股票将于次日在纳斯达克交易所开始交易。埃隆·马斯克的火箭公司很可能很快就会有另外两家大型公司上市。人工智能实验室 Anthropic 于 6 月 1 日提交了首次公开募股的草案文件；其竞争对手 OpenAI 预计也将很快跟进。有传闻称，这两家公司各自寻求高达 600 亿美元的资金。这三家超级IPO 合计可能在未来几个月内使美国上市公司的市值增加多达 4 万亿美元。

股市究竟将如何应对？头条新闻预测将出现“交易狂潮”。全球最大在线交易平台之一 Interactive Brokers 的首席策略师史蒂夫·索斯尼克（Steve Sosnik）警告称，这些上市带来了“生存风险”。一个特别的担忧是，股票指数编制机构将允许这三家巨无霸快速纳入其基准指数。这将促使拥有数万亿美元资产的追踪基金在这些新股发行几天后就买入。在立即耗尽大量买家之后，还会剩下谁呢？

答案是：在一个极其深厚且流动性强的市场中，还有众多投资者。尽管超级IPO 的供应量前所未有，但美国非凡的股市将能够消化它。不过，在接下来的几年里，预计会出现一些消化不良。

首先，将超级IPO 的规模放在背景中看。按名义价值计算，首次上市募资纪录由沙特阿美（Saudi Aramco）保持，该公司于 2019 年在利雅得上市时筹集了 290 亿美元（按今天的货币计算为 380 亿美元）。SpaceX、Anthropic 和 OpenAI 共同的目标是筹集约 2000 多亿美元。然而，这在美国证券交易所中只是一个舍入误差。广泛的罗素 3000 指数中的公司总市值为 77 万亿美元；范围较窄（但追踪更广泛）的标普 500 指数中的大公司市值为 65 万亿美元。

因此，指数基金的投资者不会立即看到他们的投资组合发生太大变化。尽管纳斯达克已将指数纳入前的“成熟期”缩短至 15 个交易日，而富时罗素（FTSE Russell）已将其等待时间缩短至五天（据报道标普道琼斯也在考虑类似举措），但大多数股票指数仅根据公司已公开发行交易的价值（“自由流通量”）对公司进行加权。对于 SpaceX 而言，这意味着仅是其 6 月份计划发行的约 750 亿美元股票——因此其在标普 500 指数中的初始权重约为 0.1%。纳斯达克 100 指数是个例外，它已修改规则，将公司权重提高至其自由流通量的三倍，这显然是为了吸引马斯克先生。即便如此，SpaceX 在这个 40 万亿美元指数中的初始权重可能仅为 0.5% 左右。

随着更多股票被释放用于交易，这种情况将会改变。美国所有上市的科技巨头的自由流通量均高于 85%（见图表 1）；最低的是 Meta，该公司于 2012 年上市，其创始人马克·扎克伯格仍持有其 13% 的股份。起初，SpaceX、Anthropic 和 OpenAI 的 IPO 招股说明书中的“锁定期”条款将阻止公司内部人士和早期投资者出售他们现有的股份并增加自由流通量。然而，随着时间的推移，这些条款将会到期，价值数万亿美元的新股将进入市场。SpaceX 计划分批次释放其锁定的股票。如果其 I...

item.title: 印度人现在可以押注季风了
item.description:
Finance & economics

BY THE MIDDLE of June Mumbai, India’s financial capital, should be drenched. The south-west monsoon, the seasonal storm which provides most of the year’s water in South Asia, will bring torrential downpours to the city. Street food-hawkers and builders will curse. Slum-dwelling migrant workers may h...
item.content:encoded:
印度人现在可以押注季风了

财经 | 天气市场到 6 月中旬，印度金融中心孟买应该已经湿透了。西南季风是南亚一年中大部分降水的来源，它将给这座城市带来倾盆大雨。街头小吃摊贩和建筑工人会咒骂。住在贫民窟的农民工可能会回村等待雨季过去。与此同时，一些商人和金融家会拍打着装满卢比的潮湿口袋。5 月 29 日，印度国家商品及衍生品交易所（NCDEX）允许交易者开始对今年孟买季风每个月的降水量是否比过去 30 年的平均水平更湿或更干下注。

天气衍生品根据某些明确定义的气象测量值进行支付，自 20 世纪 90 年代中期以来在美国就已存在。早期美国能源公用事业放松管制导致了一个利基市场——温度衍生品，公司可以用它来对冲“致冷度日”（空调需求飙升时）或“致热度日”（家庭和企业启动暖气时）的风险。

与传统保险形式相比，持有人无需证明自己遭受了损失。相反，当满足某些预先约定的参数时，衍生品合约会自动触发。这些参数可以是特定地点（通常是官方气象站）记录的门槛温度、风速或其他变量。这避免了资金在到达最需要的地方时出现长时间延迟。去年，牙买加政府在飓风梅丽莎的中心气压和风暴路径符合该国发行的“巨灾债券”定义的标准后，获得了 1.5 亿美元的赔付。

降雨衍生品不太常见。位于以刺骨寒风闻名的城市的芝加哥商品交易所，于 2011 年推出了降雨、降雪和霜冻衍生品，但因缺乏需求于 2014 年废止。在富裕国家，农民是此类保护最明显的受益者，他们通常依赖农作物保险和其他更传统的工具。印度的大量小农不太可能急于购买孟买季风衍生品（尤其是因为他们关心的是季风对印度-恒河平原某处他们小块土地的影响，而不是沿海大都市）。

相反，NCDEX 预计会从大公司那里获得客户。拥有农业贷款组合的银行可能是买家之一。水坝从整个流域蓄水的水电公司可能是另一类。它建议，太阳能发电商可能是卖家。对冲基金也可能是卖家。

无论哪一方签订合约，都必须准备好被雨淋透。天气衍生品比股票期权或商品期货更难定价。用于定价传统衍生品的金融数学不起作用，因为没有基础资产。建模者必须依赖天气预报。对于降雨，由于对微小的大气变化很敏感，准确预测比预测温度更难。试图预测季风降雨的气象学家需要应对“爆发”（云层突然在一个地点倾泻雨水）和“变幻莫测”（陆地和空气之间的反馈可能导致降雨时间和强度的突然变化）。

NCDEX 可能一开始就关注了错误的气候相关风险。温度似乎与...

item.title: 欧洲电力市场权力过大
item.description:
Finance & economics

WHEN EUROPEAN regulators were tweaking the continent’s wholesale electricity markets some years ago, they added a price floor to short-circuit trading snafus. At minus €500 ($580) per megawatt-hour (MWh), it was more of a price basement. It was set so low in order to be triggered only in exceptional...
item.content:encoded:
欧洲电力市场权力过大

财经 | 负电价峰值几年前，当欧洲监管机构调整欧洲大陆的批发电市场时，他们为短路交易故障增加了一个价格下限。设定为每兆瓦时（MWh）-500 欧元（-580 美元），这更像是一个价格底线。它设置得如此之低，以便仅在特殊情况下触发。5 月 1 日，当明媚的阳光和强风遇上享受公共假日的欧洲人对电力的低需求时，似乎相当普通。然而，德国的批发电价达到了每兆瓦时 -499 欧元。如果这转化为零售价格，你给电动汽车充电可以赚到 50 欧元。

对经济学家来说，数字零并不是特别特殊。如果需要负数价格才能使市场出清，那就随它去吧。当阳光明媚、风吹拂时，太阳能发电厂和风力发电场以接近零的边际成本发电。但因为这未必是人们在需要电力的时候，而且停止发电的成本很高，所以他们可能需要付钱给某人来吸收多余的电力。随着过去几年更多可再生能源接入欧洲电网，批发电市场中的买家（如公用事业公司和重工业）被付钱来吸纳电力的时间开始增加。

显然，负电价为任何能够储存电力并在需求恢复时以高于零的价格出售的人提供了强大的激励。在阳光明媚的加利福尼亚，电池正在取代化石能源以覆盖白天充电后的晚间需求峰值，负电价的小时数去年开始下降。在欧洲大部分地区，尽管有五一劳动节，负电价小时数开始趋于平稳（见图表 1）。市场终于开始适应了。

2025 年，欧洲的电池装机容量增加了 33,000 兆瓦时，达到约 90,000 兆瓦时（见图表 2）。这足以储存整个欧洲（包括英国）平均每 15 分钟产生的电量。研究公司 BloombergNEF 预测，今年容量将再增加 55,000 兆瓦时，足以吸收大约另外十分钟的发电量。

终端电力使用也正在成功转移到一天中更便宜的时间段。更好地反映批发电市场价格的动态电价越来越受欢迎，尤其是对热泵和电动汽车的车主而言。自 2025 年 1 月起，德国供应商被要求向客户提供至少一种动态电价。一项丹麦研究发现，尽管普通家庭大多不会根据价格变化调整需求，但用电量大的家庭会调整。另一项研究查看了 2015-2019 年的德国数据，当时受可变电价影响的主要是工业等大用户，发现每兆瓦时约 25 欧元的价格变化导致了约 4% 的需求变化。咨询公司麦肯锡最近的一项分析估计，如果欧洲的商业和工业消费者能够利用可变电价，到 2030 年他们每年可以节省 80 亿欧元。

电子可以跨越空间和时间移动。这需要强大的电网。欧洲姗姗来迟地开始认真扩大电网。去年瑞典和芬兰之间安装的一条新电缆是解释为什么这两个国家负电价小时数（类似于加利福尼亚）已经在下降的一个因素。法国和西班牙之间的比斯开湾互联电缆正在建设中，预计于 2028 年完工。2025 年，德国批准了...

item.title: 想知道未来？别相信股市
item.description:
Finance & economics

“If economists wished to study the horse,” a dismal scientist once joked, “they wouldn’t go and look at horses. They’d sit in their studies and say to themselves: ‘What would I do if I were a horse?’” But at least horses tend to be spared such attention; finance types are not. And one economic idea ...
item.content:encoded:
想知道未来？别相信股市

财经 | 梧桐树专栏“如果经济学家想研究马，”一位沉闷的科学家曾开玩笑说，“他们不会去看马。他们会坐在书房里对自己说：‘如果我是一匹马，我会怎么做？’”但至少马通常不会受到这种关注；金融人士则不然。有一个经济思想尤其容易让他们不耐烦地哼着鼻子，问引用它的人是否去过交易大厅。

这就是有效市场假说，其正式版本认为，投资者总体上会完美且及时地将新信息纳入资产价格。引用该假说的人通常可能意味着更强烈的含义：因此，市场提供了对公司基本面（如企业盈利）的最佳可能预测。换句话说，价格总是正确的，如果真由经济学家像马一样小跑着做出所有决定，那确实会是这样。

如今，这种柏拉图式的理想感觉尤其遥远。散户交易者争相购买 meme 股票，推高股价只是为了打击卖空者。GameStop（一家病态的视频游戏销售商，在 2020 年被选中享受这种青睐）的股价仍然是当时的 20 多倍。它们的表现与英伟达（迄今为止人工智能革命的最大受益者）几乎一样好。英伟达的科技巨头同行们正在竞相发行新股并出售给公众——这明确表明他们认为牛市接近顶峰。然而，投资者仍在愉快地涌入。

那些确实参观过马厩的金融经济学家近半个世纪以来一直知道，如果新信息是唯一推动市场的因素，那么市场的波动性会大得多。2013 年获得诺贝尔奖的罗伯特·席勒（Robert Shiller）在 1979 年发表的一篇论文中展示了债券收益率的这种情况，并在 1981 年的论文中展示了股票价格的情况。在他研究的大约一百年的数据中，股票价格多次下跌，跌幅远超过即使是萧条级别的经济低迷所证明的合理性。这使得投资者仅基于对其股息的冷静预测来定价股票的说法变得不可信。

最近，席勒先生的知识继承者帮助解释了原因——除了人们偶尔倾向于逃离并加入踩踏之外。最令人信服的理论，越来越多地被研究人员和有学术头脑的投资者所接受，是“无弹性市场假说”，由哈佛大学的泽维尔·加贝克斯（Xavier Gabaix）和芝加哥大学的拉尔夫·科伊延（Ralph Koijen）提出。其核心是，股价并非由投资者预期的股息（或盈利）决定，而是受到资金流的显著和持久冲击。加贝克斯和科伊延估计，用新现金购买 1 美元股票的人会将整体股市市值推高 3 至 8 美元。

为了理解原因，想象三种类型的投资者。一种是追逐回报者，他们在股票大涨时买入更多，在价格下跌时卖出（想想散户交易者或趋势跟踪对冲基金）。第二种维持固定的资产配置：比如 60% 的股票和 40% 的债券（想想养老金计划）。第三种是价值投资者，只对在崩盘后以最低价买入股票感兴趣（想想沃伦·巴菲特）。眯起眼睛看，这种风格化的组合看起来很像主宰现实市场的群体。重要的是，任何套利者——有效市场爱好者想象他们可以消除扭曲并根据基本面重新定价资产——都很少，一...

item.title: 一些亿万富翁缴税太少
item.description:
Finance & economics

Suppose you are the billionaire founder of Veblen Luxe SA, a European company selling solid-gold luggage tags. How should you organise your financial affairs? One option would be to hold your Veblen shares directly. But then you must pay income tax immediately when the company pays you dividends.

Y...
item.content:encoded:
一些亿万富翁缴税太少

财经 | 自由交流专栏假设你是一家销售纯金行李牌的公司 Veblen Luxe SA（欧洲公司）的亿万富翁创始人。你应该如何安排你的财务事务？一个选择是直接持有你的 Veblen 股票。但这样一来，当公司向你支付股息时，你必须立即缴纳所得税。

你的会计师可能会告诉你，将股票放入你的控股公司 Hespérides S.à r.l 更明智。在控股公司中，股息可以累积而不会触发大量所得税账单。确实，你不能花这笔现金。但它仍然可以用于投资和一些开支。如果你说服一家银行以你的 Hespérides 股票为抵押借给你生活费，并且股息的累积速度快于你的债务，你可能可以不断借款并无限期地推迟缴纳所得税。

正是这种安排，巴黎经济学院的加布里埃尔·祖克曼（Gabriel Zucman）在他的短篇新书《我们需要对亿万富翁征税》中瞄准了目标。本专栏作者为我们的“内部经济学”节目采访了祖克曼先生，他可以说已经超越了他的同胞和曾经的合著者托马斯·皮凯蒂（Thomas Piketty），成为各地左派最喜欢的经济学家。他最新的论点是，控股公司允许超级富豪以远低于大多数公众的税率纳税，甚至那些支持单一税率（而非强烈累进税率）的人也应该支持对财富征收新税以创造公平的竞争环境。

例如，根据祖克曼的计算，在他的祖国法国，控股公司允许亿万富翁缴纳约 25% 的所得税，包括在全球缴纳的企业税。相比之下，普通法国人的全面有效税率为 51%。祖克曼认为这是一种不公正，并提议将超级富豪的年度税单补足至其净值的至少 2%。去年他在法国推动了这样的征税。

控股公司对欧洲税务机构来说比对美国国税局更成问题。自 1934 年以来，美国对个人控股公司的未分配收入征收 20% 的税，此前公众对富豪银行家 J.P. 摩根连续两年不缴纳所得税感到愤怒。尽管如此，祖克曼表示，罗斯福的解决方案并不完整。他指出，沃伦·巴菲特的上市控股公司伯克希尔·哈撒韦自 1967 年以来就没有宣布过现金股息。收益累积起来，免征所得税。

富有的美国人也可以通过借贷抵押增值资产来维持生活方式。当他们去世时，他们的继承人受益于“递增基础”，该基础在继承股票时忽略所有之前的资本收益。如果资产增值足够快，并且利润被再投资，理论上一个王朝可以永远避免缴纳所得税和资本利得税。祖克曼表示，美国最富有的 400 人（出现在福布斯富豪榜上的人）支付的税率是 24%，而普通公民的税率是 30%。

祖克曼的工作经常引起争议，因为财富税在经济学家中不受欢迎，并且他的数据经常存在分歧。他的最新研究也引发了一场数据争议。国会机构联合税收委员会的 David Splinter 表示，祖克曼和他的合著者低估了美国亿万富翁缴纳的税额。Splinter 对资本收益、福布斯财富在家庭成员之间的分配方式以及支付给州和地方政府的税款做出了不同的假设。他还将所有美国人的收入转移纳入考虑...

item.content:encoded:
农业技术投资正在增长

科学 | 食品技术全球农业创新投资正在上升。根据风险投资公司Agfunder的一份报告，2025年农业科技初创公司的资金达到162亿美元。其中，90亿美元用于提高农场产量的新研究，而2016年这一数字为25亿美元。

这一增长恰逢其时。近年来粮食市场受到波动困扰，先是全球疫情，然后是乌克兰战争，现在是中东的新战争。此外，全球变暖正在导致干旱、土壤盐渍化以及日益不稳定和极端天气。然而，粮食生产的基本原理上一次全面改革是在20世纪中期。

幸运的是，不确定性有助于推动颠覆性技术。由于新冠疫情，2021年全球农业食品技术投资激增，从2019年的220亿美元上升到550亿美元的高点。“波动对想吃东西的人很糟糕，但对技术采用有好处，”专注于食品和农业技术的荷兰风险投资公司Anterra Capital的管理合伙人Adam Anders说。

上个月底，在荷兰瓦赫宁根大学及研究中心举行的F&A Next聚会上，有600多名农业科技精英和投资者（包括200多家初创公司）参加，出现了几个主题。创新者正在基于对自然界中保护植物的分子更深入的理解，开发模仿自然界中发现的分子农药。受到个性化医疗兴起的启发，他们还在根据植物的遗传学和特定环境条件，设计针对单个田地的定制化肥、农药和其他作物辅助剂。

“关于可持续发展的焦点正在从‘我们应该保护环境’转向‘由于气候变化，价格将飙升’，”荷兰工业生物技术加速器Planet-B.io的Cindy Gerhardt说。“这不再是关于防止气候变化。而是关于应对它并寻找解决方案，否则价格将会涨得太高。”

对一些人来说，这意味着通过开发替代自20世纪中期绿色革命以来占主导地位的合成农药和化肥的产品来提高产量和减少损失。根特大学衍生公司B-COS正在通过基因工程改造细菌，使其生产化学上类似几丁质的分子，几丁质是一种存在于昆虫外骨骼和真菌细胞壁中的化合物。喷洒了这些分子的番茄和马铃薯植物会被欺骗，以为自己受到攻击，并激活其天然防御机制来对抗病原体。B-COS正在将这种方法应用于两种新产品：一种用于提高生长和耐旱性，另一种据称可以减少40-50%的疾病。

不可避免的是，初创公司正在探索人工智能带来的机遇。许多人认为它将加速这个历史上改革缓慢的行业的颠覆。“它将帮助农民将田间每平方米的情况与天气预报、碳捕获和消费者需求等联系起来，”Anders先生说。

这种“精准农业”的总体思路是收集大量数据，从单个田地的环境条件（湿度、紫外线水平、温度等）到土壤中存在的细菌和病原体的基因序列，再到植物的基因序列……（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

As its engines ignited a series of flashes could be seen. Then the entire rocket detonated, leaving ...
item.content:encoded:
火箭爆炸；登月计划也随之破灭

科学 | 蓝色起源火箭发射总是壮观，但这次非同寻常。5月28日，杰夫·贝佐斯旗下的火箭公司蓝色起源在佛罗里达州卡纳维拉尔角测试其一枚新格伦火箭。当引擎点燃时，可以看到一系列闪光。然后整个火箭爆炸，在发射场上空留下一团愤怒的蘑菇云。

不久之后，蓝色起源以官方的航天语言宣布遭遇了一次“异常”。贝佐斯先生证实没有人受伤。但这次爆炸照亮了十几英里外的夜空，并摧毁了该公司唯一可用的发射台，可能是自1969年苏联大型N1火箭在发射时爆炸以来航天领域最大的一次爆炸。

这次爆炸对蓝色起源来说是一个重大挫折，该公司在多年缓慢进展后似乎刚刚步入正轨。这也让贝佐斯创立的另一家公司亚马逊头疼，该公司正试图将其卫星互联网企业Leo（旨在与埃隆·马斯克的Starlink竞争）送入轨道。此外，它可能推迟美国国家航空航天局的登月计划。就在爆炸前两天，美国航天局在一次精心准备的新闻发布会上详细介绍了其永久月球基地的计划，其中蓝色起源占据突出位置。

在测试新火箭时，爆炸并不罕见。但发射台上的爆炸会摧毁昂贵的地面硬件以及火箭本身。2016年，马斯克的火箭公司SpaceX建造的一枚火箭在卡纳维拉尔角爆炸，该公司花了15个月修复损坏。SpaceX可以使用第二个发射台，因此事故并没有使其火箭停飞。蓝色起源没有。

损坏的全部程度尚不清楚。事后照片显示，一台被毁的运输-起竖车（将火箭运送到发射台并直立竖起以便发射的巨型车辆）、一座避雷塔的残骸以及另一座塔的严重损坏。蓝色起源的老板Dave Limp在X上写道，附近的推进剂和水箱似乎没有受损，距离发射台不远的机库内的一个助推级也没有受损。然后他为蓝色起源设定了年底前重新发射的目标。

在此期间，不仅仅是蓝色起源会遭受损失。2022年，亚马逊签署了有史以来最大的火箭发射合同，为其Leo卫星网络预订了多达83次发射，其中最多27次由蓝色起源执行。Leo计划发射3000多颗低轨道卫星，从太空提供互联网接入。（Starlink已经拥有约10000颗。）该公司正在大力投资。今年4月，它以116亿美元收购了另一家卫星运营商Globalstar（苹果是其客户），部分原因是为了获得其宝贵的无线电频谱权。

Leo已经晚了。亚马逊的许可证要求其在7月前部署一半星座，这是一个不可能完成的任务（该公司正在争取延期）。现在它会更晚。蓝色起源计划为亚马逊执行12次任务，另有15次可选。

在最坏的情况下，部署速度可能放缓至爬行。在其83次预定发射中，亚马逊预订了38次使用联合发射联盟的Vulcan Centaur火箭。Vulcan Centaur使用与New Glenn相同的由蓝色Origin制造的BE-4发动机。如果爆炸追溯到发动机问题，那么Vulcan Centaur也可能最终停飞。

然后是NASA，它认为自己正在与时间赛跑登月……（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

The technology is cheap, easy to use and accessible, with groups like Hizbullah enthusiastically deploying small quadcopters to hit Israeli tanks. ...
item.content:encoded:
如何击落廉价低空飞行的无人机

科学 | 寂静之夜小型无人机无处不在。不仅在乌克兰，还飞越美国和英国本土的空军基地，并袭击中东各地的目标。这项技术廉价、易用且容易获得，像真主党这样的组织积极部署小型四旋翼无人机攻击以色列坦克。更糟糕的是，现有的防空传感器主要设计用于探测载人飞机和导弹等更大威胁。

因此，挑战在于开发能够探测小型低空飞行无人机的系统，这些无人机像鸟一样可能掠过树梢并在其他杂波中穿梭。一种方法是重新设计雷达系统。另一种方法涉及巧妙地使用声学技术。

雷达发射无线电波脉冲并检测返回的反射波。它们在夜间和恶劣天气下同样有效，并且能探测到空中的任何物体。但是，智库RUSI的电子战专家Thomas Withington说，雷达通常会过滤掉小型低空飞行的物体，这些物体通常被认为是鸟。

位于华盛顿州柯克兰的Echodyne公司正在开发一种更智能的替代方案。该公司老板Eben Frankenberg说，其雷达使用三项独特创新来识别“更小、更慢、更低”的威胁。

大多数现代雷达系统使用固态发射器阵列（类似LED的器件，发射无线电波而非光）产生波束，而不是曾经是标准的移动天线盘。这些有效但昂贵。Echodyne的变通方法是使用少量发射器与专门的天线相结合，调整它们发射的波。这适用于低功耗、低成本、短距离工作的系统。Frankenberg先生声称他们的雷达比传统系统便宜一个数量级。

Echodyne的雷达还快速改变其脉冲的“波形”，即长度、强度和频率。这使得波束在扫过天空时可以在模式之间切换。Frankenberg先生说，不同的波形可用于探测目标，例如在空旷空间或以建筑物等繁忙背景为背景。一些波形旨在探测旋转的旋翼叶片，这是区分无人机和鸟的好方法。

最后，该系统使用机器学习模型对其跟踪的物体进行分类。它学习与每种空中轨迹类型（从鸟到气球、四旋翼、固定翼飞机）相对应的模式，从而提高可靠性。这对于从杂波中提取微弱信号特别有用，例如在风中摇曳的植被背景下飞行的无人机。

这些技术使Echodyne的EchoShield雷达（一台笔记本电脑大小的设备）能够探测、跟踪和分类甚至小到约五公里范围内的微型无人机。跟踪精度足以将摄像头或武器对准移动的无人机。

另一种搜寻无人机的方法是使用声音，这是乌克兰首创的方法。乌克兰的田野和森林中布满了麦克风，监听俄罗斯无人机的嗡嗡声。总部位于多伦多的初创公司Prandtl Dynamics一直在研究进一步开发声学技术的方法，并声称其设备可以在隐藏的无人机甚至通电之前就揭示其存在。

这是一个非凡的技巧。Prandtl的系统名为Dome，它会发出听不见的超声波脉冲。如果该区域有无人机，这种“声学询问”会使其电子和机械组件振动，产生特征性的吱吱声……（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

item.title: 你应该使用睡眠追踪器吗？
item.description:
Science & technology

Nearly half of all Americans and around 40% of Britons now use a smartwatch, smart ring, phone app or another similar device to track their sleep. Are these gadgets accurate—and do their users get a better night’s rest?

Not getting enough sleep can cause all manner of health problems, from dementia...
item.content:encoded:
你应该使用睡眠追踪器吗？

科学 | 信息灵通现在，近一半的美国人和约40%的英国人使用智能手表、智能戒指、手机应用程序或其他类似设备来追踪睡眠。这些小玩意准确吗？它们的使用者能获得更好的夜间休息吗？

睡眠不足会导致从痴呆症到糖尿病等各种健康问题。发表在《自然》杂志上的一项新研究发现，人们的睡眠时长与生物衰老标志物之间存在U形关系。研究人员使用了英国生物样本库（UK Biobank）的数据，该数据库包含约50万人的健康和生活方式信息。每晚睡眠时间在6.4至7.8小时之间的人，大脑和身体的衰老速度似乎比睡眠时间更长或更短的人更慢。

睡眠追踪器有望帮助人们达到这个最佳点。应用程序通常记录运动声音，有时从音频中推断呼吸频率。智能手表记录运动并使用光电容积描记法——通过向皮肤发射低强度光并检测反射量来测量血流量。这用于估计心率和呼吸频率。戒指通常也会测量皮肤温度。

大多数追踪器非常擅长区分睡眠和清醒状态。几项研究将它们与多导睡眠图（polysomnography）进行了比较，多导睡眠图使用电极记录眼球运动、大脑活动、肌肉张力和心率，是测量睡眠的金标准。2024年发表在专业期刊《传感器》（Sensors）上的一篇论文测试了三款流行的可穿戴追踪器，发现它们在整个夜间区分睡眠和清醒状态时，与多导睡眠图的一致性约为95%。

在识别不同睡眠阶段时，追踪器的准确性较低。一个好的夜晚需要在快速眼动睡眠和几个非快速眼动睡眠阶段之间循环。可穿戴设备在睡眠阶段分类上与多导睡眠图的一致性仅为约50-80%。哈佛医学院的睡眠科学家Rebecca Robbins参与了其中一项研究，她说这相当于C+到B+的成绩。虽然不算很好，但许多设备仍将这些指标纳入其睡眠分数的计算中。

尽管追踪器存在缺陷，但大多数睡眠研究人员和治疗师对其持积极态度。Robbins博士说，它们让人们对自己睡了多长时间有了更客观的认识（并可能揭示他们实际上睡眠充足）。此外，它们似乎确实改善了睡眠习惯。在美国睡眠医学学会的一项调查中，55%报告使用睡眠追踪器的成年人表示，他们在从数据中学习后改变了行为。2020年发表在《临床睡眠医学杂志》上的一项小型研究发现，佩戴睡眠追踪器一周可以改善自我报告的睡眠质量。

然而，过多的数据也有缺点。与努力健康饮食或锻炼不同，在睡眠上投入更多思考和精力可能会适得其反。多达30%的睡眠追踪者报告对他们收集的数据感到焦虑，研究人员称这种现象为“完美睡眠症”。对睡眠质量差的担忧是失眠最常见的原因之一；只有财务忧虑更常让人彻夜难眠。但睡眠数据不值得让你失眠，因为有一种替代睡眠追踪的方法：你醒来时是否感到休息充分是衡量夜间睡眠质量的最佳指标。■

在免费、循证的健康和福祉指南之后……（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

item.title: 你一天会想到亚历山大大帝几次？
item.description:
Culture

How do you measure the greatness of Alexander the Great? Perhaps by the size of the empire he conquered (it stretched 4,800 kilometres, from Athens to India). Or the speed with which he conquered it (about a decade). Or the cities he founded (between six and 17, many called “Alexandria”).

Though, a...
item.content:encoded:
你一天会想到亚历山大大帝几次？

文化 | 亚历山大大帝的极致娱乐性你如何衡量亚历山大大帝的伟大？也许是他征服的帝国规模（从雅典到印度，绵延4800公里）。或者是他征服的速度（大约十年）。或者是他建立的城市（6到17座，许多名为“亚历山大”）。

然而，正如达勒姆大学古典学和古代史教授Edmund Richardson的一本新书所显示的那样，对这个人也存在更阴暗的衡量标准。他被称“疯子”、“并非那么伟大的亚历山大”和“世界已知的最伟大杀手之一”。这是有理由的：一些人估计，近1%的古代世界人口死于他的征战。

但这并没有阻止对他的崇拜。如果男人们一天想到罗马帝国多次，历史学家似乎几乎同样频繁地想到亚历山大。他让人们着迷：故事片美化他；纪录片追随他的足迹；将近5000本书剖析了他。他的追随者从尤利乌斯·恺撒到拿破仑再到现代商业大师。像所有历史一样，这些文本反映了它们的时代。马基雅维利钦佩亚历山大阳刚的领导风格（他杀死敌人）。现代文本采取更具管理性的方法：欧洲工商管理学院的一位教授写了一篇题为“亚历山大大帝的十一条领导力课程”的文章，其中包括“巩固成果”和“投资于人才管理”的建议。而且，你可能会补充说，“避免杀死已知世界的1%”。（科技兄弟和政客们，请注意。）古代统计数据不可靠。但这本书——对亚历山大从摇篮到（醉酒）坟墓的引人入胜的审视——也提供了其他统计数据。在书中，有11次各种身体部位被切断（大部分是头，但有时是四肢和阴茎）；“谋杀”一词出现了38次，“杀”出现了大约100次。它是残酷、暴力、令人震惊的血腥。换句话说，非常有趣。

在某种程度上，它也不寻常。每个人都知道历史（有战争的历史）被划分为时代：古典、中世纪、现代。但历史（有书籍的历史）也被划分为时代。仅在过去一个世纪，就流行过马克思主义历史、女权主义历史，以及最近的“焦虑式”历史。近年来，人们对从圣雄甘地到臭名昭著的反派简·奥斯汀等人的罪恶感到忧心忡忡。

古典学曾被指控为“白人至上主义的脚手架”，尤其显得道歉意味浓厚，并急于纠正其“偏见”。最近一本关于亚历山大的书宣称，它对该人的兴趣不如对“在其统治下受苦”的人的兴趣。这无疑非常高尚。但它并不有趣。

相比之下，Richardson先生的《亚历山大大帝》并不焦虑。它欢快活泼。它欢快地度过他的童年（他驯服一匹无法驯服的马）；欢快地度过他的早期战役（他征服一座无法征服的城市）；欢快地度过他的神话制造（他解开无法解开的“戈尔迪乌姆之结”）。当然，它也欢快地度过他的纵情享乐。亚历山大的情人包括他的朋友赫菲斯提安、“达里乌斯前妃嫔中的360人（对应波斯年的每一天）以及一位名叫巴戈阿斯的美艳绝伦的年轻波斯人”。凡有精彩故事可讲，Richardson先生既不解构也不批评。他兴高采烈地讲述它。以推罗围城战为例。当亚历山大开始攻击这座城市时，他还没有成为……（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）

item.content:encoded:
The hidden tastemakers of the literary world

Culture | Jackals, parasites or heroes?


COCKTAIL PARTIES have seen worse pickup attempts. In 1989 Andrew Wylie, a literary agent, set his sights on Philip Roth. (“Every time I turned around, there was this guy,” the novelist later said. “I discovered what it was like to be a pretty girl.”) When Mr Wylie made his move, he declared that he could get Roth a three-book deal worth $2m.

Later, over lunch, he formally wooed him. Roth was underappreciated by his publisher, Mr Wylie asserted, and his potentially lucrative foreign rights were being neglected. He could handle the rights to Roth’s 14 novels in 30 territories, which amounted to 420 contracts renegotiated every seven years. Roth’s revenue could increase by up to 500%. It was an offer the writer—who had a mighty reputation but a puny bank balance—could not refuse.

Mr Wylie is famous, infamous even, in the publishing world: he earned the nickname “the Jackal”, after persuading several authors to ditch their agents and join him. When he wanted to expand his network of contacts in China, he went so far as to call Henry Kissinger to suggest that he could become his agent and that Kissinger should write a book on China. That book went on to sell well, and Mr Wylie gained footing and a stronger Rolodex for future business there. Mr Wylie’s strategy of focusing on foreign rights and sales “not only changed the fortunes of the writers on his list, but the shape of American literature abroad”, writes Laura McGrath, an assistant professor of English at Temple University, in a new survey of literary agents.

Agents, Ms McGrath argues, have many functions. They are spotters, identifying promising writers. They are confidants, helping those writers to produce their best work. And they are negotiators, doing deals on behalf of authors and getting them more money so they can have more time to write.

That means agents are often controversial figures within the publishing world. In 1897 a British publisher described agents as “generally a parasite”. (They take a commission of around 15% of an author’s earnings.) They retain an aura of mystery. The literary agent’s job is to “be invisible”, Ms McGrath contends, working behind the scenes to create a star and thereby shape what gets written and what people read.

“Middlemen” is one of a pile of recent books offering a behind-the-scenes account of how literature comes to people’s shelves. Ms McGrath is a lively writer, eschewing academic jargon in favour of anecdotes. She heads to the world’s largest book fair in Frankfurt. She watches a group of agents evaluate the unsolicited manuscripts in the “slush pile”. (Every agent’s dream is to find a “Harry Potter”-like gem among the dross, as J.K. Rowling’s agent did.) She describes the evolution of the “publishing lunch”: Candida Donadio, who found Joseph Heller in the slush pile, once joked that she took three lunches in a day. (Today there are fewer stiff drinks and more talk about limp sales.)

Agents try to devise creative answers to marketing problems. For example, how do you sell a book by an unknown writer? Sterling Lord, Jack Kerouac’s agent, started a trend when he worked with publishers to build hype around “On the Road”; they advertised Kerouac as “the voice of a new age”. Agents ever since have hoped their debut novelists can make waves: first novels now account for between 15% and 25% of the fiction published every year. Many of these books fetch high advances that sales cannot recoup. Most American novelists now publish only one title.

Literary agents are never objective, and their personal preferences shape what is printed. Because most agents and editors live in New York, in 2000-22 more novels were set there than in the next 30 most populous American cities combined. And certainly the proliferation of agents—there are now more than 1,500 in America—has something to do with the proliferation of mediocre books. Many should have never have been printed. But what is striking, at a time when taste is increasingly shaped by algorithms, is just how much an individual agent’s judgment still matters. ■

item.title: Why you should never skip a TV intro
item.description:

Technology forges new art forms and destroys them. The printing press galvanised literature and rubbed out illuminated manuscripts. Cinema killed the music hall. Today a popular gizmo is threatening another intricate craft. The art form is the TV title sequence; the menacing tech is the little “Skip...
item.content:encoded:
Why you should never skip a TV intro

Culture | Back Story


Technology forges new art forms and destroys them. The printing press galvanised literature and rubbed out illuminated manuscripts. Cinema killed the music hall. Today a popular gizmo is threatening another intricate craft. The art form is the TV title sequence; the menacing tech is the little “Skip Intro” button that you reflexively click. The outcome is changing the way stories are told and watched on screen.

Once upon a time, TV titles were simple cards displaying static text. By the 1950s they served as prologues, introducing characters and catchphrases: “It’s a bird! It’s a plane! It’s Superman!” say the wowed onlookers in the opening of “The Adventures of Superman”. Titles incorporated cutesy animations (as in “Bewitched”), split-screen effects (“The Brady Bunch”) and stunts (like the much-emulated bonnet-slide in “The Dukes of Hazzard”). Many came with earworm tunes, like the finger-clicking theme for “The Addams Family”.

The form peaked in the era of prestige TV at the turn of the millennium. In the titles for “The Sopranos”, the protagonist, Tony, is glimpsed through cigar-smoke and in a rear-view mirror. He is close yet elusive, as he remains for six seasons. The falling figure in “Mad Men” (pictured) embodies both glamour and mental disintegration. Finest of all is the ghostly imagery in the first season of “True Detective”, a concise montage of its Louisianan themes: sleaze, pollution, faith, guilt and downright weirdness.

Such ingenious sequences are at once a compliment and a brag. Your time is so valuable, they flatter the audience, that even the credits will be exquisite. The brag is about the show, for which, implicitly, only a sublime introduction will do. They are summaries, mood-setters and advertisements, deft enough to intrigue new viewers and resonate with returning ones. Like the overture to an opera, they are an integral part of the drama.

Some of these shows aired without adverts, freeing up minutes for luxuriant openings. But the exigencies of streaming are changing. Adverts are creeping back, making time scarcer again. Meanwhile title sequences are an obstacle to binge-watching. Gorging fans do not need to be reintroduced to a story every hour. Many just want to get on with it.

Thanks to Skip Intro, they can. Noticing that users were fast-forwarding manually through titles themselves, Netflix devised the button in 2017; other streamers followed suit. By 2022 Netflix viewers were clicking it 136m times a day. Since then intro-skipping has snowballed. Across all the output on the BBC’s iPlayer, use of Skip Intro in March was roughly double the level two years earlier. It has soared in the past six months. The underlying impatience is bad news for elaborate opening titles. “It sucks,” says one exponent of this haiku-like genre.

Extended sequences are still airing. The cleverest are games or puzzles, such as the opening credits for “The White Lotus”, in which the lewd images flit away just before you decipher them. But briefer alternatives are on the rise. In “Pluribus”, a sci-fi parable, the title is formed by eerie, swirling dots; that is all. Some shows are reverting to the plain cards of yore. In “The Pitt”, a hospital drama, this approach fits the air of austere verisimilitude. “Steal”, a heist thriller, has only a brief flash of its title.

In the best known sequence of all, a tuxedoed man is tracked down the barrel of a gun. The James Bond titles will endure, as will others in cinema, where the audience is captive. But as they dwindle on TV, something is being lost. It isn’t just that—as in the new series of “The Night Manager”—they may be the best bit of a show. Shrinking them undermines cliffhangers: roll straight into the next episode and you can’t dangle in tingly anticipation for long.

More than that, titles can be a kind of spell; discard them and you may miss the magic. Like the flight to a holiday or dressing for a party, a title sequence is an in-between moment. It eases you from your own world, slumped on the sofa after putting the kids to bed, into the imaginary world of the show, whether that is a louche office in the 1960s or a Cajun crime scene. It is a crossing on which you suspend your disbelief.

Like making phone calls and shopping, watching TV has become immeasurably easier. These days you can see an abundance of programmes on a whim. Somehow, though, speeding things up has only made people more impatient; the yen for instantaneity is insatiable. If you are always hurrying, boundaries are skipped and nothing is special. ■

item.content:encoded:
The best, and worst, TV series and films of 2026 (so far)

Culture | Best TV/film


“Amandaland”Amanda is back—as pretentious, dishonest and delusional as ever in the second season of this sitcom. Her pitiable attempts to make it as an influencer are extremely entertaining, thanks to the sharp script.

“Babies”This show is heart-wrenching and beautifully acted. It explores how isolating infertility can be and reveals the cold and unsympathetic manner that couples encounter from doctors as they navigate the medical system.“The Boroughs”A widower discovers that otherworldly creatures are stealing precious years from the residents of a retirement community. The most unsettling thing about this series is not supernatural: it is the normal, natural process of ageing. “The Christophers” The greedy children of Julian Sklar (Sir Ian McKellan), an artist, want to forge the last series of his renowned paintings and sell them for a fortune. For all its talk of fakes, this film—about ageing, inheritance and artistic taste—is a real masterpiece.“Dreams”A wealthy female philanthropist (Jessica Chastain) has a secret affair with a young ballet dancer from Mexico, who crosses the border illegally to be with her in San Francisco. This film is a taut, chilling morality tale about passion and power.

“Half Man”Niall and Ruben grow up together and develop an intense and twisted sort of brotherhood. This series is a nerve-shredding exploration of obsession, masculinity and trauma from Richard Gadd, the creator of “Baby Reindeer”.“Henry David Thoreau”This three-part documentary from Ken Burns explores why the American naturalist is so alluring today. In an era when many are searching for meaning, Thoreau’s life and writing offer succour. “I Swear”A biopic that is funny and full of heart. Robert Aramayo deservedly won awards for his performance as John Davidson, a Scottish campaigner who was diagnosed with Tourette syndrome as a boy. “Kokuho”This historical drama about kabuki, traditional Japanese theatre, has the compressed intensity of a story told in verse. Lush and painstakingly shot, the film follows the orphaned son of a gangster in his effort to become an actor. “Legends” In the early 1990s Britain was losing its war on drugs, so the government turned to an unusual bunch of fighters: civil servants. This is a thrilling and pacy series about little-known British heroes.“Love Story”This controversial hit series imagines what happened beyond the public eye, as John F. Kennedy junior, America’s most eligible bachelor, wooed an elegant outsider before their deaths in a plane crash in 1999. A doomed fairy tale that is enthralling to watch.“No Other Choice” After a year of humiliating unemployment, a middle-aged man hits on a plan: he will murder everyone who is qualified for the job he is applying for. Ingenious, grisly fun, this film is the best South Korean satire since the Oscar-winning “Parasite”.“The Pitt”This popular medical drama about an overworked, underfunded emergency room in Pittsburgh celebrates not brilliance or glory, but the simple act of being dedicated to your job. The show may remind older viewers of “ER”, but it is grittier and more addictive than its long-running predecessor.

“Ponies”The KGB surveils any Americans of any influence in Moscow. But Bea and Twila, as women, are classified as “persons of no interest”. Thanks to a cold-war setting and ample skulduggery, this satirical comedy series is a lot of fun. “Project Hail Mary”This film is both a science-fiction caper and a buddy comedy about an astronaut and an alien. Though the film is too long, it stands out for its cinematography and droll script; Ryan Gosling is brilliant in the lead role.“The Sheep Detectives”This charming family-friendly film is a love letter to farm animals and golden-age murder mysteries. The script delivers both big laughs and unexpectedly moving moments, as it explores loss and memory.“The Stranger”A sumptuous and rich adaptation of Albert Camus’s classic existential novel. This black-and-white film boasts beautiful cinematography, but also captures the ennui and despair of the book.

To save you time, we wasted ours

“The Bride!”In this frightfully bad film, a dead woman is reanimated to marry a lonely monster. The movie mixes too many genres, from sci-fi and Gothic noir to “Bonnie and Clyde”-style capers. This remake of a film from 1935 never fully comes to life.“Imperfect Women”This show is like buttered popcorn: bingeable but unsatisfying. Its big ideas—of how well you know your partner and what women hide from their closest friends—are handled simplistically. “Ladies First”A man whacks his head and wakes up in a world where gender roles are flipped. This over-the-top film offers endless scenes of men being sexually harassed and getting cosmetic surgery, while women eat burgers and pass wind. “Michael” This nauseating biopic is a sanitised and sanctified version of Michael Jackson’s life story. For a movie about an oddball megastar who befriended a chimpanzee, much of it is also surprisingly dull. “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie” This video-game-inspired film is already the year’s highest-grossing movie worldwide. It is also a gross misuse of your time. The plotless film carries you on a hallucinogenic and frenetic journey that only nostalgic gamers will enjoy.“Wuthering Heights”Emerald Fennell turns a haunting tale of class, obsession and revenge into a bodice-ripper. She rounds off the sharpest edges of the story and focuses on the erotic awakening of Cathy and Heathcliff.“Your Friends & Neighbours”Coop (Jon Hamm), a financier-turned-thief, does not know when to quit stealing from his neighbours. The writers of this show also don’t know when to quit. The new season has all the flaws of the first, plus another: redundancy.■

All shows and films were released in America or Britain in 2026 and are available to watch in cinemas or on streaming platforms.

item.title: Travel is becoming a competitive sport
item.description:
Culture

Tuvalu, made up of nine tiny islands in the South Pacific, is not your usual holiday destination. The former British colony, about halfway between Hawaii and Australia, is a haul to get to, served by only a few flights a week.Tourismbarely exists. The main attractions are the airport runway in the c...
item.content:encoded:
Travel is becoming a competitive sport

Culture | Passport to everywhere


Tuvalu, made up of nine tiny islands in the South Pacific, is not your usual holiday destination. The former British colony, about halfway between Hawaii and Australia, is a haul to get to, served by only a few flights a week. Tourism barely exists. The main attractions are the airport runway in the capital, Funafuti, which transforms into a picnic spot and football pitch most afternoons, and the sleepy post office, which attracts enthusiastic stamp collectors. It is one of the least visited countries in the world.

None of that was enough to dissuade Ted Nims, an American who recently spent a week there and, in the process, checked off another country on his list: his 191st. The UN has 193 member states. Mr Nims is among a growing number of “country counters” trying to visit them all. Last year a record 82 people claimed to have achieved the feat of travelling to all 193 countries, according to NomadMania, an online hub for obsessive adventurers.

When the Travellers’ Century Club launched in 1954, only a fortunate few could boast of having been to 100 countries, the minimum required to join. Today the social group is nearly 2,000-strong, having enjoyed what it calls a “pretty significant upswing” in recent years. Serious travellers are whiling away hours on platforms such as NomadMania and Most Travelled People, where there are leaderboards and debates about what counts as a visit. (An airport transit is acceptable to some but dismissed by the most hardcore as too easy.)

So much time on the road may sound like solitary play. But hostels and homestays offer a lot of fun and social contact, says Carol Wong, a Malaysian who recently visited Samoa (her 142nd country). It is the “fancy hotel” that is “very lonely”, she says. Online, travel addicts share tips and socialise. Some destinations are so obscure that visitors seek advice from Facebook groups such as Every Passport Stamp, where questions range from the mundane (“Is the ferry from Kazakhstan to Azerbaijan operating?”) to the unusual (“Has anyone ever explored Enewetak Atoll in the Marshall Islands?”).

Seeing new places is all the rage, even if you do not want to fill your whole passport with new stamps. About half of Brits polled last year by ABTA, a travel industry association, planned to visit a new country, compared with 18% a decade earlier. “There’s a braggadocious element,” says Seth Borko of Skift, a travel-news website, who points to the impact of social media.

The scourge of overtourism plays a part, too, as travellers want to skip packed piazzas. Rising numbers of Americans travelling to Europe are opting for small towns or the countryside, according to Skift. The world’s top ten most visited countries saw their share of international arrivals decline from about 60% in 1980 to 40% in 2024.

“I like to see places that aren’t as touched by tourists,” says Shang Qian Song, a 34-year-old Singaporean visiting Tuvalu, which may become one of the first countries to disappear because of rising sea levels. If you’re counting on becoming a country counter, better pack your bag. ■

item.title: 桑尼·罗林斯认为爵士乐就是一切
item.description:
Obituary

Though he lived a mere two blocks away, Sonny Rollins hadn’t noticed those steps on Delancey Street before. One summer day in 1959, he climbed up. There, at the top, he found himself on the Williamsburg Bridge above New York’s East River. Subway cars and traffic were rattling over, hooting boats pas...
item.content:encoded:
桑尼·罗林斯认为爵士乐就是一切

讣告 | 最后的巨人尽管他住的地方离德兰西街仅两个街区，桑尼·罗林斯此前却从未注意到那些台阶。1959年夏日的一天，他爬了上去。在顶端，他发现自己正站在纽约东河上方的威廉斯堡大桥上。地铁车厢和车辆在桥上隆隆驶过，船只在桥下鸣笛穿行。四周是可供他躲藏的桥柱和桥台。头顶上方是开阔的天空。无论是否老套，身处此地都带给他一种精神上的感受。

这里是练习他音乐的理想之地，而他的音乐并非普通音乐。他的次中音萨克斯管，充满无穷创意，既流畅旋律化，又具有打击感或浪漫气息，早已闻名遐迩。自1953年起，他就以小乐队领队身份录制唱片，而1956年的《萨克斯巨人》将他提升到了与偶像查理·“鸟”·帕克和约翰·柯川同等的地位。此后的职业生涯中，他始终保持着这一地位，发行了超过60张专辑并两获格莱美奖。然而，无论收获多少掌声，他从未对自己的演奏方式感到满意。内心不断响起的声音时常告诉他需要提升自我。正因如此，他后来去了印度的一处冥想静修所，也正因为如此，他每天都会前往威廉斯堡大桥。

这样的日子持续了两年。有时他会连续演奏15个小时甚至更久，只有上厕所或去他喜欢的酒吧喝杯白兰地时才下来。冬天他戴着手套演奏。一些路人注意到他高大的身躯挤在钢架间，所有人都听到了他的音乐，但很少有人与他交谈。这没关系，因为他唯一需要的伙伴就是他的萨克斯管，他不断地将它推向更远。在某个地方，也许在海底深处，也许在群星之外——远超出桑尼·罗林斯目前所能触及之处——存在着一种终极音色。他并不清楚那会是什么样，但一旦听到他便能辨认出来。也许每年在舞台上能捕捉到一两回那样的瞬间。那一刻他将感到彻底的满足，并知道，终于，自己演奏得很好了。但仅此而已。

他的头脑早已塞满了多年来积累的音乐片段素材。他哥哥用小提琴演奏的练习曲；家庭自动钢琴卷上的胖子沃勒；酒吧点唱机里的曲子；廉价留声机播放的流行歌曲和民谣；以及从哈莱姆区俱乐部和敞开的窗户中传出的爵士乐。钢琴家塞隆尼斯·蒙克指导过他，萨克斯管演奏家科尔曼·霍金斯住在附近。他敬仰这两人，并从八岁起，带着母亲送给他的中音萨克斯管，他就知道音乐生涯也属于自己。

他的即兴演奏汲取了所有这些元素。他喜欢插入引用的片段，在无数次节奏与和声的变化之后，每个片段都可以与另一个相连。这里一段咏叹调，那里一首百老汇歌谣，一句厚脸皮的半听半就的连复段。仿佛所有音乐都有一种自然的统一性，而他相信确实如此。他每次走上舞台时脑中一片空白，等待一个全新的想法或一个全新的音符降临。他完全信任自己的萨克斯管技巧——潜意识中，无论多么复杂或快速。他与他的萨克斯管之间有一种默契，一种交融。（当他和妻子露西尔在9/11事件中不得不逃离公寓时，他只带走了他的萨克斯管。）但任何乐曲的其他部分——情感与精神——他则完全交由更高的力量来提供。

因为他曾与鸟、柯川、小号手迈尔斯·戴维斯以及鼓手马克斯·罗奇一起演奏，他常被称为比波普明星。但他不愿被束缚...（以下内容因长度限制截断，未翻译部分保留英文原文）
